- the only place we need to update an issue file when the issue is partially complete is the "current behavior" section. We don't need to add append-logs to the end, it's better to update the main body to align with the current design, and the current behavior with the current status.

```

### feedback_comprehensive_first_pass.md

```markdown
---
name: Don't tier work into cheap / medium / expensive
description: For new features, do every fold of the work in one comprehensive slice rather than splitting into easy-now / hard-later tiers
type: feedback
originSessionId: 1c5a19da-96cd-4e77-88ea-625e76d201fa
---
When scoping a new feature, resist the instinct to propose a
"slice 1 covers cheap fields; slice 2 covers expensive fields"
split unless the user explicitly asks for it.

**Why:** The user's framing: "they should all be configurable
with the same interface, so... don't split up the work in that
way. Just do it comprehensively the first time so we don't
forget anything on the return trip." Tiered work means coming
back, and round-trips are where details get forgotten —
especially the cross-cutting plumbing that connects the easy
and hard paths.

**How to apply:** When writing an issue file, if a feature
spans cheap-and-hard variations of the same surface (e.g. all
fields of a schema, all kinds of a polymorphic type), describe
slice 1 as covering the whole surface. The implementation may
still ship incrementally on a per-commit basis, but the issue
should not encode a "we'll do the rest later" plan unless the
user has explicitly asked for that staging.

```

### feedback_cross_language_pitfalls.md

```markdown
---
name: Cross-language design pitfalls
description: Three approaches the user rejected when designing SoraMech's cross-language wire format
type: feedback
originSessionId: e9ed70c7-2b63-425c-987c-6431040bedfb
---
When designing anything that touches the cross-language data path, avoid these three shapes — the user pushed back on each and the rejections are load-bearing for the architecture.

**1. Don't propose runtime "handles" that route operations back to the originating spec.**

**Why:** Real library functions in the wild (qsort, libcurl, anything from libc) expect actual native values — a real `int (*)(int,int)` function pointer, a real `char *` — not a SoraMech-issued id string. They can't be modified to participate in our runtime's routing scheme. The wire must carry data the destination spec can fully reconstruct into a native value, not opaque tokens.

**How to apply:** When a value seems hard to serialize (function pointers, coroutines, opaque pointers), decompose to data primitives (address + signature, bytecode + upvalues, ptr + length). If the destination needs a callable, the destination spec synthesizes one at reconstruction time (libffi trampoline for C, `ffi.cast` for LuaJIT). The "phone home" callback that the trampoline performs internally is fine — it's an artifact of the destination spec's reconstruction, not exposed in the wire format. What's forbidden is a wire primitive that says "operations on this value cross back to the source."

**2. Don't propose pair-wise language conversion paths (lua→c, c→lua, etc.).**

**Why:** N languages means N² conversion paths, which means adding a new language breaks the existing ones. The wire must use a language-agnostic intermediate (JSON) and every spec must implement only the two pair-symmetric callbacks (`to_json`, `from_json`). New language = implement those two functions, nothing else touches.

**How to apply:** Never write code that names two specific languages in a conversion context. Specs only ever see JSON on the wire. If a JSON primitive needs an extension (like `$function_pointer`), it lives in the universal JSON contract, not as a lua-spec-specific or c-spec-specific concept.

**3. Don't propose per-function annotations for type ambiguities (lengths, discriminators, callback signatures).**

**Why:** The user pointed out that "discriminator" is a vocab word the system has no general way to ask about. We can't prompt "which param is the length?" because that pairing convention lives in the function's English documentation, not its types. Asking the user to write annotations means asking them to know specialized vocabulary they didn't sign up for.

**How to apply:** When a function signature has ambiguous types (`char *` with no length, `union` with no tag, `void *` with no signature), expose each parameter as a separate input slot on the box. The user wires the slots according to the function's documentation — `p` from one source, `n` from another. The system never infers pairings; the user expresses them by wiring. If the destination needs a length and no length wire is provided, the wire compile fails with a plain-English fix-it message ("destination needs length, source provides only a pointer — wire a length input here").

**Common thread:** all three rejections are the same principle in different clothes — **SoraMech bends to the language, not the other way around.** Users write idiomatic code in their language. Libraries are used as-is. Specs are self-contained and pair-symmetric. The system stays out of the user's vocabulary.

```

### project_cross_language_wire.md

```markdown
---
name: Cross-language wire format
description: Dual-ring slot per port (native ring + JSON ring + ordering ring). JSON only at language borders. Per-edge classification at graph load; per-cell precision at runtime.
type: project
originSessionId: 5670858b-274f-49c4-89b8-a4b83ce33d7c
---
Design corrected 2026-05-21 — replaces the older "JSON always" framing.

**Each input slot is a dual-ring buffer.** Per port: one `ring_native` (consumer-language native bytes), one `ring_json` (JSON bytes from cross-language producers), and one `ring_order` of `(which_ring, idx)` tuples in arrival order. Allocate `ring_json` and `ring_order` lazily — same-language-only ports pay nothing for them.

**Push selects ring by per-edge bit.** Producer's spec writes native bytes to `ring_native` if `output_edge_native[j]` is true; otherwise calls `native_to_json` and writes to `ring_json`. Either way, pushes a `(which_ring, idx)` tuple to `ring_order`.

**Pop reads ordering ring first.** Dispatch pops `ring_order`, gets `(which_ring, idx)`, then pops the indicated cell. The consumer's spec receives `(input_data[i], input_native[i])` per input port and dispatches per flag — decode native or decode JSON.

**Why dual-ring instead of per-port classification.** Per-port (slot is all-JSON if any fan-in is cross-lang) is the pessimistic approximation — same-language values eat JSON cost on mixed-fan-in ports. Dual-ring is precise per cell: a port fed by one Lua box and one C box keeps the Lua cells native and JSON-encodes only the C-sourced cells.

**Why JSON for the cross-language ring (not pair-wise paths, not type-annotated raw bytes).** JSON's structure is self-describing — every language has a natural mapping for object/array/number/string/bool/null. Adding language K means K's spec implements its own `native_to_json` and `json_to_native`. N spec-pairs, not N² language-pair paths. The native ring's format is each spec's private choice — Lua may pick msgpack or `cjson.encode` or a custom binary form; C uses `memcpy` of the wrapper struct; Bash uses strings.

**Sentinel primitives for non-JSON-mappable values.** `$ref` (pointer + length into the large-value heap), `$function_pointer`, `$lang_opaque` ("these bytes are language-X-internal"). Carried inside the JSON ring as object-shaped sentinels. Cross-language receivers that can't reconstruct fail at wire compile.

**`$function_pointer` reconstruction — wrapper binary + persistent subprocess (issue 318, amended 2026-05-22).** Earlier design had the consumer's spec FFI-cast the raw process-local address. Rejected: FFI is language-pair-specific, biases SoraMech toward the Lua↔C corner, breaks the N-not-N² rule. Replacement: at map-compile time the compiler asks the *producing* spec to compile the referenced function + its enumerable dependencies into a standalone wrapper binary on disk that speaks a small line protocol on stdio. The consumer spec spawns one persistent subprocess per `$function_pointer` it receives and talks to it over the same socket-like channel used for any out-of-process spec. Every language pays the same price; new languages only implement "compile a function to a wrapper binary" — no pair-wise FFI knowledge required.

**Spec `invoke` signature change.** Collapses `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` into one `invoke` with per-input/per-output flags: `int invoke(handle, ..., const int *input_native, int n_inputs, int output_native, void *out_buf, ...)`. The spec dispatches per input internally. This is the contract change that unblocks 306/307's typed marshalling.

**Two compile-time layers stack:**
- **Per-edge classification (issue 312, this design)** — graph loader computes `input_edge_native[]` and `output_edge_native[]` on each box; dispatch routes pushes accordingly. This issue is the wire-format design.
- **Same-language source merge (issue 313, research / blocked)** — concatenate every same-language box's source into one translation unit per language. Boxes still run as separate thread-pool tasks; what 313 thins is the spec invocation overhead inside the merged region (direct call into the worker's `lua_State` instead of dlsym + marshal + bridge). The dual-ring slot machinery does NOT collapse — tasks still need slots to wait for sibling inputs. 313 makes the ring cells cheaper to read/write; it doesn't remove them.

**Three rejected design shapes** (kept here so they don't get reinvented):
1. **Handles back-routing to the owning spec** — library functions in the wild can't be modified to use SoraMech-shaped handles. Rejected.
2. **Pair-wise language paths** — every new language would have to grow N-1 translation paths against existing languages. Rejected. The dual-ring's "two rings per slot" is the dimension-cap that prevents this.
3. **Per-function discriminator / length annotations on the wire** — the system has no universal vocabulary to ask "is param 2 the length?" Rejected; the user expresses these by wiring two separate input slots.

**How to apply:** When discussing wire format, slot store shape, dispatch routing, or spec callbacks: think dual-ring (native, JSON, ordering) per slot, per-edge classification at push time, per-cell tag at pop time, JSON-only-at-borders, language-private native bytes everywhere else.

```

### project_custom_translation_specs.md

```markdown
---
name: Custom translation specs per port
description: Users can override the default native/JSON wire path on any input port for any reason — a knob in the wire format vocabulary (issue 246)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**Per-port custom translation specs** let the user intervene at a specific input port and replace the default dual-ring decode path with user-written code. The override applies to that one port; the rest of the graph uses the default native-or-JSON path from issue 312.

**Motivating cases (any reason qualifies, not just cross-language):**
- Cross-language ambiguity the default specs can't infer: a C++ class with methods landing at a C box (drop methods? expose as fn pointers? restructure?), a `void *` carrying a libcurl handle, a union whose discriminator is on a separate wire.
- Same-language reshape: massaging a value into a different shape on its way in (rename fields, drop a layer, project a subset) without adding a transform box on the canvas.
- Validation / coercion: clamp a number, enforce a schema, fail loudly on unexpected shapes.

**How it composes with the dual-ring design:**
- The custom spec runs at *pop* time on the consumer side, after the ordering ring has been consulted and the cell has been read from the appropriate ring. The user's code receives the decoded value (native or JSON-decoded) and produces whatever the consumer's `invoke` will see.
- A port with a custom translation gets its own wire color in the editor (issue 245) — visible signal that this port doesn't use the default path.

**Why:** The default native/JSON contract covers the cases JSON's structure handles cleanly. Everything outside that needs a user escape hatch — *and* the same hatch is useful for purely-local "I want this input shaped differently" cases. One mechanism, many uses.

**How to apply:** When the design needs an override knob on the cross-language path, propose "custom translation spec on the destination port" rather than inventing per-function annotations, type discriminator metadata, or producer-side conversion hints (all three were rejected — see feedback_cross_language_pitfalls). The port is the unit of override; the spec is user code; the rest stays default.

```

### project_editor_visual_language.md

```markdown
---
name: Editor visual language for wires
description: Wire color in the canvas editor encodes language pairing across the edge, not just routing kind — a UI invariant future work should respect (issue 245)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**Wires are colored by language pairing across the edge**, with a separate color for wires whose destination port carries a user-written custom translation (issue 246). Pre-245 wires were colored purely by routing kind (default slate-blue, comparator branches orange/blue/green).

**The pairing-based palette:**
- **Same-language hop** — the wire carries native bytes; default neutral color.
- **Cross-language hop (forest green, ~`#228b22`)** — different producer/consumer languages; runtime translates via JSON at the wire. The color is a standing reminder that encode + decode is happening on that hop.
- **Custom-translation hop** — a third distinct color signaling the destination port has a user-written translation spec overriding the default path.
- Branch-routing colors (orange/blue/green from comparator boxes) compose on top — routing kind and language pairing are orthogonal axes the editor must show simultaneously.

**Why:** The runtime treats same-lang and cross-lang hops very differently (dual-ring slot design, issue 312), but pre-245 the editor gave the box author no visual signal that the JSON translation step existed. It was invisible until someone read the dispatch code. Translation cost should be legible from the canvas.

**How to apply:** Any future editor work that touches wire rendering must preserve "color encodes language pairing." Don't propose recoloring schemes that overload the cross-language signal onto another concept. New routing concepts get new axes (line style, glyphs, animation) rather than stealing color. When discussing wire visuals, name both axes — routing kind AND language pairing — even if only one is changing.

```

### project_encapsulated_map.md

```markdown
---
name: Encapsulated map as box
description: A sub-map opens as a single box on a parent canvas. Data boxes marked externally-supplied become input ports; write boxes marked externally-consumed become output ports. The documented exception to single-output-per-box (issue 248, amended 2026-05-23)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**A map directory has two ways to be opened:** as the top-level graph (existing map-select UI), or as an **encapsulated box** on the currently-edited parent map (issue 248). Opening through the file browser while a parent map is open instantiates the sub-map as a single box on the parent's canvas.

**The encapsulation contract — symmetric input and output toggles:**
- **Inputs:** any `data` box inside the sub-map can be toggled "externally-supplied" in its inspector. Each such box becomes a typed input port on the encapsulated box.
- **Outputs:** any `write` box inside the sub-map can be toggled "externally-consumed" in its inspector. Each such box surfaces as a **distinct output port** on the encapsulated box. A write box with the toggle on can still write to its `path` if one is set — the file destination and the parent-wire destination are independent.

**Encapsulated maps are the documented exception to issue 218's "single output per box" rule.** They have *N* output ports — one per externally-consumed write box, where *N* may be zero (pure side-effect map), one, or many. Every other box kind still has exactly one output.

**Rejected earlier design (2026-05-21):** packing all write-box outputs into a single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, single wire out. Rejected 2026-05-23 because it would have repurposed file-writing machinery to emit strings into wires — substituting one mechanism for another. The symmetric toggle design preserves the `write` box's "terminate a value" semantics and treats the destination kind as a mode toggle.

**Why:** Encapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph. The parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals — it sees declared input ports, declared output ports, and known semantics. Sub-maps can be edited independently, reused across parents, and packaged once for distribution. This is the closest SoraMech gets to "user-defined functions" while staying graph-native.

**How to apply:** When discussing map composition, reuse, or "how do users build libraries of behavior" — encapsulation is the answer. Don't propose alternative function-abstraction mechanisms (named subgraphs as text references, macro-style inlining, blob-packed outputs) without explicitly weighing them against the symmetric-toggle shape. Both toggles (`externally-supplied` on data boxes, `externally-consumed` on write boxes) are the user-facing port-declaration mechanism — don't invent a separate "ports manifest" file.

```

### project_soramech.md

```markdown
---
name: SoraMech project context
description: Core architecture decisions, file layout, and execution model for SoraMech, across phase 2 (current) and phase 3 (designed)
type: project
originSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a
---
SoraMech is a visual FSM/dataflow editor and execution engine at /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/.

**Why:** Primary use case is LLM orchestration on the SoraMind Alpine cluster. Strings flow between boxes like variables. History is explicit, loaded from disk only when a box needs it.

**Three independent programs sharing a map directory:**
- `src/006-server-main.lua` — thin HTTP file CRUD proxy. No runner management.
- Runner — phase 2: `src/007-runner-main.lua` (synchronous Lua). Phase 3: `soramech-pool` (C binary, designed in issues 301–311, not yet built).
- `assets/index.html` — vanilla JS canvas editor. Editor only — no run button. Compile button (issue 222) is a phase 2 placeholder; it triggers the phase 3 build pipeline (issue 219).

**Key architecture decisions (current truth):**
- Each box is its own JSON file in `boxes/<id>.json`. Connections written to BOTH endpoint files; loader validates both ends agree — hard error if not.
- **Single output wire per box** (issue 218 complete). No `outputs` array. The function returns one value; routing is by `from_branch` on the connection.
- **Comparator-based branching** (issue 210) — replaces the earlier `branch` box kind with named ports. A box may carry a `comparand`; the dispatch layer fires `lt`/`eq`/`gt` connections. No spec is invoked for comparators.
- **Iterator boxes** (issue 221) — pure routing primitives, no `ref`/`fn`. Dispatch layer cycles through `iterator_outputs` based on a per-task counter.
- **Phase 2 drivers** are shell scripts under `drivers/` (one process per call, stdout as channel). **Phase 3 language specs** are `.so` libraries under `langs/<name>/spec.so` loaded via `dlopen` (issue 303). Lua and C are in-process; Bash is out-of-process via Unix domain socket.
- Data files: per-map JSON in `data/`. Section-level `constant` flag. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua`.
- State/ephemeral: `tmp/` is a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Phase 2 writes `last-run.json` (single doc). Phase 3 writes `last-run.jsonl` (JSON Lines, issue 311) — decoupled from the editor, consumed by LLMs / CLI viewers / test harness.
- **Phase 3 runtime model**: C pool runner owns a 3d-rts task pool; per-task slots in process heap (issue 302) with refcounting and a separate large-value heap; dispatch layer (304) is the worker action; graph loader is C (305), no embedded Lua at the runner level. Phase 2's synchronous executor retires when phase 3 lands.

**How to apply:** When working on any component, respect the three-way separation. Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server. Map directory format is the only shared contract. The phase 2 driver model and the phase 3 spec model coexist conceptually (phase 2 is current, phase 3 is fully designed) but the runtime mechanism differs entirely; box JSON and the editor are unchanged across the cutover.

```

### project_threading.md

```markdown
---
name: threading_model
description: SoraMech's threading model — phase 2 synchronous, phase 3 SoraMech-owned C thread pool with per-port slots and language specs
type: project
originSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a
---
**Phase 2 (current)**: synchronous executor in `src/004-executor.lua`. Single-threaded, sequential box execution. One driver shell-out per box call. The phase 2 path goes away when phase 3 lands — no fallback, no coroutine intermediate.

**Phase 3 (designed, not yet built)**: C pool runner with a SoraMech-owned thread pool. The 3d-rts pool at `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` is the **design reference**, not vendored — SoraMech owns its pool implementation so the spawn primitive, worker context, init barrier, and iterator-pinning extensions are all under our control. The architecture is fully specified across issues 301–313.

Key phase 3 concepts:
- **Per-input-port slots** (not per-task), allocated at graph load and durable for the run. Each slot is a ring buffer (`n_cells` cells of `cell_capacity` bytes). 1-cell slots use peek-not-drain (literals, single-push wires); N-cell slots use pop-and-drain (queued / multi-push wires). No per-slot refcounting — slot lifetime is the whole run.
- **Tasks are ephemeral**: spawned dynamically by the dispatch layer when a box's input set is ready. Tasks carry just `box_id` and a counter snapshot. Box state (counter, input slots, language handle) is durable.
- **Language specs** under `langs/<name>/spec.so`, loaded via `dlopen` at startup. Uniform `lang_spec_t`. No language is privileged.
- **Same-language fast path** (issue 312): wire format defaults to JSON, but two adjacent same-language boxes use the language's native serialization (Lua `lua_dump`, C struct memcpy). Compile-time wire classification picks the path.
- **In-process specs** (Lua, C) via `lua_pcall` / `dlsym`. **Out-of-process specs** (Bash) via Unix domain sockets to a persistent per-worker subprocess.
- **Dispatch layer** (304) is the worker-side action: pop inputs → branch on box mode → invoke spec → push to downstream input slots → end. No blocking, no wait lists; tasks spawn on input arrival and run to completion.
- **Iterator and comparator routing** in the dispatch layer. Comparator runs the function and routes by output value. Iterator skips the function and routes by per-box counter (atomic spawn-time increment). Iterator tasks parallelize across workers; ordering preserved via per-push counter tags on consumer slots.
- **No-null rule** (issue 230): every input port must be wired, given a literal, or marked optional. Compile fails on missing inputs.
- **Init barrier**: pool startup waits until every worker has run every spec's `init(worker_idx)` before submitting tasks. Avoids tasks landing on uninitialized handles.
- **Hard-crash error policy**: nonzero return from any spec aborts the program.
- **Blocking semantics**: long-running operations tie up a worker. Pool size is the budget. Cooperative split (kickoff + check-done iterator) avoids holding a worker. See `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.

**Effil is explicitly NOT used.** Coroutines are not used. The C pool is the chosen mechanism. 3d-rts is referenced as design inspiration, not vendored.

**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC: phase 2 is synchronous shell-out drivers; phase 3 is the SoraMech-owned C pool runner with `lang_spec_t`, per-port slot stores, and dispatch-layer routing. Never suggest effil. 3d-rts is a reference, not a dependency. Issues 301–313 carry the design.

```

### project_yarq_and_third_ring.md

```markdown
---
name: YARQ and the third input ring (issue 320)
description: Per-port third ring carries box-JSON reconfigure messages; YARQ (yield-and-requeue) is the project name for the cooperative-with-scheduler barrier that protects in-place box mutation
type: project
originSessionId: 1c5a19da-96cd-4e77-88ea-625e76d201fa
---
Issue 320 introduces two pieces of project vocabulary that
recur in other code-paths:

**YARQ** (yield-and-requeue) — the synchronization primitive
that protects in-place box mutation. Acquire is a CAS from 0
to 1 on a per-box atomic word. On acquire failure, the
contended worker does NOT busy-wait — it re-submits its own
task to the **tail** of the pool queue and returns, letting
the scheduler drain other work first. Same barrier is acquired
by every path that mutates a box's record (reconfigure,
runtime_connect from 319d). The point: synchronization
*cooperative with the scheduler*, not adversarial to it.
The user named it; the joke is that they want to name a dog
YARQ too.

**The third input ring** — every input slot grows a third ring
alongside the native + JSON pair from issue 312. Carries
box-JSON-shaped reconfigure messages. Per-PORT placement (not
per-box) — any input port can receive reconfigure cells, and
the per-cell ring-selector tag from issue 312/318a grows a
third value (`RING_RECONFIGURE`). When the consumer's
input-gather encounters a reconfigure cell, it retains
already-popped values, acquires YARQ, applies the reconfigure,
releases YARQ, and resumes gathering under the new config.

**Why:** Together with issue 319 (create_box / connect),
issue 320 gives the runtime its full "graph as a living
artifact" surface: 319 grows the graph (additive), 320
mutates what's already there (in-place). Many future features
will read or write these primitives — runtime DSLs, planner
boxes, the editor's live-mutation feedback path.

**How to apply:** When other issues touch box mutation,
slot rings, or per-cell ordering, treat YARQ and the third
ring as established vocabulary — don't reinvent the
primitive or the name. When the user mentions "reconfigure,"
"the third ring," or YARQ, they mean these specific pieces
of the design.

```

### reference_strategems.md

```markdown
---
name: Strategems directory

1	# 248 — Encapsulated map as box
2	
3	## Status
4	in progress · input-side load-time inlining shipped; output-side
5	(ext-consumed write boxes), editor UI, and recursion across mixed
6	ext-consumed wires deferred
7	
8	## Current behavior
9	
10	Input-side encapsulation runs at graph load. The loader recognizes
11	`kind: "map"` with a `ref` to a sub-map directory. A new pass between
12	`load_boxes` and `resolve_topology` walks every BOX_MAP record,
13	loads the sub-map's boxes into the parent's arena, prefix-renames
14	their ids with `<encap_id>__<sub_id>`, splices them into the parent's
15	flat box list, then rewires each parent producer's connection that
16	targeted the encapsulating box. The rewire splices THROUGH the
17	externally-supplied data box: each parent wire to `encap.port` is
18	replaced with copies pointing to the matching data box's
19	downstreams, preserving each from_branch tag. Externally-supplied
20	data boxes are matched to the encapsulating box's input ports by
21	the issue's three binding kinds (positional / numbered by index,
22	named by string).
23	
24	After inlining, the encap box stays in the index but is inert
25	(connections cleared, `ref` stripped — the loader skips it on
26	subsequent passes, dispatch's BOX_MAP case is a logged no-op). The
27	ext-supplied data box is also orphaned (its outgoing connections
28	were absorbed into the parent producer; the cache pass skips it so
29	the "neither value nor path" check doesn't reject the value-less
30	shape).
31	
32	The end-to-end fixture `tests/maps/248-encap-input-only/` proves
33	the splice reaches disk: a parent read box wires
34	`"encapsulated-greeting"` to a BOX_MAP whose sub-map has one
35	externally-supplied data box feeding a write box; the parent's
36	bytes land in `/tmp/soramech-248-encap-out.txt`.
37	
38	Output-side encapsulation (externally-consumed write boxes
39	surfacing as the encap's output ports) is not yet wired. Wires
40	the user drew from `encap.port_x` to a parent consumer don't fire
41	in this slice. The editor toggles, file-browser Encapsulate
42	action, and the multi-output exception to issue 218 also remain
43	ahead.
44	
45	## Concept
46	
47	A map directory is normally opened via the map-select UI as the
48	top-level graph being edited. **This issue adds a second way to
49	open a map:** through the file browser, as an *encapsulated box*
50	on the currently-edited parent map. The opened map becomes a
51	single box on the parent's canvas. Its inputs come from `data`
52	boxes inside the sub-map that have been marked
53	**externally-supplied**; its outputs come from `write` boxes
54	inside the sub-map that have been marked **externally-consumed**.
55	The two markings are symmetric: one redirects an input from "file
56	on disk" to "wire from parent," the other redirects an output
57	from "file on disk" to "wire to parent."
58	
59	Encapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph.
60	The parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals; it sees one box
61	with declared input ports, declared output ports, and known
62	semantics. The sub-map can be edited independently, reused across
63	parent maps, and packaged once for distribution.
64	
65	**Encapsulated boxes are the documented exception to issue 218's
66	"single output per box" rule.** Every other box kind has exactly
67	one output (with fan-out via multiple wires leaving that one
68	output). An encapsulated map has *N* distinct output ports, one
69	per `write` box marked externally-consumed. *N* may be zero (the
70	map is a pure side-effect sink), one (matches the common case),
71	or many. The exception exists because an encapsulated map's
72	outputs are independent values produced by independent
73	`write` boxes — packing them into a single blob (the earlier
74	design in this issue) would have repurposed file-writing
75	machinery to emit strings into wires, which is the wrong shape:
76	`write` boxes should keep their semantics ("terminate a value")
77	and the destination kind ("file vs. parent wire") should be a
78	mode toggle, not a substitution.
79	
80	## Marked input ports inside the sub-map
81	
82	A **data** box inside the sub-map (kind: `data`, the existing
83	language-agnostic file-IO source) can be marked as
84	**externally-supplied** via a small toggle on the box's
85	inspector. Toggling declares: "this data box's value comes from
86	the encapsulating context, not from its `path` or `value`
87	field."
88	
89	The toggle is intentionally scoped to `data` boxes — those are
90	the natural entry points for external values into a map. Call
91	boxes / read boxes / write boxes don't carry the toggle, which
92	keeps the inspector uncluttered for the common cases. Each
93	external input becomes a small shared-memory chunk seeded by
94	the encapsulating call's invoke; the marked data box reads from
95	that chunk on each fire, treating it identically to a value
96	loaded from disk.
97	
98	The toggle records the port's binding kind on the box JSON:
99	
100	```json
101	{
102	    "id": "sum_input",
103	    "kind": "data",
104	    "external": {
105	        "kind": "named",            // or "positional" / "numbered"
106	        "name": "count",            // for named
107	        "index": 0                  // for positional / numbered
108	    },
109	    "...": "..."
110	}
111	```
112	
113	Three binding kinds capture how the encapsulating box's input
114	maps to this internal port:
115	
116	- **`positional`** — bound by argument order. The encapsulating
117	  box has N input ports; the *k*th port's value flows to the
118	  internal box whose `external.index` is *k*. Conceptually
119	  matches positional function arguments.
120	- **`numbered`** — bound by an explicit integer index. Same shape
121	  as positional but the user picks the number (so they can leave
122	  gaps, reorder freely, etc.).
123	- **`named`** — bound by a string name. The encapsulating box's
124	  input port has a label; the matching internal box's
125	  `external.name` is the same string.
126	
127	A single sub-map can mix kinds across its marked boxes — some
128	positional, some named — and the parent map's encapsulated box
129	exposes the union as its input ports.
130	
131	## Marked output ports inside the sub-map
132	
133	A **write** box inside the sub-map (kind: `write`, issue 229's
134	file-write kind) can be marked as **externally-consumed** via a
135	small toggle on the box's inspector — the mirror of the
136	externally-supplied toggle on data boxes. Toggling declares:
137	"this write box's value goes to the encapsulating context, not
138	to its `path` field."
139	
140	The toggle is intentionally scoped to `write` boxes — those are
141	the natural exit points for values out of a map. Each
142	externally-consumed write box surfaces as one **distinct output
143	port** on the encapsulating box. The port carries that one
144	value, on its own wire, to whichever downstream box(es) the
145	parent wires it to.
146	
147	The toggle records the port's binding kind on the box JSON, in
148	the same shape as the input-side toggle:
149	
150	```json
151	{
152	    "id": "result_value",
153	    "kind": "write",
154	    "external": {
155	        "kind": "named",            // or "positional" / "numbered"
156	        "name": "result",           // for named
157	        "index": 0                  // for positional / numbered
158	    },
159	    "...": "..."
160	}
161	```
162	
163	Three binding kinds — same vocabulary as the input side:
164	
165	- **`positional`** — bound by argument order. The encapsulating
166	  box's *k*th output port is the externally-consumed write box
167	  whose `external.index` is *k*.
168	- **`numbered`** — bound by an explicit integer index, allowing
169	  gaps and reordering.
170	- **`named`** — bound by a string name. The encapsulating box's
171	  output port carries that label.
172	
173	A write box marked externally-consumed **also** writes to its
174	`path` if one is set — the two destinations are independent. The
175	write box can opt out of the file write (set `path: null`) if it
176	exists solely to surface a value to the parent.
177	
178	Each externally-consumed write box's emitted value becomes an
179	independent output wire on the encapsulating box. The earlier
180	design in this issue packed all write-box outputs into a single
181	byte-blob with a leading size index; that design is rejected —
182	see the "Concept" section for why. No packing, no unpacking
183	library; the wire format is the same per-port wire format every
184	other box uses.
185	
186	## File layout in the parent map
187	
188	**The encapsulating box is a normal `call` box.** From the
189	editor's perspective it has the same JSON shape as any other
190	call box — `kind: "call"`, `lang`, `ref`, `fn`, `inputs`,
191	`connections`, `routing`. What makes it an encapsulation is
192	that its `lang` is `map` and its `ref` points to a sub-map
193	directory rather than a source file. The map-language spec
194	(`langs/map/spec.so`) is responsible for the "behind the
195	scenes" processing — running the sub-graph and packing the
196	outputs.
197	
198	```json
199	{
200	    "id": "stats_pipeline",
201	    "kind": "call",
202	    "lang": "map",
203	    "ref": "../shared-maps/stats-pipeline",
204	    "fn": null,                                  // unused for map kind
205	    "inputs": [
206	        { "name": "count", "type": "int" },
207	        { "name": "label", "type": "string" }
208	    ],
209	    "outputs": [
210	        { "name": "mean",  "type": "float" },
211	        { "name": "stdev", "type": "float" },
212	        { "name": "n",     "type": "int" }
213	    ],
214	    "...": "..."
215	}
216	```
217	
218	The `outputs` array on the encapsulating box JSON is the
219	documented exception to the single-output-per-box rule. The
220	graph loader treats each entry as a distinct output slot,
221	allocates one ring buffer per output port (same machinery as
222	input slots, but on the producer side), and lets the parent
223	wire each output independently.
224	
225	The map-language spec is registered in the spec registry the
226	same way `lua` / `c` / `bash` are. Its `file_ext` is `.map`
227	(or no extension if the ref points to a directory). The graph
228	loader resolves the `ref`, the map spec's `init` (per worker)
229	loads the sub-graph, and its `invoke` runs the sub-graph and
230	packs the outputs. From the dispatch layer's view, an
231	encapsulating call is just another spec invocation.
232	
233	The sub-map's input ports (derived from its marked data boxes)
234	and output ports (derived from its marked write boxes) are
235	exposed on the encapsulating box's JSON as `inputs` and `outputs`
236	arrays. The user doesn't write either array themselves — the
237	editor generates them from the sub-map on first encapsulation
238	and re-syncs them when the sub-map changes.
239	
240	## Editor UI
241	
242	### File browser
243	
244	The file browser (issue 207's source-file-browser, or its
245	descendant) shows map directories with a distinct icon — a
246	folder-like glyph annotated to suggest "this is a runnable
247	graph, not a source file." Clicking opens a small menu:
248	
249	- **Edit this map** — switches the editor's active map (the
250	  existing map-select behaviour).
251	- **Encapsulate** — adds the map as a `kind: "map"` box to the
252	  currently-edited parent map. The new box appears on the
253	  canvas at the cursor position; the user wires it in like any
254	  other box.
255	
256	### External-binding toggle (inputs and outputs)
257	
258	The inspector for a `data` box's value-input grows a small
259	toggle that marks it externally-supplied; the inspector for a
260	`write` box's value-input grows the same toggle that marks it
261	externally-consumed. Both surface in the same visual idiom:
262	
263	```
264	  ┌─────────────────────────────┐
265	  │ count   [● external]        │ ← toggle on, port is externally-bound
266	  │   kind:    named            │
267	  │   name:    "count"          │
268	  └─────────────────────────────┘
269	```
270	
271	When the toggle is on, the inspector reveals the kind selector
272	(positional / numbered / named) and the name / index field.
273	When off, the port behaves normally (wires-in / literal value on
274	the data box; `path` write on the write box).
275	
276	A map with no marked data boxes encapsulates to a no-input box
277	(just a source of values). A map with no externally-consumed
278	write boxes encapsulates to a box with no output (side-effecting
279	only — legal but unusual; useful for "fire and forget"
280	sub-pipelines).
281	
282	### Visual on the canvas
283	
284	The encapsulating box renders distinctly — different border,
285	maybe a small "sub-map" badge — so the user sees at a glance
286	that this isn't a leaf call. Hovering shows the sub-map's name
287	and a small thumbnail of its graph.
288	
289	## Runtime model — two paths, needs a decision
290	
291	Two implementation paths exist. The encapsulating box being a
292	normal `call` box from the editor's perspective doesn't pick
293	between them; the choice lives in what the map-language spec
294	does behind the scenes and what (if anything) the compile
295	pipeline does at build time.
296	
297	### Path A — Compile-time inlining
298	
299	The compile pipeline (issue 309) recognizes encapsulating call
300	boxes and **expands them into their sub-graphs at build time**.
301	Steps the compile step takes per encapsulating box:
302	
303	1. Load the sub-map's graph from `ref`.
304	2. Rename every internal box with a parent-namespaced id:
305	   `stats_pipeline__compute`, `stats_pipeline__filter`, etc.
306	3. Copy every internal wire across, with the renamed ids.
307	4. For each marked data box inside the sub-map: replace it with
308	   a wire that brings the encapsulating box's matching input
309	   value directly to wherever the data box's output was wired.
310	5. For each externally-consumed write box inside the sub-map:
311	   route its emitted value to the matching output port on the
312	   encapsulating box (so downstream consumers in the parent map
313	   see the value on a distinct wire per write box). The write
314	   box still performs its disk-write if `path` is set.
315	6. Remove the encapsulating call box from the parent's graph.
316	
317	After expansion, the compiled artifact is **one flat graph**.
318	The runtime never sees `lang: "map"`. The map-language spec
319	exists only for the editor's sake (validating refs, listing
320	the sub-map's inputs/outputs for the inspector).
321	
322	**Pros:**
323	
324	- No new runtime machinery. The dispatch, slot store, and spec
325	  registry all operate on flat graphs as today.
326	- Best per-call performance — no sub-graph startup cost, no
327	  nested dispatch.
328	- **Composes cleanly with issue 313** (whole-program same-
329	  language merge). The inlined sub-graph's same-language regions
330	  merge into the parent's merge as if they were always one map.
331	- Debugging stack traces inside the inlined region point to
332	  flat box ids — readable once you know the naming convention.
333	
334	**Cons:**
335	
336	- The sub-map gets baked into every parent that uses it. Edit
337	  the sub-map → every parent must recompile.
338	- No hot-reload of sub-maps. The editor would have to
339	  re-expand on every parent map edit, or accept that the
340	  parent's last-compiled artifact lags the sub-map source.
341	- Compile time grows with sub-map size × number of
342	  encapsulations.
343	- Deep recursion (sub-maps inside sub-maps inside sub-maps)
344	  inflates the parent's compiled output proportionally.
345	- The multi-output exception to issue 218 has to be carried
346	  through compile-time inlining as well: after expansion, the
347	  parent's flat graph has wires going from internal sub-graph
348	  boxes directly to whichever parent consumers were wired to
349	  the encapsulating box's output ports. The compile-time
350	  artifact loses the "encapsulated box" identity entirely but
351	  preserves the per-output routing.
352	
353	### Path B — Runtime sub-graph dispatch
354	
355	The encapsulating box stays as one box in the parent's flat
356	graph. The map-language spec's `invoke` runs the sub-graph at
357	call time:
358	
359	1. **`map_init(worker_idx)`** — load every sub-map referenced
360	   by the running program (or lazily on first invoke). Each
361	   worker gets its own copy of the sub-graph state (slot store,
362	   dispatch context).
363	2. **`map_invoke(handle, sub_map_dir, ..., inputs, ..., outputs, ...)`** —
364	   for each input, write the bytes into the shared-memory chunk
365	   that the matching marked data box reads from. Then drive the
366	   sub-graph to quiescence using the existing pool's dispatch
367	   loop (the sub-graph's tasks are normal pool tasks distinguished
368	   by a nested namespace). When quiescent, walk each
369	   externally-consumed write box and push its emitted value onto
370	   the matching output port of the encapsulating box. Each output
371	   port surfaces on its own wire to the parent — no packing.
372	
373	The sub-graph's parallelism uses the same thread pool as the
374	parent's. A sub-graph's tasks compete for workers alongside the
375	parent's tasks. From the pool's perspective, the difference is
376	just box-id prefix.
377	
378	**Pros:**
379	
380	- Sub-map loaded once per worker, reused across many parent
381	  invocations and across many parent maps.
382	- Hot-reload friendly: change the sub-map, parent picks up the
383	  new version on next run (no parent recompile).
384	- The multi-output boundary is clean — each externally-consumed
385	  write box pushes onto its own output port wire as it would
386	  if it were a leaf box in the parent graph, no packing or
387	  unpacking required.
388	- Debugging stack traces preserve the sub-map identity (the
389	  task's namespace says "this came from `stats-pipeline`").
390	- Recursion is natural — the spec's invoke can nest-invoke its
391	  own spec for a sub-sub-map.
392	
393	**Cons:**
394	
395	- New runtime machinery: the map spec's `invoke` runs a nested
396	  dispatch loop. Either the dispatch layer grows a re-entrancy
397	  contract, or the map spec replicates enough of the dispatch
398	  machinery to drive the sub-graph itself.
399	- Each encapsulating-box call pays sub-graph startup cost —
400	  seeding inputs, possibly resetting slot state from a previous
401	  invocation, collecting outputs at the end. Small but real.
402	- Does NOT compose with issue 313's same-language merge — the
403	  sub-map's source can't merge with the parent's, because at
404	  build time they're separate compilation units. (313 could be
405	  extended to merge across encapsulation boundaries, but that's
406	  a separate design.)
407	- Re-using the sub-graph across invocations requires reset
408	  semantics. Either the sub-graph's slots and counters get
409	  reset between invocations (cost), or each invocation gets a
410	  fresh sub-graph instance (allocation cost).
411	
412	### What to weigh
413	
414	The choice turns on whether encapsulation is **a build-time
415	abstraction (like a C macro or a Lua-function-inlined-by-LuaJIT)**
416	or **a runtime composition (like calling a function in a shared
417	library)**.
418	
419	Path A treats it as a build-time abstraction. Encapsulation is
420	how the user organizes source; the compiled artifact is one
421	flat program. Best for raw performance and integration with
422	the existing machinery. Cost: rebuild propagation.
423	
424	Path B treats it as a runtime composition. Encapsulation is a
425	real boundary at execution time, with the packed-blob output
426	as the wire format across the boundary. Best for modularity,
427	hot-reload, and clear semantics. Cost: per-call overhead and
428	loss of cross-boundary optimization.
429	
430	A third option exists — **support both, picked per encapsulating
431	box** via a small flag in the box JSON (`encap_mode: "inline" |
432	"runtime"`). The compile pipeline expands inline-mode boxes;
433	runtime-mode boxes stay encapsulated. Each user picks per
434	encapsulation based on their needs. Higher implementation cost
435	but maximally flexible. Probably not in the first slice; flag it
436	for later if either A or B alone proves too narrow.
437	
438	Recursion (a sub-map encapsulates another sub-map) works under
439	either path. Cycles between maps are a compile-time (or
440	load-time, under B) error.
441	
442	## Relationship to existing issues
443	
444	- **Issue 207 (source-file-browser)** — the file browser is the
445	  entry point for the "encapsulate" action.
446	- **Issue 239 (literal port shrinks to nodule)** — the
447	  external-input slider reuses the same visual idiom on the
448	  input-port row.
449	- **Issue 229 (data box as language-agnostic file IO)** —
450	  encapsulation adds an "externally-supplied" toggle to data
451	  boxes and an "externally-consumed" toggle to write boxes. The
452	  boxes' default behaviour (read from / write to disk) is
453	  unchanged; the toggles route the value through a parent-wire
454	  instead of (or in addition to) the disk file.
455	
456	- **Issue 218 (single output per box)** — the encapsulated
457	  `kind: "map"` box is the documented exception. Every other box
458	  has exactly one output; an encapsulated box has one per
459	  externally-consumed write box (zero or more).
460	- **Issue 309 (build system / compile pipeline)** — the
461	  compile-time inlining path (option A above) extends the
462	  pipeline with an "encapsulation expansion" step.
463	- **Issue 313 (whole-program same-language merge)** — composes
464	  with compile-time inlining; the inlined sub-graph's same-
465	  language regions merge into the parent's merge as if they
466	  were always part of one map.
467	
468	## Relevant files
469	
470	- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box state, the `kind: "map"` box,
471	  the per-input-port external-binding state.
472	- `assets/js/005-app.js` — file browser; menu with Edit /
473	  Encapsulate actions.
474	- `assets/index.html` — inspector UI for the external-binding
475	  toggle.
476	- `src/006-server-main.lua` — HTTP backend; resolving sub-map
477	  paths, validating bindings.
478	- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — graph loader; recognise
479	  `kind: "map"`, resolve the sub-map, build the encapsulated
480	  shape.
481	- `src/012-dispatch.c` — encapsulating-box dispatch (runtime
482	  path) or compile-time expansion (compile path).
483	- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — encapsulation expansion if the
484	  compile-time path wins.
485	
486	## Suggested implementation sequence
487	
488	1. **Box JSON schema**: add `kind: "map"`, the `ref` field, and
489	   the per-input `external` block. Graph loader rejects with a
490	   clear error if any field is missing where required.
491	2. **External-binding toggles**: inspector toggle on data boxes
492	   (externally-supplied) and write boxes (externally-consumed);
493	   kind / name / index selectors when on. Same visual idiom for
494	   both.
495	3. **File browser "Encapsulate" action**: adds a `kind: "map"`
496	   box to the parent at the cursor position. Reads the sub-map's
497	   marked data boxes and marked write boxes to populate the new
498	   box's `inputs` and `outputs` arrays.
499	4. **Graph loader sub-map resolution**: load the sub-map's
500	   `meta.json` and `boxes/`; record its marked-input and
501	   marked-output lists on the parent box record.
502	5. **Multi-output slot allocation**: the encapsulated box gets
503	   one output slot per externally-consumed write box (the
504	   documented exception to issue 218). Graph loader and slot
505	   store accept this shape only for `lang: "map"` boxes.
506	6. **Pick A or B**: compile-time inlining or runtime sub-graph
507	   dispatch. Prototype the simpler of the two end-to-end on a
508	   trivial sub-map (`maps/encap-trivial`).
509	7. **Recursion**: nested encapsulation; cycle detection at
510	   compile (or load) time.
511	8. **Editor visualization**: distinct canvas rendering for
512	   encapsulating boxes; tooltip / thumbnail.
513	
514	## Open questions
515	
516	- **Sub-map identity for the editor**: when the parent
517	  encapsulates `maps/<sub>`, what happens if the user later
518	  renames or moves `<sub>`? The reference path is brittle.
519	  Options: store a stable id in the sub-map's `meta.json` and
520	  reference that, plus a path hint; or require the sub-map to
521	  live inside the parent's map directory tree.
522	- **Re-sync behaviour when the sub-map changes**: if the user
523	  edits the sub-map and changes its marked inputs, the parent's
524	  encapsulating box's `inputs` array drifts out of date. Likely
525	  resolution: on parent map load, the loader re-derives the
526	  inputs from the sub-map and warns the user if wiring needs
527	  fixing.
528	- **`.map` packaging format**: this issue assumes sub-maps are
529	  directories. A single-file `.map` archive (tarball / zip)
530	  would be more portable for distribution. Out of scope here;
531	  separate ticket if it becomes relevant.
532	- **Output naming consistency**: outputs use the same
533	  positional / numbered / named binding kinds as inputs. The
534	  question is whether a single encapsulated box can mix kinds
535	  across outputs (e.g. two named, one positional), or whether
536	  all outputs must share a kind. Inputs already allow mixing —
537	  preferable to keep outputs symmetric.
538	- **Side-effect ordering**: the sub-map's write boxes run as
539	  part of the sub-graph and write to disk. The encapsulating
540	  box's output emits *after* those side effects complete. If
541	  the parent wires the encapsulating box's output forward, the
542	  downstream task can rely on the writes having happened. Worth
543	  documenting; not a design choice so much as a consequence of
544	  the existing dispatch model.
545	
546	## Design history
547	
548	The original 2026-05-21 design packed all write-box outputs into
549	a single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, and
550	the encapsulated box had a single output wire carrying that blob:
551	
552	> "the write data slots are the outputs, written to a chunk of
553	> heap memory. At the beginning is an array of sizes — null
554	> terminated. Then, immediately afterwards, is the first index
555	> of data..." — 2026-05-21
556	
557	That design was reconsidered on 2026-05-23 while specifying the
558	self-construction built-ins (issue 319). The reconsideration:
559	boxes never "return" values to the outside world under the
560	existing model — they push values onto wires that other boxes
561	consume, and `write` boxes specifically terminate values to
562	files. Repurposing the file-writing destination to emit strings
563	into wires would have been a substitution of one mechanism for
564	another. The symmetric design — mark write boxes
565	externally-consumed, surface each as its own output port —
566	preserves the `write` box's semantics ("terminate a value") and
567	treats the destination as a mode toggle. Cost: multi-output boxes
568	exist for this kind alone; benefit: one mechanism does both jobs
569	cleanly.
570	
```

# 319 — Built-in library for map self-construction

## Status
open — planning stub. Several design questions need user resolution
before implementation can begin. See **Open design questions**
below.

## Concept

A map should be able to build more of itself while running.
Two built-in primitives, exposed by the runtime to every language
spec, are enough to bootstrap that capability:

- **`create_box(filepath, function_name) -> box_handle`**
  Spawn a new box on the currently-running map. The first argument
  is the file holding the function the box will run; the second is
  the name of that function inside the file. The runtime does any
  build-pipeline work that's needed (compile the source, register
  the spec, allocate the box's input port slots) before returning
  a handle the caller can use to wire the box up.

- **`connect(from_box, to_box_a, to_box_b, ...) -> bool`**
  Attach a wire from the single output of `from_box` to each of
  the destination boxes. Variadic on the destinations, since fan-out
  from a single producer is the common pattern. Returns true if
  every connection succeeded, false otherwise.

Together these let a running map grow new sub-graphs in response
to runtime conditions: a planner box decides what sub-pipeline to
build, calls `create_box` for each node, calls `connect` to wire
them, and the dispatch layer picks up the new region on the next
push.

## Why this shape works (and the parts that need to be checked)

**Single-output-per-box is already the law.** Issue 218 collapsed
boxes to one output. Variadic destinations on `connect` is just
fan-out across that single output — no new concept on the wire
side. The variadic part of the API matches the data model.

**`filepath + function_name` matches box JSON.** That's already how
language specs locate the code a box runs. The API takes the same
two strings the box JSON would hold.

**Handle-as-return mirrors `data` boxes' encapsulation contract
(issue 248).** Encapsulated maps already expose typed handles
to externally-supplied inputs. A `create_box` handle is the same
kind of thing — a reference the caller uses to identify the box
in follow-up calls.


==> /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/315-compiled-artifact-reference-counting.md <==
# 315 — Reference-counted compiled-map artifacts

## Status
open

## Current behavior

`scripts/soramech-compile.sh` from issue 309 is destructive at the
top:

```bash
rm -rf "$COMPILED"
mkdir -p "$COMPILED" "$COMPILED/boxes" "$COMPILED/src" ...
```

Whatever lived in `<map>/compiled/` before the rebuild is gone. If
another process — a long-running runner, a different shell, a
sibling tool that opened the artifact yesterday — had pinned to
that exact compiled layout (a particular `pool-runner` binary, a
particular `spec.so` ABI, a particular set of pre-compiled C
boxes), the rebuild yanks the rug. The holder either crashes,
silently retains stale `dlopen` handles, or starts reading new
files mid-flight.

This is fine in single-user development. It stops being fine the
moment a SoraMech artifact is the kind of thing other programs
hold onto across time.

## Intended behavior

A compiled artifact carries its own reference count. Other
programs that depend on a particular build of a map are expected
to *acquire* a reference on startup and *release* it on shutdown.
When `soramech-compile` is asked to rebuild a map that has any
live references, it does NOT clobber the existing directory.
Instead it builds a sibling directory next door, leaving the
referenced one untouched until its holders are done with it.

The reference count is **expected to be unreliable**. A crashing
holder doesn't get the chance to release; an SSH session that
drops doesn't either. The design accepts that staleness is the
common case, not the exception — every reference entry carries
enough metadata to be independently validated and (eventually)
reaped. The reference count is a hint and a courtesy, not a
guarantee.

This is conceptually a copy-on-write filesystem for compiled
artifacts: writes (rebuilds) fork the universe when readers
exist; readers can keep reading the version they pinned to;
generations get garbage-collected when nothing observable still
```

Here's where we left off on the encapsulated-map-as-box issue, and what I think the next move is.

**Input side is done and on disk.** The most recent commit shipped load-time inlining: when the graph loader sees a sub-map referenced as a box, it slurps the sub-map's boxes into the parent's arena with prefixed ids, then rewrites every parent wire that targeted the encapsulating box so it goes *through* the matching externally-supplied data box and lands on whatever the data box was feeding inside the sub-map. There's an end-to-end fixture under `tests/maps/248-encap-input-only/` that proves bytes from the parent reach a write box inside the sub-map.

**Three things are still deferred** — listed in the issue's status header and now on the todo list:

1. **Output-side encapsulation.** Wires the user drew *from* the encapsulating box's output ports don't fire yet. The symmetric splice — every externally-consumed write box inside the sub-map surfaces as its own distinct output port on the parent's view of the encap box — is the natural next slice, since it mirrors the machinery the input side already proves out.
2. **Editor UI.** The inspector toggle (externally-supplied on data boxes, externally-consumed on write boxes) and the file-browser "Encapsulate" action that drops a `kind: "map"` box onto the parent at cursor position.
3. **Recursion** across nested encapsulations + cycle detection at load time.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The decision to inline at *load time* rather than compile time (path A in the issue) or with a true nested dispatch loop (path B) is a third path — splicing happens after the parent's JSON is read but before topology is resolved, so the runtime never sees `kind: "map"`. It gets path-A's flat-graph simplicity without depending on issue 309's compile pipeline being in shape.
- The reason encapsulated maps are the *one* documented exception to issue 218's "single output per box" rule is that each externally-consumed write box is genuinely an independent value with its own semantics — bundling them into a packed blob would have been file-write machinery doing wire-emit work, the wrong shape. Keeping the multi-output exception on this one kind preserves both invariants.
- Reference-counted artifacts (issue 315) and self-construction (319) are blockers for a real release because together they're what lets *other programs* hold onto a SoraMech artifact across time and let a running map mutate itself — until those land, SoraMech is single-user, single-shot.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

I also queued 319 and 315 on the todo list as you asked. Want me to dive into the **output-side splice** for 248 next? That's the smallest self-contained step that unblocks the rest of 248 (the editor toggle is mostly a UI affordance over data the loader already needs to read), and it'll let me show you a fixture where a wire leaving the encap box actually carries a value into the parent. Or would you rather I poke at 319 / 315 first since those are the release blockers?

1	# 243 — Multi-band comparator routing
2	
3	## Status
4	open · design carried forward from issue 233
5	
6	## Current behavior
7	
8	Issue 233 ships the comparator routing kind with a single
9	threshold and three fixed branches (`lt` / `eq` / `gt`). The
10	generalisation — N thresholds defining N+1 numeric bands — is
11	the natural next step but ships separately so the schema-and-
12	inspector work it carries doesn't bloat 233.
13	
14	## Intended behavior
15	
16	A comparator with a list of thresholds defines N+1 output
17	branches, each named for the band it fires on:
18	
19	```json
20	"routing": {
21	  "kind":       "comparator",
22	  "thresholds": [3, 7, 11, 17]
23	}
24	```
25	
26	Five output ports get named `below_3`, `between_3_7`,
27	`between_7_11`, `between_11_17`, `above_17`. The single-
28	threshold case (`thresholds: [c]`) reduces to the band `[below_c,
29	above_c]` — different shape from today's three-branch lt/eq/gt.
30	To recover the lt/eq/gt semantics, **doubled thresholds** mark
31	zero-width equality bands:
32	
33	```
34	thresholds: [3, 3]         → < 3      / == 3   / > 3
35	thresholds: [3, 3, 7, 7]   → < 3 / == 3 / 3<x<7 / == 7 / > 7
36	```
37	
38	This means the comparator shipped in 233 is exactly
39	`thresholds: [c, c]` under the multi-band shape, and the editor
40	can present the single-comparand UI while storing the doubled
41	form so the dispatch layer sees one consistent representation.
42	
43	### Schema
44	
45	```json
46	"routing": {
47	  "kind":       "comparator",
48	  "thresholds": [3, 7, 11, 17]
49	}
50	```
51	
52	`thresholds` is a non-empty array of numbers. Non-decreasing
53	(doubled values are valid, decreasing values are rejected). The
54	schema also accepts the legacy single-comparand form for one
55	release as a transition aid:
56	
57	```json
58	"routing": { "kind": "comparator", "comparand": 5 }
59	```
60	
61	The editor normalises this to `thresholds: [5, 5]` on next save.
62	
63	### Branch picker (dispatch layer)
64	
65	Linear scan over thresholds; zero-width bands require equality
66	checks. For `thresholds: [t0, t1, …, t_{n-1}]`:
67	
68	```
69	value <  t0          → below_<t0>
70	value == t0 == t1    → == <t0>          (when t0 == t1)
71	t_i < value < t_{i+1}→ between_<t_i>_<t_{i+1}>
72	value > t_{n-1}      → above_<t_{n-1}>
73	```
74	
75	Doubled thresholds match equality; non-doubled boundaries match
76	the open interval. The picker is straight-line code; profiling
77	might justify a binary search if thresholds gets long, but
78	typical use is N ≤ 8.
79	
80	### Inspector UI
81	
82	Two control modes share the same dropdown selection:
83	- **Simple comparator** (the 233 UI): a single number input.
84	  Stores `thresholds: [c, c]`.
85	- **Multi-band**: a sortable list of number inputs, with `+
86	  threshold` and `× threshold` buttons. Reordering enforces non-
87	  decreasing order on save.
88	
89	A toggle between the two presentations sits next to the
90	threshold list. The "Simple" mode is the default for new
91	comparator boxes; the user opts into multi-band when they need
92	it.
93	
94	## Suggested implementation steps
95	
96	1. `src/001-schema.lua` — accept `thresholds` array as a
97	   comparator alternative to the legacy `comparand`. Validate
98	   non-decreasing.
99	2. `src/010-graph-loader.c` — read the thresholds array into the
100	   box's `routing` struct.
101	3. `src/012-dispatch.c` — replace the lt/eq/gt picker with a
102	   threshold-band lookup. The single-threshold doubled case
103	   reduces to the same code path.
104	4. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — add the multi-band UI under
105	   the comparator dropdown choice. Keep the simple-comparand UI
106	   as the default visible to the user.
107	5. `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — render output ports named
108	   `below_<t>` / `between_<a>_<b>` / `above_<t>` based on the
109	   thresholds array.
110	6. Migration: the editor reads legacy `comparand` and emits
111	   `thresholds: [c, c]` on the next save. Hand-migrate any
112	   maps not opened in the editor.
113	7. Fixture: `tests/maps/multi-band-comparator/` — four
114	   thresholds, sample inputs hitting every band including
115	   doubled-equality.
116	
117	## Relevant files
118	
119	- `issues/completed/233-unified-routing-schema.md` — parent.
120	- `src/001-schema.lua`, `src/010-graph-loader.c`,
121	  `src/012-dispatch.c` — runtime side.
122	- `assets/js/004-inspector.js`, `assets/js/002-boxes.js` —
123	  editor side.
124	
125	## Open questions
126	
127	- **Edge inclusion**: `x == threshold` (non-doubled) — which
128	  side does the value land on? Lean toward
129	  `less-than-or-equal` for consistency. Document the choice in
130	  the dispatch code's comment so a reader doesn't have to guess.
131	- **Port-name length**: long threshold values produce long
132	  port names (`between_-1234567_2345678`). The canvas already
133	  truncates with ellipsis (issue 235's MAX_LABEL_CHARS rule).
134	  Probably fine; flag if it becomes ugly.
135	- **Threshold mutation invalidates wires**: changing a
136	  threshold renames a port (e.g. `between_3_7` → `between_3_8`).
137	  The editor should rewrite outgoing wire `from_branch` to
138	  match — same machinery as the iterator slot rename used to
139	  use under the legacy schema.
140	
```

Wrote `issues/250-routing-kind-nonlinearity.md`, mirroring the format from 240–243.

The shape of the issue: schema + branch-picker + inspector sections like its siblings, but with the recognition that **this is the first routing kind that rewrites the wire value** instead of just selecting a branch — which is the most interesting architectural note in there.

A few design notes I want to flag for your decision (all also expanded as open questions in the file):

- **Auto vs fixed bounds is the most interesting axis.** Auto means non-deterministic outputs across runs (a value early in the run remaps differently than the same value late in the run, once min/max have widened). That's a real cost — debugging downstreams becomes "what did the box see before this value?" One mitigation: a "freeze observed bounds" action that snapshots auto → fixed on save.
- **Sigmoid wants something to bend.** If you sigmoid a normalised `t ∈ [0,1]` directly, the output range is roughly `[0.5, 0.73]` — barely curved. You almost always want to center the input (`t - 0.5`) and apply a steepness `k`. So the "default sigmoid" needs a default `k`, and the question is whether to expose `k` to the user or pick something opinionated (I'd lean opinionated — `k ≈ 6` gives a satisfying S — and let power users edit the JSON directly).
- **Shape choice has implications for output range.** Sigmoid is `[0,1]`, tanh is `[-1,1]`. Either pick one and let `out_range` field map between them, or let the shape dictate. The first is more flexible, the second is less surprising.
- **The first value seen under `auto`** has no `[min, max]` yet. I picked "emit 0.5" as the bootstrap; alternatives are "emit input unchanged" or "suppress the emit" (breaks the "every fire emits one value" contract every other routing kind upholds).
- **Hard-error on non-numeric input** matches your preferences exactly — no silent coercion, no skip-on-bad-input fallback. `strtod` is "good enough" but accepts `"3.14abc"` as 3.14; strict parse (reject trailing junk) is the more consistent choice.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Generalising the dispatch layer from "routing picks a branch" to "routing may also rewrite the value" is the architectural shift this issue introduces. If you ever want **square**, **log**, **abs**, or **quantise** as routing kinds, factor that path as a first-class concept now rather than special-casing this one kind.
- The auto-mode running min/max is the first slot kind in the project (that I'm aware of) where CAS-update semantics are load-bearing on shared state. Per-worker bounds would be faster but produce drifting output streams — shared with atomic CAS is the right shape but worth knowing it's the precedent it sets.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**Which open question do you want to nail down first?** My read is the name (`nonlinearity` / `squash` / `remap`) and the bounds-mode default (`auto` vs `fixed`) are the two that have to settle before any code lands — everything else can be tuned after the first fixture runs.

091da6e 248 — input-side encapsulation: sub-maps as boxes via load-time inlining
---
commit 091da6e6e3abe0ca371fe3ce273c9fcfcd4c169d
Author: gabrilend <gabrilend@gmail.com>
Date:   Sat May 23 21:35:55 2026 -0700

    248 — input-side encapsulation: sub-maps as boxes via load-time inlining
    
    A map directory can now appear as one box in a parent map. The loader
    recognizes kind: "map" and an external block on the sub-map's data
    boxes; a new pass between load_boxes and resolve_topology splices the
    sub-map's boxes into the parent with namespaced ids, then rewires any
    parent wire that landed on the encapsulating box to flow directly to
    the matching ext-supplied data box's downstreams (preserving routing
    branch tags). The result by the time topology resolution starts is
    one flat graph with the encapsulating record left inert.
    
    Verified end-to-end with a fixture whose parent reads a literal and
    wires it into a sub-map whose write box deposits the value on disk —
    the file contains exactly what the parent sent. Output-side
    (externally-consumed write boxes surfacing as the encap's output
    ports) and editor UI are tracked as deferred on the issue.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

12	 * primitives — they have no function to invoke.

15	 * function names, branch tags, paths, input port names) lives in a
16	 * single json_arena_t owned by the graph_t. graph_destroy frees the
17	 * arena, the box / connection / input arrays, and the graph_t in

310	 * malloc'd `box` pointer to this function. After the call the box
311	 * is owned by the graph; graph_destroy will free it. Returns the
312	 * new box's index (>= 0) or -1 on allocation failure.
313	 *
314	 * box_add_connection appends a connection entry to the given box's
315	 * `connections` array via atomic copy-and-publish: a new array is
316	 * allocated at current_n+1 entries, the old entries are copied in,
317	 * the new entry is appended, and the new array pointer is published
318	 * before the new count. The old array is parked on the graph's
319	 * stale-list and freed at graph_destroy. Concurrent dispatch reads
320	 * of the producer's connections see either the pre-append snapshot
321	 * or the post-append snapshot, never a half-published state.

324	 * connections concurrently from two workers (single-spawn CAS guard

343	 * any feeder has output_capacity == 0 (variable-size). Multi-spawn

1	# 010-graph-loader.c — public surface
2	
3	C graph loader (phase 3). Reads a map directory, parses every
4	JSON file, and produces an in-memory `graph_t` the dispatch layer
5	and pool runner consume. Replaces `src/003-loader.lua`.
6	
7	## Lifecycle
8	
9	- `graph_t *graph_load(const char *map_dir, char **err)` — read +
10	  parse + validate. Returns NULL on any failure and sets `*err` to
11	  a malloc'd `"<file>:<line>: <message>"` diagnostic. The caller
12	  frees `*err`.
13	- `void graph_destroy(graph_t *g)` — frees every byte the graph
14	  owns (the box and connection arrays, the input declarations, the
15	  underlying JSON arena holding every string).
16	
17	## Accessors
18	
19	- `const char *graph_name(g)`
20	- `const char *graph_description(g)`
21	- `const char *graph_entry_box_id(g)`
22	- `int          graph_n_boxes(g)`
23	- `const box_t *graph_box(g, i)`
24	- `const box_t *graph_box_by_id(g, id)`
25	
26	## Public types
27	
28	- `box_kind_t` — `BOX_CALL` / `BOX_READ` / `BOX_WRITE`.
29	- `routing_kind_t` — `ROUTING_PLAIN` / `ROUTING_COMPARATOR` /
30	  `ROUTING_ITERATOR`; randomizer / weighted / distributor enum
31	  values exist but the parser doesn't accept them yet.
32	- `routing_t` — `kind` plus per-kind params (`n_outputs`,
33	  `comparand`).
34	- `input_decl_t` — `name`, `type`, `literal`, `optional`.
35	- `connection_t` — outgoing connection. Stores string refs
36	  (`to_box`, `to_input`); resolved-to-integer-index forms come in
37	  the topology iteration.
38	- `box_t` — all of the above per box.
39	
40	## Schema currently enforced
41	
42	- `meta.json` must be a JSON object containing at least `name`.
43	- Every file under `boxes/` ending in `.json` is a box file with a
44	  top-level object, `id` (string), `kind` ∈ `{call, read, write}`.
45	- `call` boxes: require `ref` and `routing`. `fn` is optional (a
46	  language without function-name dispatch is fine). `lang` is
47	  optional too — falls back to inference from `ref` extension once
48	  the spec registry lands.
49	- `read` boxes (issue 229): an inline `value` literal OR a `path`
50	  field; no `ref` / `fn` / `routing`. With `value` set, the box
51	  emits the literal directly and the `path` port hides on the canvas.
52	- `write` boxes (issue 229): no kind-specific required fields beyond
53	  inputs `path` and `value`. Pushes the boolean string `"true"`
54	  downstream after a successful write.
55	- `routing.kind` ∈ `{plain, comparator, iterator}` (issue 233's
56	  shipped surface). `comparator` requires `comparand` (number or
57	  string-form number per the issue's example shape).
58	  `iterator` requires `n_outputs` (>= 1).
59	- Box ids must be unique across the map. O(n²) scan; n is small.
60	
61	## What's NOT here (deferred to follow-on iterations within 305)
62	
63	- **Phase 4 — topology validation.** Connection endpoints aren't
64	  resolved to integer indices yet; we don't verify that every
65	  `to_box` refers to a real box, nor that the `to_input` matches a
66	  declared port. Cycle detection (excluding iterator-rooted
67	  cycles) lands here too.
68	- **Phase 5 — slot size class enumeration.** The slot store's
69	  `slot_alloc` consumes a `cell_capacity`; the loader's job is to
70	  scan box outputs and enumerate the distinct sizes the graph
71	  needs.
72	- **Phase 6 — entry-box detection.** Boxes with no inputs (or
73	  inputs fed only by `data` boxes) get auto-detected as entry
74	  points.
75	- **Phase 7 — language enumeration.** Walk every call box,
76	  collect distinct `lang` values, hand the set to the spec
77	  registry.
78	- The remaining routing kinds (`randomizer`, `weighted`,
79	  `distributor`) — issue 233 deferred them to their own
80	  follow-ons; the parser rejects them with a precise message.
81	
82	None of these block issues 301 / 303 / 306 from starting.
83	
84	## Related
85	
86	- Issue 305 — design.
87	- Issue 233 — unified routing schema this loader implements.
88	- Issue 229 — data / file_write box kinds.
89	- Issue 314 — the JSON parser this depends on.
90	- Issue 302 — slot store; the loader will eventually hand size
91	  class enumeration to it.
92	
```
