1259	 *      then rewrite each sub-box's connections.to_box strings that
1260	 *      reference sibling sub-boxes to the renamed form.
1261	 *   4. For each parent producer, walk its connections; any that target
1262	 *      encap_id get replaced (1→N) by the corresponding ext-supplied
1263	 *      data box's downstream targets.
1264	 *   5. Append sub-boxes to parent's box array (grow capacity if needed).
1265	 *   6. Orphan the encap box (clear its connections; kind stays BOX_MAP
1266	 *      so dispatch's no-op case never confuses it for a live producer).
1267	 *
1268	 * Output-side (externally-consumed write boxes) is deferred to the
1269	 * next slice. Wires originally leaving encap.port_x are dropped.
1270	 */
1271	static int inline_one_encapsulation(graph_t *g, int encap_idx, char **err)
1272	{
1273	    box_t **boxes = atomic_load_explicit(&g->boxes, memory_order_relaxed);
1274	    box_t  *encap = boxes[encap_idx];
1275	
1276	    if (!encap->ref) {
1277	        *err = err_fmt("box '%s': BOX_MAP missing 'ref'", encap->id);
1278	        return -1;
1279	    }
1280	
1281	    char sub_dir[4096];
1282	    if (encap->ref[0] == '/') {
1283	        int w = snprintf(sub_dir, sizeof sub_dir, "%s", encap->ref);
1284	        if (w < 0 || w >= (int)sizeof sub_dir) {
1285	            *err = err_fmt("encap '%s': sub-map path too long", encap->id);
1286	            return -1;
1287	        }
1288	    } else {
1289	        int w = snprintf(sub_dir, sizeof sub_dir, "%s/%s",
1290	                         g->map_dir, encap->ref);
1291	        if (w < 0 || w >= (int)sizeof sub_dir) {
1292	            *err = err_fmt("encap '%s': sub-map path too long", encap->id);
1293	            return -1;
1294	        }
1295	    }
1296	
1297	    box_t **sub_boxes = NULL;
1298	    int     sub_n     = 0;
1299	    if (load_sub_map_boxes(g, sub_dir, &sub_boxes, &sub_n, err) != 0) {
1300	        return -1;
1301	    }
1302	
1303	    /* Save the pre-rename ids so we can rewrite intra-sub-map
1304	     * connection refs before clobbering the ids on the box records. */
1305	    const char **old_ids = calloc((size_t)sub_n, sizeof(const char *));
1306	    char       **new_ids = calloc((size_t)sub_n, sizeof(char *));
1307	    if ((sub_n > 0 && !old_ids) || (sub_n > 0 && !new_ids)) {
1308	        free(old_ids); free(new_ids);
1309	        for (int k = 0; k < sub_n; k++) free(sub_boxes[k]);
1310	        free(sub_boxes);
1311	        *err = err_fmt("out of memory");
1312	        return -1;
1313	    }
1314	
1315	    const char *prefix = encap->id;
1316	    size_t      plen   = strlen(prefix);
1317	    for (int i = 0; i < sub_n; i++) {
1318	        old_ids[i] = sub_boxes[i]->id;
1319	        size_t need = plen + 2 + strlen(old_ids[i]) + 1;
1320	        char *nid = malloc(need);
1321	        if (!nid) {
1322	            for (int k = 0; k < i; k++) free(new_ids[k]);
1323	            free(old_ids); free(new_ids);
1324	            for (int k = 0; k < sub_n; k++) free(sub_boxes[k]);
1325	            free(sub_boxes);
1326	            *err = err_fmt("out of memory");
1327	            return -1;
1328	        }
1329	        snprintf(nid, need, "%s__%s", prefix, old_ids[i]);
1330	        new_ids[i] = nid;
1331	    }
1332	
1333	    /* Rewrite intra-sub-map connection refs to use the renamed ids.
1334	     * Connections that already target an outside-the-sub-map id (which
1335	     * shouldn't happen at this layer, but guard anyway) are left alone. */
1336	    for (int i = 0; i < sub_n; i++) {
1337	        int n_c = atomic_load_explicit(&sub_boxes[i]->n_connections,
1338	                                       memory_order_relaxed);
1339	        connection_t *cs =
1340	            atomic_load_explicit(&sub_boxes[i]->connections,
1341	                                 memory_order_relaxed);
1342	        for (int k = 0; k < n_c; k++) {
1343	            for (int j = 0; j < sub_n; j++) {
1344	                if (strcmp(cs[k].to_box, old_ids[j]) == 0) {
1345	                    cs[k].to_box = new_ids[j];
1346	                    break;
1347	                }
1348	            }
1349	        }
1350	    }
1351	
1352	    /* Adopt the renamed ids onto the sub-box records. From this point
1353	     * on, the sub-boxes look like normal parent boxes with namespaced
1354	     * ids. The malloc'd new_ids strings move into the graph's
1355	     * owned-strings list. */
1356	    for (int i = 0; i < sub_n; i++) {
1357	        sub_boxes[i]->id = new_ids[i];
1358	        if (track_owned_str(g, new_ids[i]) != 0) {
1359	            /* Leak the rest of new_ids on this rare failure; we're
1360	             * about to error out anyway. */
1361	            free(old_ids); free(new_ids);
1362	            *err = err_fmt("out of memory");
1363	            return -1;
1364	        }
1365	    }
1366	    free(new_ids);    /* the strings live on; only the temp array goes */
1367	
1368	    /* INPUT-side rewiring. Each parent producer's connection that
1369	     * targets (encap_id, port) becomes one-or-more new connections
1370	     * targeting the matching ext-supplied data box's downstreams. */
1371	    uint32_t cur_n = atomic_load_explicit(&g->n_boxes, memory_order_relaxed);
1372	    for (uint32_t p = 0; p < cur_n; p++) {
1373	        box_t *prod = g->boxes[p];
1374	        if (prod == encap) continue;
1375	
1376	        int n_c = atomic_load_explicit(&prod->n_connections,
1377	                                       memory_order_relaxed);
1378	        if (n_c == 0) continue;
1379	        connection_t *cs =
1380	            atomic_load_explicit(&prod->connections, memory_order_relaxed);
1381	
1382	        /* First pass: compute the new array's size. Each connection
1383	         * to encap explodes to N entries where N = matched data box's
1384	         * out-degree (potentially 0; that prunes the wire). */
1385	        int new_cap = 0;
1386	        int touches_encap = 0;
1387	        for (int k = 0; k < n_c; k++) {
1388	            if (strcmp(cs[k].to_box, encap->id) != 0) {
1389	                new_cap += 1;
1390	                continue;
1391	            }
1392	            touches_encap = 1;
1393	            int port_idx = find_input_port_index(encap, cs[k].to_input);
1394	            if (port_idx < 0) {
1395	                *err = err_fmt("encap '%s': producer '%s' wires to unknown "
1396	                               "port '%s'",
1397	                               encap->id, prod->id, cs[k].to_input);
1398	                free(old_ids);
1399	                return -1;
1400	            }
1401	            box_t *D = find_ext_supplied_for_port(sub_boxes, sub_n,
1402	                                                  encap, port_idx);
1403	            if (!D) {
1404	                *err = err_fmt("encap '%s': port '%s' has no matching "
1405	                               "externally-supplied data box in sub-map",
1406	                               encap->id, cs[k].to_input);
1407	                free(old_ids);
1408	                return -1;
1409	            }
1410	            new_cap += atomic_load_explicit(&D->n_connections,
1411	                                            memory_order_relaxed);
1412	        }
1413	        if (!touches_encap) continue;
1414	
1415	        /* Second pass: build the new array. */
1416	        connection_t *new_cs =
1417	            (new_cap > 0) ? calloc((size_t)new_cap, sizeof(connection_t)) : NULL;
1418	        if (new_cap > 0 && !new_cs) {
1419	            free(old_ids);
1420	            *err = err_fmt("out of memory");
1421	            return -1;
1422	        }
1423	        int new_n = 0;
1424	        for (int k = 0; k < n_c; k++) {
1425	            if (strcmp(cs[k].to_box, encap->id) != 0) {
1426	                new_cs[new_n] = cs[k];
1427	                new_cs[new_n].to_box_idx   = -1;
1428	                new_cs[new_n].to_input_idx = -1;
1429	                new_n++;
1430	                continue;
1431	            }
1432	            int port_idx = find_input_port_index(encap, cs[k].to_input);
1433	            box_t *D = find_ext_supplied_for_port(sub_boxes, sub_n,
1434	                                                  encap, port_idx);
1435	            int dn = atomic_load_explicit(&D->n_connections,
1436	                                          memory_order_relaxed);
1437	            connection_t *dc =
1438	                atomic_load_explicit(&D->connections, memory_order_relaxed);
1439	            for (int j = 0; j < dn; j++) {
1440	                new_cs[new_n].to_box      = dc[j].to_box;
1441	                new_cs[new_n].to_input    = dc[j].to_input;
1442	                new_cs[new_n].from_branch = cs[k].from_branch;
1443	                new_cs[new_n].to_box_idx   = -1;
1444	                new_cs[new_n].to_input_idx = -1;
1445	                new_n++;
1446	            }
1447	        }
1448	
1449	        free(cs);
1450	        atomic_store_explicit(&prod->connections, new_cs,
1451	                              memory_order_release);
1452	        atomic_store_explicit(&prod->n_connections, new_n,
1453	                              memory_order_release);
1454	    }
1455	    free(old_ids);
1456	
1457	    /* Orphan each ext-supplied data box: its outgoing connections
1458	     * (now spliced into the parent producer's array) must be cleared
1459	     * so build_read_predecessor_lists doesn't double-count them as
1460	     * a feeder of the same consumer the parent producer is also
1461	     * feeding. The string pointers inside the original connection
1462	     * entries are arena-owned and remain valid for the parent's
1463	     * copies; only the array itself goes. */
1464	    for (int i = 0; i < sub_n; i++) {
1465	        box_t *d = sub_boxes[i];
1466	        if (d->kind != BOX_READ) continue;
1467	        if (d->external.kind == EXTERNAL_NONE) continue;
1468	        connection_t *dc =
1469	            atomic_load_explicit(&d->connections, memory_order_relaxed);
1470	        if (dc) free(dc);
1471	        atomic_store_explicit(&d->connections, NULL, memory_order_release);
1472	        atomic_store_explicit(&d->n_connections, 0, memory_order_release);
1473	    }
1474	
1475	    /* Grow the parent's box pointer array if needed and append the
1476	     * sub-boxes. No atomic publish ordering needed at load time
1477	     * (single-threaded), but we keep the same shape as graph_add_box
1478	     * for consistency. */
1479	    uint32_t cap = atomic_load_explicit(&g->box_capacity,
1480	                                        memory_order_relaxed);
1481	    uint32_t want = cur_n + (uint32_t)sub_n;
1482	    if (want > cap) {
1483	        uint32_t new_cap = cap ? cap : 16u;
1484	        while (new_cap < want) new_cap *= 2u;
1485	        box_t **new_arr = calloc((size_t)new_cap, sizeof(box_t *));
1486	        if (!new_arr) {
1487	            for (int k = 0; k < sub_n; k++) free(sub_boxes[k]);
1488	            free(sub_boxes);
1489	            *err = err_fmt("out of memory");
1490	            return -1;
1491	        }
1492	        box_t **old_arr =
1493	            atomic_load_explicit(&g->boxes, memory_order_relaxed);
1494	        if (old_arr) {
1495	            memcpy(new_arr, old_arr, cur_n * sizeof(box_t *));
1496	            struct stale_arr *st = malloc(sizeof *st);
1497	            if (st) { st->ptr = old_arr; st->next = g->stale_box_arrs;
1498	                      g->stale_box_arrs = st; }
1499	        }
1500	        atomic_store_explicit(&g->boxes, new_arr, memory_order_release);
1501	        atomic_store_explicit(&g->box_capacity, new_cap,
1502	                              memory_order_release);
1503	    }
1504	    box_t **arr = atomic_load_explicit(&g->boxes, memory_order_relaxed);
1505	    for (int i = 0; i < sub_n; i++) {
1506	        arr[cur_n + (uint32_t)i] = sub_boxes[i];
1507	    }
1508	    atomic_store_explicit(&g->n_boxes, cur_n + (uint32_t)sub_n,
1509	                          memory_order_release);
1510	    free(sub_boxes);
1511	
1512	    /* Orphan the encap box. Its outgoing connections (if any) were
1513	     * the output-side wiring path which this slice doesn't implement
1514	     * yet; dropping them means any wires the user drew from encap's
1515	     * output ports won't fire. The box itself stays in the index
1516	     * (so its slot id remains valid for any unfixed references) but
1517	     * becomes inert — BOX_MAP has a no-op dispatch case. */
1518	    int n_old_out = atomic_load_explicit(&encap->n_connections,
1519	                                         memory_order_relaxed);
1520	    connection_t *old_out =
1521	        atomic_load_explicit(&encap->connections, memory_order_relaxed);
1522	    (void)n_old_out;
1523	    if (old_out) {
1524	        free(old_out);
1525	        atomic_store_explicit(&encap->connections, NULL,
1526	                              memory_order_release);
1527	        atomic_store_explicit(&encap->n_connections, 0,
1528	                              memory_order_release);
1529	    }
1530	    /* Strip the encap's `ref` so inline_encapsulations' find-loop
1531	     * doesn't pick this same record up on the next iteration and
1532	     * inline its sub-map a second time. The record stays in the
1533	     * box list as an inert BOX_MAP; the no-op dispatch case
1534	     * handles the (should-not-happen) reach. */
1535	    encap->ref = NULL;
1536	
1537	    return 0;
1538	}
1539	/* }}} */
1540	
1541	/* {{{ inline_encapsulations() — splice every BOX_MAP into the graph
1542	 *
1543	 * Iterates until no BOX_MAP remains. Sub-maps that themselves contain
1544	 * a BOX_MAP get picked up on the next iteration once their boxes are
1545	 * in the parent list. A high iteration bound guards against
1546	 * pathological recursion (which would also imply a cycle, caught
1547	 * later by detect_cycles in the flat form). */
1548	static int inline_encapsulations(graph_t *g, char **err)
1549	{
1550	    for (int iter = 0; iter < 1024; iter++) {
1551	        uint32_t n = atomic_load_explicit(&g->n_boxes,
1552	                                          memory_order_relaxed);
1553	        box_t **boxes =
1554	            atomic_load_explicit(&g->boxes, memory_order_relaxed);
1555	        int found = -1;
1556	        for (uint32_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
1557	            /* `ref` cleared after inlining → skip already-handled boxes.
1558	             * Without this, the orphaned BOX_MAP record keeps matching
1559	             * and the pass loops forever inlining the same sub-map. */
1560	            if (boxes[i]->kind == BOX_MAP && boxes[i]->ref) {
1561	                found = (int)i; break;
1562	            }
1563	        }
1564	        if (found < 0) return 0;
1565	        if (inline_one_encapsulation(g, found, err) != 0) return -1;
1566	    }
1567	    *err = err_fmt("inline_encapsulations: exceeded recursion limit (1024) "
1568	                   "— likely a sub-map cycle");
1569	    return -1;
1570	}
1571	/* }}} */
1572	
1573	/* {{{ graph_load() */
1574	graph_t *graph_load(const char *map_dir, char **err)
1575	{
1576	    if (err) *err = NULL;
1577	    if (!map_dir) {
1578	        if (err) *err = err_fmt("graph_load: NULL map_dir");
1579	        return NULL;
1580	    }
1581	
1582	    graph_t *g = calloc(1, sizeof *g);
1583	    if (!g) { if (err) *err = err_fmt("out of memory"); return NULL; }
1584	    pthread_mutex_init(&g->graph_mu, NULL);
1585	    atomic_init(&g->boxes,        NULL);
1586	    atomic_init(&g->n_boxes,      0u);
1587	    atomic_init(&g->box_capacity, 0u);
1588	    g->stale_box_arrs = NULL;
1589	
1590	    g->arena = json_arena_create();
1591	    if (!g->arena) {
1592	        if (err) *err = err_fmt("out of memory");
1593	        free(g);
1594	        return NULL;
1595	    }
1596	
1597	    g->map_dir = strdup(map_dir);
1598	    if (!g->map_dir) {
1599	        if (err) *err = err_fmt("out of memory");
1600	        graph_destroy(g);
1601	        return NULL;
1602	    }
1603	
1604	    if (load_meta(g, map_dir, err)            != 0) { graph_destroy(g); return NULL; }
1605	    if (load_boxes(g, map_dir, err)           != 0) { graph_destroy(g); return NULL; }
1606	    /* Issue 248 — splice any BOX_MAP into the parent's flat box list
1607	     * before topology resolution. After this pass the graph is one
1608	     * flat program with namespaced sub-map ids; resolve_topology
1609	     * never has to know encapsulation existed. */
1610	    if (inline_encapsulations(g, err)         != 0) { graph_destroy(g); return NULL; }
1611	    if (resolve_topology(g, err)              != 0) { graph_destroy(g); return NULL; }
1612	    if (detect_cycles(g, err)                 != 0) { graph_destroy(g); return NULL; }
1613	    if (cache_read_box_values(g, err)         != 0) { graph_destroy(g); return NULL; }
1614	    if (build_read_predecessor_lists(g, err)  != 0) { graph_destroy(g); return NULL; }
1615	    if (detect_entry_boxes(g, err)            != 0) { graph_destroy(g); return NULL; }
1616	
1617	    /* Compute the same-language fast path flag per call box (issue
1618	     * 312). A box is "native-eligible" iff every adjacent call box —
1619	     * any producer feeding its inputs AND any consumer reading its
1620	     * output — shares the box's language. Read boxes and
1621	     * write boxes don't constrain (they emit/consume JSON-shaped
1622	     * bytes that any spec interprets through its bridges).
1623	     *
1624	     * Computed in graph_load (not graph_attach_runtime) because
1625	     * it's purely topology-derived and doesn't need the slot
1626	     * store or registry. The dispatch reads these per-cell to
1627	     * pick the producer's push ring (native vs JSON) and to set
1628	     * the consumer's `input_native[i]` flag at read time. */
1629	    for (int i = 0; i < g->n_boxes; i++) {
1630	        box_t *b = g->boxes[i];
1631	        b->input_edge_native  = NULL;
1632	        b->output_edge_native = NULL;
1633	        if (b->kind != BOX_CALL || !b->lang) continue;
1634	
1635	        /* Allocate per-port input bits and per-connection output
1636	         * bits. malloc rather than calloc — we fill every entry
1637	         * explicitly below. */
1638	        if (b->n_inputs > 0) {
1639	            b->input_edge_native = malloc((size_t)b->n_inputs * sizeof(int));
1640	            if (!b->input_edge_native) { if (err) *err = err_fmt("oom"); return NULL; }
1641	            for (int j = 0; j < b->n_inputs; j++) b->input_edge_native[j] = 0;
1642	        }
1643	        if (b->n_connections > 0) {
1644	            b->output_edge_native = malloc((size_t)b->n_connections * sizeof(int));
1645	            if (!b->output_edge_native) { if (err) *err = err_fmt("oom"); return NULL; }
1646	            for (int j = 0; j < b->n_connections; j++) b->output_edge_native[j] = 0;
1647	        }
1648	
1649	        /* Outgoing edges: for each connection, the consumer's lang
1650	         * is native iff it's also a call box in this box's
1651	         * language. Read / write consumers are not native
1652	         * (they don't carry a language). */
1653	        int all_outs_native = 1;
1654	        for (int j = 0; j < b->n_connections; j++) {
1655	            int dst = b->connections[j].to_box_idx;
1656	            if (dst < 0) { all_outs_native = 0; continue; }
1657	            const box_t *c = g->boxes[dst];
1658	            int native = (c->kind == BOX_CALL && c->lang
1659	                          && strcmp(c->lang, b->lang) == 0);
1660	            b->output_edge_native[j] = native;
1661	            if (!native) all_outs_native = 0;
1662	        }
1663	
1664	        (void)all_outs_native;   /* slice 5 of 312 removed the per-box bit */
1665	
1666	        /* Incoming edges: for each input port the port is native iff
1667	         * it has at least one feeder AND every feeder is a call box
1668	         * sharing this box's language. A mixed-language fan-in
1669	         * downgrades the port to JSON — the slot can carry only one
1670	         * format and JSON is the common denominator.
1671	         *
1672	         * NOTE (issue 318 follow-on): this per-edge classification is
1673	         * the FALLBACK on single-ring slots. For dual-ring slots
1674	         * (issue 312), the consumer's read path uses the per-cell
1675	         * which_ring tag returned by slot_pop_ordered instead. The
1676	         * dual-ring path is what makes intra-Lua $lang_opaque survive
1677	         * a producer that was forced to JSON by a cross-language
1678	         * sibling consumer — each cell carries its own format flag,
1679	         * so the consumer doesn't have to trust a per-edge
1680	         * approximation that lies when the producer's per-call
1681	         * output_native is 0. */
1682	        for (int port = 0; port < b->n_inputs; port++) {
1683	            input_feeders_t f = scan_input_feeders(g, i, port, b->lang);
1684	            b->input_edge_native[port] = (f.n_feeders > 0 &&
1685	                                          f.n_native == f.n_feeders) ? 1 : 0;
1686	        }
1687	    }
1688	    return g;
1689	}
1690	/* }}} */
1691	
1692	/* {{{ graph_destroy() */
1693	void graph_destroy(graph_t *g)
1694	{
1695	    if (!g) return;
1696	    box_t **boxes = atomic_load_explicit(&g->boxes, memory_order_relaxed);
1697	    uint32_t n    = atomic_load_explicit(&g->n_boxes, memory_order_relaxed);
1698	    if (boxes) {
1699	        for (uint32_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
1700	            box_t *b = boxes[i];
1701	            if (!b) continue;
1702	            free(b->inputs);
1703	            free(b->connections);
1704	            free(b->input_slot_ids);
1705	            free(b->input_slot_modes);
1706	            free(b->input_edge_native);
1707	            free(b->output_edge_native);
1708	            free((double *)b->routing.weights);
1709	            /* per-box compile hint pointer arrays (strings inside
1710	             * are arena-owned; only the array itself is heap) */
1711	            free((void *)b->link_libs);
1712	            free((void *)b->headers);
1713	            /* 244 read-box cache + predecessor lists */
1714	            free(b->cached_value);
1715	            if (b->read_predecessor_ids) {
1716	                for (int j = 0; j < b->n_inputs; j++) {
1717	                    free(b->read_predecessor_ids[j]);
1718	                }
1719	                free(b->read_predecessor_ids);
1720	            }
1721	            free(b->n_read_predecessors);
1722	            free(b->read_pred_counter_slot);
1723	            free(b);
1724	        }
1725	        free(boxes);
1726	    }
1727	    /* Free any stale pointer-arrays parked by runtime growth. The
1728	     * box records they pointed to are the same records already
1729	     * freed above (growth never deep-copies records). */
1730	    struct stale_arr *st = g->stale_box_arrs;

693	        if (ends_with(e->d_name, ".json")) n++;
694	    }

883	static int cache_read_box_values(graph_t *g, char **err)
884	{

887	        if (b->kind != BOX_READ) continue;

893	         * value nor path" check below doesn't reject them. */
894	        if (b->external.kind != EXTERNAL_NONE) continue;
895	
896	        if (b->value) {
897	            int n = (int)strlen(b->value);
898	            b->cached_value = malloc((size_t)n + 1);
899	            if (!b->cached_value) { *err = err_fmt("oom"); return -1; }
900	            memcpy(b->cached_value, b->value, (size_t)n);
901	            b->cached_value[n] = '\0';
902	            b->cached_size = n;
903	            continue;
904	        }
905	        if (!b->path) {
906	            /* No value, no path — error surfaces only if a consumer
907	             * actually tries to pull from this box, but flagging at
908	             * load is louder. Future iterations may allow `path`
909	             * inputs that arrive at run time; for now an unconfigured
910	             * read box is a load failure. */
911	            *err = err_fmt("read box '%s' has neither 'value' nor 'path'", b->id);
912	            return -1;
913	        }

915	        /* Resolve `path` relative to the map directory and slurp the

920	        size_t plen = strlen(b->path);

923	        if (b->path[0] == '/') {
924	            memcpy(full, b->path, plen + 1);
925	        } else if (blen > 0) {
926	            memcpy(full, base, blen);
927	            full[blen] = '/';

929	        } else {
930	            memcpy(full, b->path, plen + 1);
931	        }
932

945	            fclose(fp);
946	            return -1;

948	        b->cached_value = malloc((size_t)len + 1);

950	            *err = err_fmt("oom");
951	            fclose(fp);
952	            return -1;
953	        }
954	        size_t got = fread(b->cached_value, 1, (size_t)len, fp);
955	        fclose(fp);
956	        b->cached_value[got] = '\0';
957	        b->cached_size = (int)got;
958	    }

#!/bin/bash
# scripts/run-tests.sh — phase 3 integration tests.
#
# Runs every fixture map under tests/maps/ through `soramech-pool`
# and asserts that the captured outputs match a hardcoded
# expectation per map. The point is to catch regressions
# end-to-end — past the spec interface, past the dispatch action,
# past JSONL writing — rather than via the in-process unit tests.
#
# Per the project convention: scripts run from any directory via a
# hard-coded ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths are
# relative to ${DIR}.

set -u

DIR="/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech"
if [[ $# -ge 1 ]]; then
    DIR="$1"
fi

cd "$DIR"

pass=0
fail=0
failures=()

# {{{ check_map() — run one fixture, verify expected substrings
check_map() {
    local map="$1"
    shift
    local expected=("$@")

    printf "  %-44s " "$map"

    local output
    # Per-map env opt-in: a map may set SORAMECH_TEST_WORKERS to
    # pin worker count for tests that depend on per-worker state
    # (e.g. issue 318's $lang_opaque, which lives in the producer's
    # Lua registry and can only be reconstructed by a consumer on
    # the same worker).
    local workers_env=""
    if [[ -f "$DIR/tests/maps/$map/.test_workers" ]]; then
        workers_env=$(cat "$DIR/tests/maps/$map/.test_workers")
    fi
    if [[ -n "$workers_env" ]]; then
        output=$(SORAMECH_WORKERS="$workers_env" "$DIR/soramech-pool" "$DIR/tests/maps/$map" 2>&1)
    else
        output=$("$DIR/soramech-pool" "$DIR/tests/maps/$map" 2>&1)
    fi
    local rc=$?

    local missing=""
    if [[ $rc -ne 0 ]]; then
        missing="exit=$rc"
    fi
    for e in "${expected[@]}"; do
        if [[ "$output" != *"$e"* ]]; then
            missing+="${missing:+; }missing '$e'"
        fi
    done

    if [[ -z "$missing" ]]; then
        printf "ok\n"
        pass=$((pass + 1))
    else
        printf "FAIL — %s\n" "$missing"
        fail=$((fail + 1))
        failures+=("$map: $missing")
    fi
}
# }}}

# {{{ pipeline_output_check() — additional: the pipeline writes to disk
pipeline_output_check() {
    local file="/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt"
    rm -f "$file"
    "$DIR/soramech-pool" "$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline" > /dev/null 2>&1
    printf "  %-44s " "pipeline write output"
    if [[ -f "$file" ]]; then
        local content
        content=$(cat "$file")
        if [[ "$content" == "11!" ]]; then
            printf "ok\n"
            pass=$((pass + 1))
        else
            printf "FAIL — expected '11!', got '%s'\n" "$content"
            fail=$((fail + 1))
            failures+=("pipeline file: $content")
        fi
    else
        printf "FAIL — output file missing\n"
        fail=$((fail + 1))
        failures+=("pipeline: $file missing")
    fi
}
# }}}

# into compiled/, then runs the artifact from /tmp (i.e. with no
```

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The `inline_encapsulations` outer loop already handled recursion correctly — it iterates up to 1024 times picking up any `BOX_MAP` with a non-NULL `ref` until none remain. Once an outer sub-map gets inlined, its inner BOX_MAP appears as a fresh entry in the parent's flat box list with the right ref, and the next iteration handles it. No code change needed; only a fixture to prove it.
- The most interesting bug today was the dangling `sub_boxes` array. The pointer-array I allocated locally got `free()`d as soon as the records inside were copied into `g->boxes` — but my new output-side splice still needed the original `sub_boxes[i]` indexing to find the ext-consumed write box. The records are still alive (they migrated to the graph), but reading them through the freed *pointer array* is UB and crashed on the first dry run. Moving the `free` after the splice fixed it. The lesson is that "the records are still owned" doesn't mean "every container I held them in is still valid" — separate lifetimes.

The write box already wrote the file and the disk-write/wire-emit pair is independent; only the bytes copied into `out_buf` had to change.

Can you write an issue file to add a third input ring buffer which accepts json but... it's a configuration style json? It should exactly match the pattern of the json on the box. It's placed in the queue the same as all the other inputs, and when that third queue is selected to be popped then instead of running the box function, the thread will re-configure the box with the new input json (which determines the nature and qualities of the box) and then check to see if the inputs are filled now with the new requirements. If so, then it will run the box. If not, then it will quietly exit after re-configuring the box. I'm thinking we'll need to put an atomic spinlock on the entire box that, instead of spinning, will ask the waiting thread to re-add the box to the end of the thread pool queue. When we're done re-configuring the box, the spinlock is removed. It's not quite a spinlock actually... but you get the idea, it's essentially "hey we're not ready yet, put yourself back at the beginning of the queue please"

Wrote `issues/320-box-reconfigure-via-third-input-ring.md`. The shape: a per-box auxiliary inbox carrying box-JSON-shaped reconfigure messages, treated as a scheduling peer to the per-port input rings, gated by a yield-and-requeue barrier instead of a spinlock.

A few design notes worth flagging for your decision (also expanded as open questions in the file):

- **Per-box vs per-port ring placement.** I went with per-box because the message concerns the whole box — but the user-facing phrase "third ring" could mean per-port (mirroring the native/JSON pairing exactly). If per-port, every port could carry config and "which port's config wins?" needs answering. Per-box is cleaner; flag if you'd rather mirror per-port symmetry.
- **Scheduler ordering between value-pops and reconfigure-pops.** Three defensible rules:
  - **Strict FIFO across all four channels** using issue 318a's per-cell ordering tags — most consistent with the "interleave naturally" model.
  - **Reconfigures get priority** — drain them before any fire; every fire runs under the latest config.
  - **Reconfigures get no priority** — values in flight keep their original interpretation under the old config.
  
  Option 1 matches your phrasing best ("placed in the queue the same as all the other inputs"); option 2 is the "configuration is always current" stance; option 3 is "values keep their original interpretation."
- **Yield-and-requeue target end.** You said both "end" and "beginning" in one sentence. End-of-queue is fairer (other tasks get to run before the contended worker retries); beginning is faster recovery. I'd default to end but it's your call.
- **Scope of reconfigurable fields in slice 1.** I proposed "cheap fields (lang/ref/fn/routing/output_capacity) + connections[]; reject changes to id/kind/inputs[] with a precise diagnostic; defer the expensive port-shape changes to a follow-on." Anything missing from that scope?
- **The "not-quite-a-spinlock" name.** I called it the "yield-and-requeue barrier" in the prose. It's a barrier in the sense that it's the gate, but cooperative-with-the-scheduler rather than blocking — your phrasing made me lean away from "lock" entirely. If you have a preferred name, the issue can adopt it.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The synchronization primitive you described is unusual in C runtimes and **interesting**: instead of a thread blocking when it can't make progress, it returns to the scheduler with a "retry me later" hint. This is the same shape Go's goroutine yield uses, and what `async/await` runtimes do when a future returns `Pending`. The cost is one extra trip through the scheduler; the benefit is no busy-wait, no priority inversion, no thread parking. For SoraMech's pool-based dispatch where every fire is a small unit of work, this is genuinely the right primitive — and naming it something other than "lock" (since it isn't one) matters for keeping the mental model honest.
- This issue is the symmetric counterpart to 319: 319 grows the graph (additive — `create_box`, `connect`), 320 mutates what's already there (replacing). Together they cover the full "graph as a living artifact" surface, which is what makes the runtime feel mutable in a coherent way rather than as a pile of escape hatches.
- The "JSON exactly matching the box's own schema" choice means **the box-file parser is doing double duty** — it parses the load-time JSON files AND the runtime reconfigure messages. One parser, one validator, one schema. If you ever change the box JSON shape, both paths get the change for free. That's the same economy of design as your `external` block being a single struct used by both ext-supplied data boxes and ext-consumed write boxes — one mechanism, two destinations.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The per-port placement is conceptually stronger than per-box because it preserves the **single ordering scheme** that already governs value cells: if the producer pushes "value, value, reconfigure, value" onto a port, the consumer sees them in exactly that order. A per-box config inbox would have been a parallel scheduling channel, requiring its own ordering rules to interleave with port pops. Per-port means "one fewer thing to coordinate" — same scheduler, same FIFO, just one extra tag value.
- YARQ being **cooperative with the scheduler** rather than blocking is the move that unlocks per-cell reconfigure interleaving. A traditional lock would have meant "while reconfiguring, every other worker that touches this box stalls a thread"; YARQ means "while reconfiguring, every other worker that touches this box returns to the pool and gets used for other work." The barrier holder doesn't pay a coordination cost; the contended workers each pay one extra scheduler trip. That's a much friendlier accounting for a runtime where thousands of tiny tasks compete for tens of workers.
- The comprehensive-first-slice preference is the right call **because the cross-cutting plumbing IS the work**. Splitting "cheap fields now, port-shape changes later" would mean writing the input-gather → YARQ → reconfigure-apply pipeline twice (once for the easy case, once again with slot-store growth/shrink threaded through). Doing both in one pass means the plumbing is shaped correctly from the start — slot store calls live next to JSON parse calls live next to producer re-resolution calls, all in one function, one mental model.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

1	# Strategem — a contract must fit every implementer, not just the simplest
2	
3	## The pattern
4	
5	When designing a contract that several implementers will satisfy
6	(spec interfaces, abstract types, system protocols), check whether
7	the contract's assumptions hold for *every* class of implementer,
8	not just the cleanest case in front of you. A contract that works
9	for one class and almost-works for another is a contract that
10	forces the awkward class into shims, hacks, or special-cases. The
11	right move is to weaken the contract until it fits everyone
12	honestly.
13	
14	The trap is subtle: the cleanest implementer often comes to mind
15	first when you're designing. C and Bash specs in this project both
16	treat values as bytes — their bridges write to and read from `dst`
17	buffers. The proposed amendment to issue 312 designed the
18	dispatch-side normalisation around this: "dispatch calls the
19	consumer spec's `json_to_native` with a buffer, gets native bytes
20	back, hands them to invoke." Clean, symmetric, byte-oriented.
21	
22	The amendment failed when Lua showed up. Lua's `json_to_native`
23	doesn't write to a buffer — it pushes a value onto the worker's
24	`lua_State` stack. There is no "Lua native byte form" external
25	to the state for dispatch to hand to invoke. And Lua isn't an
26	outlier: every runtime that owns its values (Python, Ruby,
27	JavaScript, anything with a private GC heap) would have the same
28	shape. The amendment assumed buffer orientation; half of all
29	possible future specs don't have buffer orientation; the contract
30	was wrong.
31	
32	## How to apply
33	
34	When sketching a new contract:
35	
36	- List the implementers you can imagine. Not just the ones you
37	  have today — the ones a future user might bring.
38	- For each, ask: does the contract's central abstraction (bytes,
39	  callbacks, state ownership, etc.) actually fit how that
40	  implementer naturally works?
41	- If even one implementer needs a shim — "we'll just say its
42	  buffer is empty," "it'll ignore that half of the signature,"
43	  "we'll define a convention where..." — the contract is doing
44	  half the work and the implementer is doing the other half.
45	  That asymmetry is a smell.
46	- Either weaken the contract so the awkward implementer fits
47	  honestly, or accept that the contract is for a narrower
48	  category (e.g. "buffer-oriented specs only") and design a
49	  separate path for the others.
50	
51	The litmus test: can the most awkward implementer satisfy the
52	contract *without lying*? If lua_json_to_native has to set
53	`*dst_size = 0` and leave dst untouched because Lua doesn't have
54	bytes to write, the signature is forcing it to satisfy a shape
55	that doesn't apply. That's the lie. The dispatch can't actually
56	use the (empty, zero-sized) result. The contract has dead
57	parameters for half its implementers.
58	
59	## Adjacent pattern — the "agnosticism" question
60	
61	When a user asks "is this design agnostic to X?", they're usually
62	asking exactly this question. The answer to "is the system
63	agnostic to runtime statefulness?" is: yes, if and only if the
64	contract doesn't assume statelessness. Buffer-oriented bridges
65	assume statelessness. Stack-protocol bridges accommodate
66	statefulness. Neither is wrong; what's wrong is mixing them and
67	hoping the awkward case will quietly degrade.
68	
69	## Why this happens
70	
71	When the contract is being designed, the people in the room are
72	usually thinking about the implementers in front of them. Future
73	implementers don't get to participate. So the contract drifts
74	toward what works for the present implementers, and the future
75	ones inherit the asymmetry. The discipline is to imagine those
76	future implementers explicitly — to write down their shape and
77	ask if the contract fits, before shipping.
78	
79	This is especially load-bearing for plugin / extension surfaces
80	(spec interfaces, hook points, anything with a `register_X` API).
81	The whole point of those surfaces is that new implementers will
82	appear. If the contract was built for the first two, the third
83	will not fit.
84	
```

{
  "content":"# Strategem — when a worker can't make progress, return the work to the scheduler, not the worker\n\n## The pattern\n\nIn a runtime where many small tasks compete for a small pool of\nworkers, synchronization primitives that *hold workers* (locks,\nspinlocks, parked threads) silently flip the cost model. The\nworker is the scarce resource; the scheduler is the abundant\ncoordinator. When a worker hits a contended boundary and can't\nmake progress, the cooperative move is to **hand the task back\nto the scheduler** — not to camp on the worker until the\nboundary clears.\n\nYARQ — yield-and-requeue, the primitive that protects in-place\nbox mutation in issue 320 — is the project's name for this\npattern in one specific place. The shape is general: any time a\nworker realises \"I can't finish this task right now,\" it should\nre-submit the task to the pool queue and return its body to the\nscheduler for the next ready unit of work.\n\nThe trap is that locks read as \"the right tool\" because they\nwork fine in the textbook setting where threads are heavyweight\nand tasks are large. Spinlock or mutex, every contended worker\neither burns CPU or parks; either way, the worker is committed\nto that task until it can proceed. When tasks are tiny and\nworkers are few, that commitment is expensive — the worker\ncould have done five other things in the time it spent waiting.\n\nSymptoms that suggest the wrong primitive:\n\n- Many short tasks per second, few workers, occasional bursts\n  of contention. The contended workers stall, throughput\n  collapses for the duration of the burst, then recovers.\n- Priority inversion: a low-priority task holds a lock, a\n  high-priority task can't proceed, the scheduler's careful\n  ordering is silently overridden by the lock contract.\n- Workers parked on locks that other parked workers depend on\n  — the deadlock-prevention dance grows around the locks\n  because the locks themselves don't compose.\n\n## How to apply\n\nWhen you reach for a lock to protect shared mutable state:\n\n- Ask: **is the worker the scarce resource, or is the lock\n  contract genuinely needed?** If workers are cheap (one per\n  CPU, OS threads, the system is throughput-bounded by CPU),\n  a lock is fine. If workers are scarce (a fixed-size pool\n  smaller than the task fanout, the system is latency-bounded\n  by scheduler trips), prefer YARQ.\n- Express acquire as a non-blocking CAS that **returns failure\n  instead of waiting**. On failure, the worker re-submits the\n  task to the scheduler (usually at the queue tail — see below)\n  and exits the task body. No spin, no park, no waiting.\n- Release is a plain atomic store. The contended worker's\n  re-submission lands later by virtue of scheduler progress,\n  not because the holder signalled.\n- Pick the requeue end thoughtfully. **Tail** is fairer (other\n  pending work runs first, the contended task doesn't\n  immediately re-collide with the holder, the system as a\n  whole keeps draining). **Head** is faster recovery for one\n  task (it retries soonest) at the cost of unfairness to\n  whatever else is queued. Default to tail; choose head only\n  when latency on this one task dominates.\n- Fold every mutation path that touches the shared state into\n  the same YARQ barrier — not just the path you noticed first.\n  If `connect` and `reconfigure` both mutate a box, they share\n  YARQ. The barrier is \"no concurrent mutator,\" not \"no\n  concurrent reconfigure.\"\n\n## Adjacent pattern — async/await is YARQ at the language level\n\nThe async-await primitive in modern runtimes is the same shape\ngeneralised: a coroutine returns `Pending` instead of blocking,\nthe executor reschedules the coroutine when its waker fires.\nThe worker (the executor thread) is freed for other coroutines\nin the meantime. The pattern's name varies — green threads,\nfibers, futures, tasks — but the core invariant is identical:\n**when a unit of work can't proceed, hand the unit back, not\nthe worker.**\n\nYARQ is the lower-level version: no waker, no future. The\ncontended task just re-submits itself and trusts the scheduler\nto eventually try again. Coarser-grained than async-await, but\nstrictly simpler to implement and reason about — there's no\nwaker chain to keep coherent, no `Poll` state machine, just\n\"try, fail, re-submit.\"\n\n## Why this happens\n\nLock-style primitives carry a hidden assumption: *workers are\ninterchangeable units of capacity, plentiful enough that\nholding one is cheap.* That assumption is right for OS threads\non big servers and wrong for almost every other context — task\npools, async executors, embedded runtimes, the actor model. In\nthe wrong context, locks turn the scheduler's careful work\ndistribution into a coordination bottleneck.\n\nThe strategem is to notice which side of that assumption the\nsystem actually lives on. If the scheduler is the load-bearing\npiece — the thing making the system fast — then synchronization\nshould be **expressed in scheduler vocabulary**: re-submit,\nyield, requeue. Locks express it in thread vocabulary: park,\nspin, wake. Mixing the two means the lock's parked workers are\ninvisible to the scheduler, and the scheduler's careful\nordering is broken by waits the lock owns.\n\n## Related issues\n\n- Issue 320 — the box reconfigure path that introduces YARQ to\n  this project.\n- Issue 319d — `box_add_connection`'s copy-and-publish atomic\n  dance; the comprehensive YARQ-folded design subsumes it\n  under the same barrier.\n- Issue 301 / 304 — the pool runner and dispatch layer whose\n  scheduler-vocabulary YARQ speaks. The fact that the pool\n  already routes tasks by re-submission is what makes YARQ\n  cheap to add — the machinery is there.\n",
  "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/strategems/yarq-return-the-work-not-the-worker.md"
}

1	# 250 — Routing kind: nonlinearity (squash)
2	
3	## Status
4	open · design carried forward from issues 240 / 241 / 242 / 243
5	
6	## Current behavior
7	
8	The routing kinds shipped or queued so far — `plain`, `comparator`,
9	`iterator`, `randomizer` (240), `weighted` (241), `distributor`
10	(242), `multi-band-comparator` (243) — all pick a **branch** and
11	forward the producer's value to the consumer **unchanged**. The
12	schema (`src/001-schema.lua`) and the dispatch picker
13	(`src/012-dispatch.c`) treat the wire payload as opaque on the
14	way out; routing has only ever decided *where* a value goes, never
15	*what* it is.
16	
17	There is no routing kind that **transforms the value** on the way
18	through. A user who wants the producer's output remapped into a
19	new numeric range — for feeding a UI slider, an audio level, a
20	heat-map cell — has to insert a dedicated call box that runs a
21	Lua / C function whose entire job is one arithmetic expression.
22	That's a lot of box for one knob.
23	
24	## Intended behavior
25	
26	A new routing kind, **`nonlinearity`** (working name; "squash"
27	is the alternative — see open questions), maps each numeric value
28	that flows through the box into a bounded output range via a
29	chosen unary function (default: logistic sigmoid). The input is
30	normalised against either:
31	
32	- **`auto`** — the running min and max observed on this wire
33	  during the current run, OR
34	- **`fixed`** — two user-supplied numeric bounds (`min`, `max`).
35	
36	After normalisation the value lands in `[0, 1]` (or `[-1, 1]` for
37	tanh — see open questions), the chosen non-linearity is applied,
38	and the result is forwarded on the box's single output port. The
39	routing kind has exactly one output — fan-out happens the same
40	way every other single-output box's fan-out happens (multiple
41	wires leaving one port).
42	
43	-- to switch between auto and fixed, the user just needs to supply one or two
44	   values - if they supply one, the minimum / maximum is set (the slots in the
45	   editor and json are specified as "min" or "max" so there's no ambiguity about
46	   which is which) if they supply both then it's set to "fixed" mode as specified.
47	   I want there to be only one mode, and auto is the fallback if no fixed values
48	   are specified. C treats NULL as zero, so if we wanted to switch back to auto
49	   after specifying a value then we'd need to have two separate flags on-top of
50	   the min and max value - they basically say "is this a fixed value or is it
51	   an auto value?" - if the flag is set to fixed, then the value won't change if
52	   we receive a higher/lower value. If the flag is unset to auto, then we will
53	   adjust the min/max value depending on the min/max value we've received.
54	
55	-- I don't know the math very well so you'll have to take the lead on this part,
56	   but we need a function that will work equally well without normalization.
57	   The vision I had, which might be more / less useful for AI purposes than some
58	   other kind of function, is essentially an S curve with the minimum and max
59	   set to certain values, and whatever inputs come in will get fairly mid value
60	   unless they're very clearly a "strong" value one way or the other. This is
61	   why 0 is selected as the midpoint usually, I think, so that values close to
62	   mid, or perhaps a fairly even mixture of two values, can be multiplied and
63	   the result will be close to 0. So, maybe we need three - one that has the
64	   midpoint at 0, one that has the midpoint at 1, and one that scales? I'm not
65	   sure, can you picture why I would want such a thing? If so, can you offer any
66	   ideas about how to create intelligent behavior with this structure?
67	
68	-- what if, for the scaling one, we also added a "dampening" effect where each
69	   time the function is run, it reduces the min/max a little toward an equilibrium.
70	   it doesn't necessarily have to be 0 or 1 or whatever, it should just adjust so
71	   that the values become normalized over time. How would we ensure that there's
72	   a decent enough gap between the min and max? How would the input values which
73	   expand the min/max be considered? We'd re-calculate the curve, probably, right?
74	
75	### Schema
76	
77	```json
78	"routing": {
79	  "kind":     "nonlinearity",
80	  "shape":    "sigmoid",        // or "tanh" / "linear" / "softsign"
81	  "mode":     "auto",           // or "fixed"
82	  "min":      0,                // present only when mode == "fixed"
83	  "max":      100,              // present only when mode == "fixed"
84	  "out_range":"unit"            // or "signed" — see open questions
85	}
86	```
87	
88	`mode: "auto"` requires no bounds — the dispatch picker maintains
89	a running min and max in two slot-store cells (issue 302) per
90	nonlinearity box, updated atomically on each fire. `mode:
91	"fixed"` requires both `min` and `max`; schema rejects either
92	missing or `min >= max`.
93	
94	### Branch picker (dispatch layer)
95	
96	There is no branch to pick — the kind always emits on the single
97	output. The dispatch code path differs from the existing
98	routing kinds in that it **mutates the value** rather than
99	**selecting an index**. Pseudocode:
100	
101	```c
102	double x = coerce_to_number(value_in);     // hard-error path on failure
103	
104	double lo, hi;
105	if (mode == AUTO) {
106	    lo = slot_min_load(min_slot);
107	    hi = slot_max_load(max_slot);
108	    slot_min_cas_update(min_slot, x);      // best-effort widen
109	    slot_max_cas_update(max_slot, x);
110	} else {
111	    lo = box->fixed_min;
112	    hi = box->fixed_max;
113	}
114	
115	double t = (hi == lo) ? 0.5 : (x - lo) / (hi - lo);   // bootstrap case
116	
117	double y;
118	switch (shape) {
119	    case SIGMOID:  y = 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-k * (t - 0.5))); break;
120	    case TANH:     y = tanh(k * (t - 0.5));               break;
121	    case LINEAR:   y = t;                                 break;
122	    case SOFTSIGN: y = (t - 0.5) / (1.0 + fabs(t - 0.5)); break;
123	}
124

1	# 315 — Reference-counted compiled-map artifacts
2	
3	## Status
4	open
5	
6	## Current behavior
7	
8	`scripts/soramech-compile.sh` from issue 309 is destructive at the
9	top:
10	
11	```bash
12	rm -rf "$COMPILED"
13	mkdir -p "$COMPILED" "$COMPILED/boxes" "$COMPILED/src" ...
14	```
15	
16	Whatever lived in `<map>/compiled/` before the rebuild is gone. If
17	another process — a long-running runner, a different shell, a
18	sibling tool that opened the artifact yesterday — had pinned to
19	that exact compiled layout (a particular `pool-runner` binary, a
20	particular `spec.so` ABI, a particular set of pre-compiled C
21	boxes), the rebuild yanks the rug. The holder either crashes,
22	silently retains stale `dlopen` handles, or starts reading new
23	files mid-flight.
24	
25	This is fine in single-user development. It stops being fine the
26	moment a SoraMech artifact is the kind of thing other programs
27	hold onto across time.
28	
29	## Intended behavior
30	
31	A compiled artifact carries its own reference count. Other
32	programs that depend on a particular build of a map are expected
33	to *acquire* a reference on startup and *release* it on shutdown.
34	When `soramech-compile` is asked to rebuild a map that has any
35	live references, it does NOT clobber the existing directory.
36	Instead it builds a sibling directory next door, leaving the
37	referenced one untouched until its holders are done with it.
38	
39	The reference count is **expected to be unreliable**. A crashing
40	holder doesn't get the chance to release; an SSH session that
41	drops doesn't either. The design accepts that staleness is the
42	common case, not the exception — every reference entry carries
43	enough metadata to be independently validated and (eventually)
44	reaped. The reference count is a hint and a courtesy, not a
45	guarantee.
46	
47	This is conceptually a copy-on-write filesystem for compiled
48	artifacts: writes (rebuilds) fork the universe when readers
49	exist; readers can keep reading the version they pinned to;
50	generations get garbage-collected when nothing observable still
51	points at them.
52	
53	## Concept
54	
55	A compiled directory contains a `.refs` file (hidden, dot-prefixed
56	so it doesn't clutter directory listings). It's append-only by
57	design — concurrent acquires never need to take a lock; concurrent
58	releases write a separate marker without rewriting the file.
59	
60	Each reference has three parts:
61	
62	1. **A date.** When the reference was acquired. Lets a janitor
63	   prune references older than some threshold even if their back
64	   pointer can't be validated.
65	2. **A back-pointer.** The identity of the holder — enough
66	   information that an outside observer can ask "is this holder
67	   still alive, and does it still want this reference?" without
68	   trusting the count alone. Concrete candidates:
69	   - process PID + start time (PID alone is not enough; PIDs
70	     recycle)
71	   - a path to a marker file the holder maintains (presence of
72	     the marker = the holder is still live and aware of the
73	     ref)
74	   - some combination (PID + a marker path)
75	3. **An opaque ref id.** A short string the holder can use later
76	   to identify *its* reference when it wants to release, so it
77	   doesn't accidentally release someone else's.
78	
79	A release writes an entry referencing the original acquire id.
80	Net live refs = acquires whose id isn't in the release set.
81	
82	## Reference file format
83	
84	A line-oriented log. Each line is one of two record types:
85	
86	```
87	acquire <id> <iso8601-date> <pid> <pid-start-time-ticks> <marker-path>
88	release <id> <iso8601-date>
89	```
90	
91	Append-only. Holders open with `O_APPEND` and write a single line
92	per operation. Atomic on POSIX as long as the line fits in
93	`PIPE_BUF` (4 KB on Linux) — well within budget for these short
94	records.
95	
96	Reading: tail through the file, build a set of acquire ids,
97	subtract release ids; remaining ids are nominally live. Then
98	validate each survivor's back pointer.
99	
100	A `.refs.lock` file is used only for compaction (rewriting the
101	log to drop matched acquire/release pairs) and for the
102	fork-to-sibling decision during compile. Steady-state reads /
103	writes don't lock.
104	
105	## Acquire / release API
106	
107	A small helper utility, probably a shell script for portability
108	since holders are written in many languages:
109	
110	```
111	scripts/soramech-ref.sh acquire <compiled-dir> [--id <id>] [--marker <path>]
112	scripts/soramech-ref.sh release <compiled-dir> --id <id>
113	scripts/soramech-ref.sh list    <compiled-dir>          # JSON, including staleness verdicts
114	scripts/soramech-ref.sh reap    <compiled-dir>          # compact + drop dead refs
115	```
116	
117	`acquire` prints the assigned id to stdout; the holder is
118	responsible for plumbing it to wherever it'll need to call
119	release. If no `--id` was supplied, the script generates one
120	(timestamp + random suffix).
121	
122	`list` walks the log and prints a JSON array of `{id, date,
123	holder, valid}` entries. Validation reads the back pointer's
124	liveness signal (PID exists & start-time matches, or marker file
125	exists).
126	
127	`reap` is destructive — it rewrites the log to remove entries
128	whose holders failed validation. Run periodically; never
129	automatically as part of compile (compile must not destroy state
130	its caller might care about).
131	
132	## Compile-time fork logic
133	
134	`soramech-compile.sh` consults `<map>/compiled/.refs` (and any
135	sibling generation directories' `.refs` files) before deciding
136	where to write:
137	
138	1. If `<map>/compiled/` doesn't exist → build there, fresh.
139	2. If it exists but has zero live references → build there, after
140	   `rm -rf`. Same destructive behavior as today.
141	3. If it exists with one or more live references → pick a sibling
142	   directory name (see below) and build there. The original
143	   `compiled/` stays intact.
144	
145	After a fork-build, the caller has a new directory; `manifest.json`
146	in the new directory records the fork relationship (`forked_from`
147	field pointing at the previous generation's path).
148	
149	### Sibling directory naming
150	
151	Two reasonable schemes; pick whichever the implementer prefers:
152	
153	- **Generation index:** `compiled.0`, `compiled.1`, `compiled.2`...
154	  Always pick `compiled.N` where N is one more than the highest
155	  existing generation. Easy to grep for; index order = build
156	  order.
157	- **Timestamp suffix:** `compiled.2026-05-19T2347` (ISO 8601
158	  compact). Order-preserving lexicographically; the name itself
159	  tells the operator when it was built.
160	
161	Whichever wins, the script should also leave a `compiled` symlink
162	pointing at the newest generation, so callers who want "the
163	latest" don't have to enumerate.
164	
165	## Stale reference handling
166	
167	A reference is stale if any of the following hold:
168	
169	- The PID no longer exists on the system.
170	- The PID exists but its start time (`/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22)
171	  doesn't match the recorded value — different process, recycled
172	  PID.
173	- The marker file path was supplied at acquire and is now
174	  missing.
175	
176	Stale refs are *tolerated*: compile-time fork still triggers if
177	ANY ref exists, stale or otherwise — the caller can run
178	`soramech-ref.sh reap` first if they want to consolidate. The
179	philosophy is: the artifact directory belongs to its readers
180	until proven otherwise, and the cost of an extra build dir is
181	trivial compared to the cost of a use-after-rebuild crash.
182	
183	## Gitignore considerations
184	
185	Every generation (`compiled/`, `compiled.0/`, `compiled.1/`,
186	`compiled.2026-05-19T2347/`, the `compiled` symlink) is a derived
187	artifact and should never be tracked. The existing
188	`.gitignore` line `tests/maps/*/compiled/` covers the canonical
189	name; add a sibling pattern to cover generations:
190	
191	```
192	tests/maps/*/compiled/
193	tests/maps/*/compiled.*/
194	```
195	
196	The `.refs` file itself lives *inside* the compiled directory,
197	so it inherits the same gitignore.
198	
199	## Suggested implementation steps
200	
201	1. Pick the back-pointer format. Recommend PID + start time +
202	   optional marker path. Document the choice with a comment at
203	   the top of the ref helper.
204	2. Write `scripts/soramech-ref.sh` with `acquire`, `release`,
205	   `list`, `reap`. Append-only writes for the first two, log
206	   rewrite under `.refs.lock` for the last.
207	3. Add a small `tests/315-refs-test.sh` that exercises:
208	   acquire → list (1 entry, valid) → release → list (0 valid) →
209	   acquire → kill the holder process → list (1 entry, stale) →
210	   reap → list (0).
211	4. Teach `soramech-compile.sh` to read `.refs` and pick the
212	   target directory. Implement the sibling-naming scheme.
213	   `compiled` becomes a symlink to the newest generation.
214	5. Add a `forked_from` field to `manifest.json` when forking.
215	6. Update `.gitignore` for the new generation pattern.
216	7. Integration check in `scripts/run-tests.sh`: compile the
217	   pipeline fixture twice — second time with a live `acquire` —
218	   assert a sibling generation was created and the original
219	   pinned generation still runs unchanged.
220	
221	## Open questions
222	
223	- Should the runner (`soramech-pool`) itself acquire a reference
224	  when it opens a compiled directory? On the one hand, yes —
225	  it's the canonical case the system protects against. On the
226	  other, soramech-pool runs are usually short-lived and the
227	  acquire/release overhead per run is unwelcome. Possible
228	  compromise: only acquire if pool runs longer than N seconds.
229	- How does a fork chain end? If `compiled.5` is built while
230	  `compiled.4` had live refs but `compiled.4`'s refs are now all
231	  stale (caller never released, then died), do we ever prune
232	  `compiled.4`? Probably yes, via `soramech-ref.sh reap-all
233	  <map>` which walks every generation and drops the ones whose
234	  refs all validate as dead.
235	- Is the `.refs` log itself something that should be versioned
236	  (`.refs.v1`)? If we ever change the line format, in-flight
237	  holders won't know how to read it. Versioning the filename
238	  avoids the problem.
239	- Does the editor (`maps/<x>/` user-facing) want the same
240	  mechanism? Probably yes eventually, but out of scope for this
241	  issue — start with `compiled/` artifacts only.
242	
243	## Relevant files
244	
245	- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — issue 309's compile pipeline,
246	  modified here to fork on live references
247	- `scripts/soramech-ref.sh` — new helper for acquire / release /
248	  list / reap
249	- `tests/315-refs-test.sh` — new
250	- `.gitignore` — extended pattern for generation directories
251	- `scripts/run-tests.sh` — new integration check
252	- `issues/309-build-system.md` — parent issue; references this
253	  one's fork behavior
254	
255	## Notes (philosophy)
256	
257	The unreliability is a feature, not a bug. A reliable reference
258	count would require a kernel-level mechanism (file locks held
259	for the lifetime of the holder), and that's a tower of
260	operational complexity for marginal value. By accepting that
261	holders sometimes lie and sometimes vanish, we get a system
262	that's robust to crashes, network drops, and SIGKILL — at the
263	cost of needing a "reap" pass to catch up with reality
264	occasionally. The back pointer is what makes that catch-up
265	possible: it's the bridge between what the log claims and what
266	the world actually shows.
267	
268	A reference is a wish, not a contract. The compile pipeline
269	honors wishes by default and only stops honoring them when
270	nothing in the world supports the wish anymore. That's how
271	respectful software treats its peers.
272

Reading 250 now and picking the educational threads. Three substantive math/design questions the user couldn't answer; four they answered well. Let me address the open ones, then move to 315.

---

## Educational notes for 250

### Why an S-curve with a midpoint? (the math vision)

Your intuition is exactly right and exactly why neural networks use sigmoid/tanh as activation functions. Here's the underlying mechanism:

A sigmoid acts as a **soft decision boundary**. Values near the midpoint say "I have no opinion." Values far from the midpoint say "I'm confident in this direction." The shape captures the difference between *uncertainty* and *commitment* in a single function — and it does it smoothly so the gradient is continuous (which matters when you compose many of them).

When you **multiply two midpoint-0 outputs together**, you get a behavior that's structurally identical to **soft AND**:
- `0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81` (both strong positive → strong positive)
- `0.9 × -0.9 = -0.81` (disagreement → strong negative)
- `0.1 × 0.9 = 0.09` (one uncertain → uncertain)
- `0.05 × 0.05 = 0.0025` (both uncertain → very uncertain)

This is the **noise-rejection** behavior you sensed. Weak evidence doesn't accumulate into strong conclusions, because uncertainty multiplied by uncertainty stays uncertain. Strong evidence reinforces because confidence × confidence stays confident. Two boxes wired into a multiply box become a soft logic gate; chain them and you have a network of weighted votes that converges on a decision.

So your three variants map cleanly:

- **Midpoint at 0** (tanh-style, output `[-1, 1]`) — for "agree/disagree/abstain" semantics. Multiplication composes like soft AND with sign-tracking. **Best for decision-making agents** where signals have a polarity.
- **Midpoint at 0.5** (sigmoid-style, output `[0, 1]`) — for "probability/confidence" semantics. Multiplication composes like a probabilistic conjunction (assuming independence). **Best for evidence-accumulation pipelines** where everything is a likelihood.
- **No midpoint, just scaling** (linear, output `[0, 1]`) — for "calibrate this range to that range" with no decision content. **Best when you're just remapping a sensor reading** to a UI slider's range.

### How do you build intelligent behavior with this?

The mechanism is **composition**. Wire many nonlinearity boxes together, each looking at different inputs, each with its own bounds and steepness. The output of each is a confident "yes/no/abstain." Combine those outputs through multiplication (soft AND), addition followed by another nonlinearity (soft OR with re-thresholding), or weighted sums followed by a nonlinearity (the perceptron — the building block of deep learning).

An RL-style agent might use:
- Sensor box → nonlinearity (raw → confidence)
- Two confidences → multiply (soft AND)
- Many such AND-ed signals → weighted sum → another nonlinearity (decision threshold)
- Decision threshold → comparator routing → action

The reason this gets called "intelligent" is that the network of soft thresholds learns to ignore irrelevant signal combinations (they multiply to near-zero) and amplify relevant ones (they multiply to near-one), without anyone hand-coding which combinations matter.

**One question back to you**: are you building toward something more like a **neural-net-style perceptron lattice** (many sigmoids feeding weighted sums feeding more sigmoids), or more like a **bayesian/probabilistic pipeline** (sigmoids producing confidences that get conjuncted/disjuncted)? The choice changes what default shape / midpoint you'd want, because the two paradigms have different multiplication semantics.

### The dampening / equilibrium idea

This is a real technique — it's called **exponential moving average** of the bounds. Concretely:

```c
// every fire, decay both bounds slightly toward the midpoint
double mid = (min + max) / 2.0;
min = α * min + (1 - α) * mid;     // 0 < α < 1, e.g. α = 0.99
max = α * max + (1 - α) * mid;

// then if the new value extends the range, snap to it
if (x < min) min = x;
if (x > max) max = x;
```

Per-fire decay rate of `1 - α = 0.01` means the bounds halve their distance from the midpoint roughly every 70 fires. So an outlier from 1000 fires ago has decayed to ~0 influence by now, but a recent outlier still counts.

**Your minimum-gap question**: enforce it as a floor on `max - min`. If decay would bring them within `ε`, freeze decay until new values widen them. Or, equivalently: only decay when `max - min > 2ε`, so the gap never falls below `2ε`.

**Your re-calculation question**: yes, the curve gets re-computed every fire — but it's just `t = (x - min) / (max - min)`, three operations. Free. No precomputation needed.

**One question back to you**: do you want decay to be **symmetric** (both bounds pulled toward the midpoint equally) or **asymmetric** (the bound furthest from the midpoint decays faster, so a single outlier on one side decays quickly while the other side stays stable)? Asymmetric tends to feel more like "settling" because outliers don't bias the midpoint after they're gone.

### The midpoint-branch idea (your line 133-136)

Yes, this is a real and useful pattern — but I'd argue it's a **separate routing kind**, not a feature of nonlinearity. What you're describing is roughly: "comparator-with-magnitude" — split into above/below branches AND carry the magnitude through. Pros: captures direction+strength in one box, matches RL agent vocabulary. Cons: blends two concerns (which branch + transformation) and couples them.

The composition path is already clean: wire your nonlinearity to a downstream comparator. The nonlinearity gives the magnitude on the wire; the comparator splits the branches based on its midpoint. Two boxes, separate concerns, fully composable.

If you want it as one box, file it as a new kind — `directional-magnitude` or similar — rather than extending nonlinearity. Same reasoning as why the issue is for "value-transforming routing" specifically: keep each kind's job small and composable.

### The out-of-range "scaling value" idea (your line 298-301)

What you're describing sounds like **elastic bounds**: the user-supplied `min` / `max` are *initial estimates*, not hard limits. When a value exceeds them, the bounds widen to include it (same as `auto`), the curve re-computes, and the value gets normalized to its new position. No clamping, no erasure — the bounds just stretch.

This collapses cleanly into your fixed/auto-flag design:
- Both flags set (`fixed_min` AND `fixed_max`) → fixed mode, sigmoid saturates naturally on out-of-range (linear/softsign error out).
- Neither flag set → pure auto, bounds track the data.
- **One flag set** → asymmetric mode: the fixed side is a hard limit, the unset side tracks the data. Out-of-range on the fixed side is a hard error; out-of-range on the auto side just widens.

That last case is genuinely useful: "I know my values are always positive (fixed_min = 0), but I don't know how big they get (auto max)." Worth surfacing as a deliberate design point rather than an emergent property.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The reason sigmoid keeps showing up across so many different domains — neural networks, logistic regression, biological neuron models, dose-response curves in pharmacology, demand curves in economics — is that it's the simplest function that captures the abstract phenomenon of "smooth transition between two regimes." Anywhere you have soft thresholds, sigmoid is the natural fit.
- Your "AND of two sigmoids = soft AND" insight is essentially the discovery the perceptron paper (Rosenblatt, 1958) was built on. Deep learning is layers of weighted sums followed by nonlinearities. Three boxes of yours, properly wired, are one neuron. Many such triples wired into a lattice are a neural network.
- The fact that you arrived at "elastic bounds with a fixed/auto flag per side" without knowing the math is a sign the design's grain is correct — when the right primitive falls out of the requirements independently of the theory, you can usually trust the primitive.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`
