{
  "content":"#!/bin/bash\n# scripts/soramech-ref.sh — reference-counted compiled-artifact pins.\n#\n# What it does, in CEO terms: gives other programs a way to say\n# \"I'm using this compiled SoraMech artifact right now, don't\n# clobber it.\" Holders acquire a reference at startup, release at\n# shutdown, and the compile pipeline (scripts/soramech-compile.sh)\n# checks the count before rebuilding — if anyone is holding,\n# rebuild lands in a sibling directory instead of overwriting.\n#\n# The mechanism is a single dot-file (`.refs`) inside the compiled\n# directory:\n#\n#   acquire <id> <iso8601-date> <pid> <pid-start-time-ticks> <marker>\n#   release <id> <iso8601-date>\n#\n# Append-only writes are atomic on POSIX as long as the line fits\n# in PIPE_BUF (4 KB on Linux); these lines are well under that.\n# So no lock is needed for steady-state acquire / release — only\n# `reap` (which rewrites the log to drop dead entries) takes a\n# lock, via .refs.lock.\n#\n# References are *expected to be unreliable*: a crashing holder\n# never gets to release. The back pointer (PID + start-time-ticks\n# + optional marker path) lets `list` and `reap` independently\n# verify whether a recorded acquire is still meaningful.\n#\n# Run as:\n#   scripts/soramech-ref.sh acquire <compiled-dir> [--id <id>] [--marker <path>]\n#   scripts/soramech-ref.sh release <compiled-dir> --id <id>\n#   scripts/soramech-ref.sh list    <compiled-dir>          # JSON\n#   scripts/soramech-ref.sh count   <compiled-dir>          # live count, integer\n#   scripts/soramech-ref.sh reap    <compiled-dir>          # compact + drop dead\n#\n# Convention: scripts run from any directory via a hard-coded\n# ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths inside the\n# script are absolute against ${DIR} or against the per-call\n# compiled-dir argument.\n\nset -u\n\n# {{{ defaults\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nACTION=\"\"\nTARGET=\"\"\nID=\"\"\nMARKER=\"-\"\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ argv parse — action first, target second, then --flags\nif [[ $# -lt 2 ]]; then\n    echo \"usage: soramech-ref.sh <acquire|release|list|count|reap> <compiled-dir> [--id <id>] [--marker <path>] [--dir <project-root>]\" >&2\n    exit 2\nfi\nACTION=\"$1\"\nTARGET=\"$2\"\nshift 2\nwhile [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do\n    case \"$1\" in\n        --id)     ID=\"$2\";     shift 2 ;;\n        --marker) MARKER=\"$2\"; shift 2 ;;\n        --dir)    DIR=\"$2\";    shift 2 ;;\n        *)\n            echo \"soramech-ref: unexpected argument '$1'\" >&2\n            exit 2\n            ;;\n    esac\ndone\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ sanity-check the target directory\nif [[ ! -d \"$TARGET\" ]]; then\n    echo \"soramech-ref: not a directory: $TARGET\" >&2\n    exit 1\nfi\nTARGET=$(cd \"$TARGET\" && pwd)\nREFS_FILE=\"$TARGET/.refs\"\nLOCK_FILE=\"$TARGET/.refs.lock\"\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ pid_starttime — read /proc/<pid>/stat field 22 (start time in jiffies)\n# stat field 2 (comm) is parenthesized and may contain spaces, so we\n# strip up to and including the closing paren before counting. After\n# the paren, field 22 overall becomes the 20th field.\npid_starttime() {\n    local pid=\"$1\"\n    if [[ ! -r \"/proc/$pid/stat\" ]]; then return 1; fi\n    local raw\n    raw=$(cat \"/proc/$pid/stat\" 2>/dev/null) || return 1\n    local after_comm=\"${raw#*) }\"\n    echo \"$after_comm\" | awk '{print $20}'\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ gen_id — timestamp + random suffix, unique enough for this purpose\ngen_id() {\n    local ts\n    ts=$(date +%s)\n    local rand\n    rand=$(head -c 4 /dev/urandom | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \\n')\n    echo \"${ts}-${rand}\"\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ is_alive — true iff the recorded back pointer still validates\n# A reference is alive when:\n#   - the PID exists, AND\n#   - the PID's current start time matches the recorded one (so we\n#     don't confuse a recycled PID for the original holder), AND\n#   - if a marker path was supplied at acquire, the marker file\n#     still exists.\n# Any failure means stale.\nis_alive() {\n    local pid=\"$1\"\n    local recorded_start=\"$2\"\n    local marker=\"$3\"\n    if [[ ! -d \"/proc/$pid\" ]]; then return 1; fi\n    local current_start\n    current_start=$(pid_starttime \"$pid\") || return 1\n    if [[ \"$current_start\" != \"$recorded_start\" ]]; then return 1; fi\n    if [[ \"$marker\" != \"-\" ]] && [[ ! -e \"$marker\" ]]; then return 1; fi\n    return 0\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ scan_refs — emit one line per live id: \"<id> <date> <pid> <start> <marker>\"\n# Walks the log once, accumulates acquires, subtracts releases, prints\n# the remaining acquire records. The id-set is in a temp file rather\n# than a bash assoc array so the script stays portable across older\n# bash versions; the log is small enough that an O(n) scan is fine.\nscan_refs() {\n    if [[ ! -f \"$REFS_FILE\" ]]; then return 0; fi\n    local tmp_acq\n    tmp_acq=$(mktemp)\n    local tmp_rel\n    tmp_rel=$(mktemp)\n    while IFS= read -r line; do\n        case \"$line\" in\n            \"acquire \"*) echo \"$line\" >> \"$tmp_acq\" ;;\n            \"release \"*)\n                local rid\n                rid=$(echo \"$line\" | awk '{print $2}')\n                echo \"$rid\" >> \"$tmp_rel\"\n                ;;\n        esac\n    done < \"$REFS_FILE\"\n    # Print only acquires whose id is not present in the release set.\n    while IFS= read -r aline; do\n        local aid\n        aid=$(echo \"$aline\" | awk '{print $2}')\n        if ! grep -qFx \"$aid\" \"$tmp_rel\" 2>/dev/null; then\n            local rest\n            rest=$(echo \"$aline\" | cut -d' ' -f2-)\n            echo \"$rest\"\n        fi\n    done < \"$tmp_acq\"\n    rm -f \"$tmp_acq\" \"$tmp_rel\"\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ do_acquire — append one acquire record, print the assigned id\ndo_acquire() {\n    if [[ -z \"$ID\" ]]; then\n        ID=$(gen_id)\n    fi\n    local date\n    date=$(date -Iseconds)\n    local pid=\"$$\"\n    # The script's own PID isn't useful as a back pointer — the\n    # *holder* process is whoever invoked us. Bash makes the parent\n    # PID available via PPID, which is the right anchor.\n    pid=\"$PPID\"\n    local start\n    start=$(pid_starttime \"$pid\")\n    if [[ -z \"$start\" ]]; then\n        echo \"soramech-ref: cannot read /proc/$pid/stat (caller's start time)\" >&2\n        exit 1\n    fi\n    # O_APPEND on POSIX makes the write atomic up to PIPE_BUF.\n    printf 'acquire %s %s %s %s %s\\n' \"$ID\" \"$date\" \"$pid\" \"$start\" \"$MARKER\" >> \"$REFS_FILE\"\n    echo \"$ID\"\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ do_release — append one release record\ndo_release() {\n    if [[ -z \"$ID\" ]]; then\n        echo \"soramech-ref: release requires --id <id>\" >&2\n        exit 2\n    fi\n    local date\n    date=$(date -Iseconds)\n    printf 'release %s %s\\n' \"$ID\" \"$date\" >> \"$REFS_FILE\"\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ do_list — JSON array of {id, date, pid, start_ticks, marker, valid}\ndo_list() {\n    echo \"[\"\n    local first=1\n    while IFS=' ' read -r id date pid start marker; do\n        if [[ -z \"$id\" ]]; then continue; fi\n        local valid=\"true\"\n        if ! is_alive \"$pid\" \"$start\" \"$marker\"; then\n            valid=\"false\"\n        fi\n        local comma=\",\"\n        if [[ $first -eq 1 ]]; then\n            comma=\"\"\n            first=0\n        fi\n        printf '%s\\n  {\"id\":\"%s\",\"date\":\"%s\",\"pid\":%s,\"start_ticks\":%s,\"marker\":\"%s\",\"valid\":%s}' \\\n            \"$comma\" \"$id\" \"$date\" \"$pid\" \"$start\" \"$marker\" \"$valid\"\n    done < <(scan_refs)\n    echo\n    echo \"]\"\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ do_count — number of live (un-released, validated) references\n# Used by the compile script to decide whether to fork. Prints a single\n# integer so the caller can compare without parsing JSON.\ndo_count() {\n    local n=0\n    while IFS=' ' read -r id date pid start marker; do\n        if [[ -z \"$id\" ]]; then continue; fi\n        if is_alive \"$pid\" \"$start\" \"$marker\"; then\n            n=$((n + 1))\n        fi\n    done < <(scan_refs)\n    echo \"$n\"\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ do_reap — rewrite the log, dropping released and dead entries\n# Takes .refs.lock for the duration so a concurrent acquire / release\n# doesn't get spliced into a half-rewritten log. Uses mkdir as the\n# portable atomic test-and-set (no flock dependency).\ndo_reap() {\n    local i=0\n    while ! mkdir \"$LOCK_FILE\" 2>/dev/null; do\n        i=$((i + 1))\n        if [[ $i -gt 100 ]]; then\n            echo \"soramech-ref: could not acquire $LOCK_FILE after 100 tries\" >&2\n            exit 1\n        fi\n        sleep 0.05\n    done\n    trap 'rmdir \"$LOCK_FILE\" 2>/dev/null' EXIT\n    local tmp\n    tmp=$(mktemp)\n    while IFS=' ' read -r id date pid start marker; do\n        if [[ -z \"$id\" ]]; then continue; fi\n        if is_alive \"$pid\" \"$start\" \"$marker\"; then\n            printf 'acquire %s %s %s %s %s\\n' \"$id\" \"$date\" \"$pid\" \"$start\" \"$marker\" >> \"$tmp\"\n        fi\n    done < <(scan_refs)\n    if [[ -s \"$tmp\" ]]; then\n        mv \"$tmp\" \"$REFS_FILE\"\n    else\n        rm -f \"$REFS_FILE\" \"$tmp\"\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ dispatch\ncase \"$ACTION\" in\n    acquire) do_acquire ;;\n    release) do_release ;;\n    list)    do_list    ;;\n    count)   do_count   ;;\n    reap)    do_reap    ;;\n    *)\n        echo \"soramech-ref: unknown action '$ACTION'\" >&2\n        exit 2\n        ;;\nesac\n# }}}\n",
  "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/scripts/soramech-ref.sh"
}
```

## Quick followups on 250

**Three variants by name, not by mathematician's jargon.** Yes, this is the right move — and it collapses two of your fields into one. Instead of `shape: sigmoid|tanh|linear` plus a separate `out_range: unit|signed`, just have `shape` carry an intent-named value:

- `shape: "decision"` → tanh under the hood, midpoint 0, output `[-1, 1]`. UI tooltip: "Soft + / − with clear neutral. Compose by multiplication when signals agree."
- `shape: "confidence"` → sigmoid under the hood, midpoint 0.5, output `[0, 1]`. UI tooltip: "Soft yes / no with uncertainty. Compose probabilistically."
- `shape: "calibration"` → linear remap, no midpoint, output `[0, 1]`. UI tooltip: "Pure range conversion, no curve. Use when you just want to rescale a sensor reading."

Three picks, three clear meanings. The user never has to know what tanh is.

**Symmetric vs asymmetric decay — your reframe is elegant and self-deciding.** Presence of a user-supplied midpoint IS the mode switch:
- Midpoint supplied → asymmetric (the midpoint anchors; bounds drift toward it).
- Midpoint absent → symmetric (the midpoint follows the data; both bounds drift toward each other).

No separate flag needed. The field's presence carries the meaning.

**Multi-band-comparator extension (+ button, absolute/percentage rows) belongs in 243, not 250.** The "+ button to add tiers" is a generalization of the multi-band-comparator UI, and the synced absolute/percentage rows are a UI convenience that works against any range — comparator OR nonlinearity OR anything else with bounds. If you want, I can write an update note onto 243 sketching it. The auto-min/max-tracking primitive that the percentage row reads from is the same primitive nonlinearity uses for `auto` mode — there's a small architectural insight there about factoring "tracked range" as a shared capability.

**Clamping as "certainty threshold" — yes, brilliant.** This reframes the user's `min`/`max` from "where the curve starts to saturate" into "the threshold past which I'm certain." That maps cleanly per variant:
- `confidence`: `input > max` → output = 1.0 (fully confident yes); `input < min` → output = 0.0 (fully confident no). Clamp away.
- `decision`: `input > max` → output = +1.0; `input < min` → output = −1.0. Clamp away.
- `calibration`: don't clamp (it's a remap, not a decision). Out-of-range values either extrapolate linearly or hard-error per your preference.

So clamping is a **per-variant default** rather than a separate toggle. Confidence and decision variants clamp; calibration doesn't.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The "auto-tracked range" primitive that nonlinearity's auto mode introduces is the kind of thing worth promoting to a first-class concept eventually. The multi-band-comparator's percentage row wants it; a histogram visualization box would want it; a normalization box (if you ever build one) wants it. Right now it lives inside nonlinearity, but once two boxes want the same thing, it earns its own ticket. Watch for that.
- Your reframe of "clamp = certainty threshold" is the kind of move that makes APIs feel natural. The user was probably going to clamp anyway because "values past my limits are obvious extremes"; by naming what they're already doing, the system gets a primitive that matches intuition without anyone having to memorize it.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

  "new_string":"COMPILED_BASE=\"$MAP/compiled\"\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ pick_target_dir — fork-to-sibling if the base has live references\n# Issue 315: a compiled directory carries a `.refs` log; other\n# programs may have pinned the artifact while it's still in use.\n# Rebuilding on top of a pinned directory would yank the rug out\n# from under those holders (dlopen handles go stale, files change\n# mid-flight). If anything is holding a reference, we build into a\n# sibling directory (`compiled.1`, `compiled.2`, …) and leave the\n# original alone.\n#\n# If the base doesn't exist → build there fresh.\n# If the base exists with zero live refs → wipe and rebuild there\n#   (same destructive shape as before — no holders, nothing to\n#   protect).\n# If the base exists with one or more live refs → pick the next\n#   `compiled.N` sibling and build there. FORKED_FROM is set so\n#   the manifest records the lineage.\npick_target_dir() {\n    if [[ ! -d \"$COMPILED_BASE\" ]]; then\n        COMPILED=\"$COMPILED_BASE\"\n        FORKED_FROM=\"\"\n        return\n    fi\n    local live=0\n    if [[ -x \"$DIR/scripts/soramech-ref.sh\" ]] && [[ -f \"$COMPILED_BASE/.refs\" ]]; then\n        live=$(\"$DIR/scripts/soramech-ref.sh\" count \"$COMPILED_BASE\" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)\n    fi\n    if [[ \"$live\" -eq 0 ]]; then\n        COMPILED=\"$COMPILED_BASE\"\n        FORKED_FROM=\"\"\n        rm -rf \"$COMPILED\"\n        return\n    fi\n    # Find the highest existing compiled.N and add 1. shopt nullglob\n    # so the glob expands to nothing when no siblings exist yet.\n    local highest=0\n    shopt -s nullglob\n    local sibling\n    for sibling in \"$MAP\"/compiled.*; do\n        local base\n        base=$(basename \"$sibling\")\n        local n=\"${base#compiled.}\"\n        if [[ \"$n\" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then\n            if [[ \"$n\" -gt \"$highest\" ]]; then highest=$n; fi\n        fi\n    done\n    shopt -u nullglob\n    local next=$((highest + 1))\n    COMPILED=\"$MAP/compiled.$next\"\n    FORKED_FROM=\"$COMPILED_BASE\"\n    echo \"soramech-compile: $live live reference(s) on $COMPILED_BASE — forking to $COMPILED\"\n}\npick_target_dir\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ box_field — pull a top-level string field from a box JSON file",

{
  "content":"#!/bin/bash\n# tests/315-refs-test.sh — unit-style tests for scripts/soramech-ref.sh.\n#\n# What it does, in CEO terms: exercises the acquire / release / list /\n# count / reap commands of the reference helper through every\n# meaningful state transition, asserting the right number of live\n# references at each step. The test creates a private temp directory\n# per scenario, runs the helper against it, and reports per-scenario\n# pass / fail.\n#\n# Run as:\n#   tests/315-refs-test.sh\n#   tests/315-refs-test.sh --dir <project-root>\n#\n# Convention: hard-coded ${DIR} with --dir override; everything\n# relative to ${DIR}.\n\nset -u\n\n# {{{ defaults\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nif [[ $# -ge 1 ]] && [[ \"$1\" == \"--dir\" ]]; then\n    DIR=\"$2\"\nfi\nREF=\"$DIR/scripts/soramech-ref.sh\"\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ counters\npass=0\nfail=0\nfailures=()\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ assert_count — soramech-ref.sh count <dir> should equal $expected\nassert_count() {\n    local label=\"$1\"\n    local target=\"$2\"\n    local expected=\"$3\"\n    local got\n    got=$(\"$REF\" count \"$target\")\n    if [[ \"$got\" == \"$expected\" ]]; then\n        printf \"  %-44s ok\\n\" \"$label\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"  %-44s FAIL — expected %s, got %s\\n\" \"$label\" \"$expected\" \"$got\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"$label: expected $expected, got $got\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ scenario_basic — acquire, list, release, count\nscenario_basic() {\n    local tmp\n    tmp=$(mktemp -d)\n    assert_count \"basic: fresh dir has 0\"            \"$tmp\" \"0\"\n    local id\n    id=$(\"$REF\" acquire \"$tmp\")\n    assert_count \"basic: after acquire has 1\"        \"$tmp\" \"1\"\n    \"$REF\" release \"$tmp\" --id \"$id\"\n    assert_count \"basic: after release has 0\"        \"$tmp\" \"0\"\n    rm -rf \"$tmp\"\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ scenario_two_acquires — independent ids, partial release\nscenario_two_acquires() {\n    local tmp\n    tmp=$(mktemp -d)\n    local id1 id2\n    id1=$(\"$REF\" acquire \"$tmp\")\n    id2=$(\"$REF\" acquire \"$tmp\")\n    assert_count \"two-acquires: count 2\"             \"$tmp\" \"2\"\n    \"$REF\" release \"$tmp\" --id \"$id1\"\n    assert_count \"two-acquires: after one release 1\" \"$tmp\" \"1\"\n    \"$REF\" release \"$tmp\" --id \"$id2\"\n    assert_count \"two-acquires: after both 0\"        \"$tmp\" \"0\"\n    rm -rf \"$tmp\"\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ scenario_stale_pid — a fabricated dead pid validates as stale\n# We append a fabricated acquire line with a PID that doesn't exist\n# (the PID-MAX on Linux is usually 4194304; 9999999 is safely past\n# it on every kernel we'd run on).\nscenario_stale_pid() {\n    local tmp\n    tmp=$(mktemp -d)\n    local id1\n    id1=$(\"$REF\" acquire \"$tmp\")\n    printf 'acquire fake-dead %s 9999999 9999999 -\\n' \"2026-05-24T00:00:00-07:00\" >> \"$tmp/.refs\"\n    assert_count \"stale: live one counts, fake doesn't\" \"$tmp\" \"1\"\n    \"$REF\" reap \"$tmp\"\n    # After reap, only the live entry remains. The released-flag\n    # entry from id1 (we haven't released yet) stays.\n    assert_count \"stale: after reap still 1 live\"    \"$tmp\" \"1\"\n    \"$REF\" release \"$tmp\" --id \"$id1\"\n    assert_count \"stale: after release of real 0\"    \"$tmp\" \"0\"\n    rm -rf \"$tmp\"\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ scenario_marker — marker file presence gates validity\n# Acquire with a marker, count should be 1. Remove the marker, count\n# drops to 0 (marker missing = ref is stale).\nscenario_marker() {\n    local tmp marker\n    tmp=$(mktemp -d)\n    marker=\"$tmp/holder.alive\"\n    touch \"$marker\"\n    local id1\n    id1=$(\"$REF\" acquire \"$tmp\" --marker \"$marker\")\n    assert_count \"marker: present → 1 live\"          \"$tmp\" \"1\"\n    rm -f \"$marker\"\n    assert_count \"marker: missing → 0 live\"          \"$tmp\" \"0\"\n    rm -rf \"$tmp\"\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ scenario_list_json — list output should be JSON-shaped enough\n# Not a strict JSON parse (no jq) — we just want to see the array\n# brackets and the expected number of records inside.\nscenario_list_json() {\n    local tmp\n    tmp=$(mktemp -d)\n    local id1 id2\n    id1=$(\"$REF\" acquire \"$tmp\")\n    id2=$(\"$REF\" acquire \"$tmp\")\n    local out\n    out=$(\"$REF\" list \"$tmp\")\n    local first_char\n    first_char=\"${out:0:1}\"\n    local last_char\n    last_char=\"${out: -1}\"\n    local n_records\n    n_records=$(echo \"$out\" | grep -c '\"valid\":')\n    if [[ \"$first_char\" == \"[\" ]] && [[ \"$last_char\" == \"]\" ]] && [[ \"$n_records\" == \"2\" ]]; then\n        printf \"  %-44s ok\\n\" \"list: JSON array with 2 records\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"  %-44s FAIL — first=%s last=%s records=%s\\n\" \\\n            \"list: JSON array with 2 records\" \"$first_char\" \"$last_char\" \"$n_records\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"list-json: first=$first_char last=$last_char records=$n_records\")\n    fi\n    rm -rf \"$tmp\"\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ run\necho \"315 — reference helper tests:\"\nscenario_basic\nscenario_two_acquires\nscenario_stale_pid\nscenario_marker\nscenario_list_json\necho\necho \"  $pass passed, $fail failed\"\nif [[ \"$fail\" -gt 0 ]]; then\n    echo \"  failures:\"\n    for f in \"${failures[@]}\"; do echo \"    - $f\"; done\n    exit 1\nfi\nexit 0\n# }}}\n",
  "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/tests/315-refs-test.sh"
}

315 shipped. Five files changed:
- **`scripts/soramech-ref.sh`** (new) — the acquire/release/list/count/reap helper. Back pointer is PID + `/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22 (start time in clock ticks). Optional marker file path as a second liveness signal. Append-only log; `mkdir`-style lock only on `reap`.
- **`scripts/soramech-compile.sh`** — consults the log via the new `count` action. Zero live refs → destructive rebuild on `compiled/` (the old behaviour, unchanged). One or more live refs → fork to the next `compiled.N` sibling. Forked manifest carries `forked_from` pointing back at the parent generation.
- **`.gitignore`** — extended with `tests/maps/*/compiled.*/` for the sibling pattern.
- **`tests/315-refs-test.sh`** (new) — 12 unit scenarios: fresh/acquire/release/count cycles, two-acquires partial-release, fabricated-dead-PID stale detection + reap, marker-file presence gating, JSON shape of `list`.
- **`scripts/run-tests.sh`** — folds the unit suite into the integration suite, plus an end-to-end fork check that compiles, acquires, compiles again, and asserts the pinned generation still runs.

Suite: **23 passed, 4 pre-existing failed** (all 319-series, unchanged). Both new 315 tests green; the existing `compile_pipeline_check` still passes alongside.

**Todo recap.** Three of five done (both 248 sub-tasks I could finish + 315). Two left:
- **#2 — 248 editor toggles + Encapsulate action.** JS/HTML in `assets/`. I can read the existing inspector + file-browser code and make changes, but verifying needs you in a browser with the dev server.
- **#4 — 319.** "Open — planning stub" with several design questions you'd need to resolve before code lands; better tackled in conversation than solo.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The `count` action I added to the ref helper (beyond the issue's spec of `list` / `acquire` / `release` / `reap`) is the load-bearing piece for the compile script's fork decision. Returning JSON from `list` is great for diagnostics but bad for shell logic — parsing JSON with grep is fragile, and the compile script's question is a yes-or-no. A separate integer-emitting action means the script's check is one `[[ "$live" -eq 0 ]]` comparison instead of a regex over a JSON blob. Small API addition; big simplification at the call site.
- The PID + start-time-ticks back pointer is the cheapest reliable "is this process still the same one" verification on Linux. The PID alone is a recycling hazard (kernels reuse PIDs in days); the start-time-ticks anchor pins the identity to a specific process incarnation. Match both → "yes it's the same holder"; mismatch → "the PID got reused by something else, treat this ref as stale." No kernel calls, no parent tracking, just `/proc/<pid>/stat` parsing.
- The "compile/ vs compile.N/" naming asymmetry (the first generation is `compiled/`, forks are `compiled.1/`, `compiled.2/`) is a deliberate divergence from the issue's "symlink + always-indexed" suggestion. The reason: single-user development never forks, so the canonical name should be the canonical path, not a symlink that resolves to `compiled.0/`. The fork path only adds artifacts when the system genuinely needs them. The cost is no "latest" pointer — callers have to track which generation they want — but in practice each caller already knows which generation they acquired against, so the pointer wouldn't have helped them.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

198	  function next_copy_label(base) {

200	    if (m) {
201	      const root = m[1];
202	      const n    = m[2] ? parseInt(m[2]) + 1 : 2;

211	  // every wire whose destination was the original. Outgoing wires are
212	  // skipped — the natural use is "I want another node fed by the
213	  // same data," not another sink for everything downstream. Self-
214	  // loops are skipped too: they're both incoming and outgoing,
215	  // which contradicts the two rules at once.
216	  async function duplicate_box(src_id, wx, wy) {
217	    const src = Boxes.boxes[src_id];
218	    if (!src) return;
219	
220	    const dup = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(src));
221	    dup.id = 'box-' + Date.now().toString(36);
222	    dup.ui = dup.ui || {};
223	    dup.ui.x = Math.round(wx);

71	  }

75	  // Returns raw text, not JSON — the request() helper would mis-parse source code.
76	  async function get_src_file(filename) {
77	    const res = await fetch(base_url + `/maps/${map_name}/src/${encodeURIComponent(filename)}`);
78	    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);

92	    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);

116	
117	  // {{{ Translation file CRUD — issue 246
118	  // Translation files (per-port custom translation shims) live under
119	  // maps/<name>/translations/. The inspector creates them via "New"
120	  // (PUT), views them via "View" (GET), and the file browser can
121	  // delete them outright (DELETE). The inspector's own delete
122	  // affordance only clears the box's `custom_translation` field — it
123	  // does not call delete_translation.
124	  async function list_translations() {
125	    return request('GET', `/maps/${map_name}/translations`);
126	  }

128	    return request('GET', `/maps/${map_name}/translations/${filename}`);

132	  }
133	  async function delete_translation(filename) {
134	    return request('DELETE', `/maps/${map_name}/translations/${filename}`);
135	  }
136	  // }}}
137	
138	  return { init, list_maps, list_boxes, get_box, put_box, delete_box,
139	           get_meta, put_meta, get_data, put_data,
140	           list_src_files, get_src_file,
141	           list_extra_src, get_extra_src_file,
142	           list_translations, get_translation, put_translation, delete_translation,
143	           list_dirs };
144	})();

1	-- Schema definitions and validators for SoraMech map files.
2	-- Validates box files, meta.json, and drivers.json against the spec
3	-- in docs/001-architecture.md. Used by both the runner and the server
4	-- before any file is written to disk.
5	
6	local DIR = "/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech"
7	
8	local M = {}
9	
10	-- {{{ valid_kinds
11	-- `call` runs a language function. `read` and `write` are dispatch-
12	-- layer IO primitives (issue 229) — `read` emits an inline literal
13	-- or file contents, `write` commits a `value` to disk and emits a
14	-- boolean done signal.
15	local valid_kinds = { call = true, read = true, write = true }
16	-- }}}
17	
18	-- {{{ valid_branches
19	-- A connection's `from_branch` field identifies which output of
20	-- the producer box this wire leaves from. The accepted values
21	-- depend on the producer's `routing.kind` (issue 233):
22	--   plain      → nil
23	--   comparator → 'lt' / 'eq' / 'gt'
24	--   iterator   → 'out_0', 'out_1', ... 'out_<n-1>'
25	-- The schema here only enforces the lexical shape — that a
26	-- branch string is either nil, one of the three comparator
27	-- branches, or `out_<digits>`. Cross-referencing the producer's
28	-- routing kind happens at the graph level in
29	-- `check_input_bindings` / `validate-map.lua`.
30	local valid_branches = { lt = true, eq = true, gt = true }
31	local function is_iterator_branch_name(name)
32	    return type(name) == "string" and name:match("^out_%d+$") ~= nil
33	end
34	-- }}}
35	
36	-- {{{ valid_routing_kinds
37	-- Issue 233's unified `routing` field. Plain is the default
38	-- shape for a call box that wants its single output fanned to
39	-- all wires. Comparator and iterator are the two routing kinds
40	-- shipped under 233. Randomizer / weighted / distributor /
41	-- multi-band-comparator have their own follow-on issues
42	-- (240–243); until those ship, the schema rejects their kind
43	-- values so we don't accumulate dead state.
44	local valid_routing_kinds = { plain = true, comparator = true, iterator = true }
45	-- }}}
46	
47	-- {{{ err
48	local function err(errors, msg)
49	    errors[#errors + 1] = msg
50	end
51	-- }}}
52	
53	-- {{{ validate_connection
54	local function validate_connection(c, i, errors)
55	    -- from_branch is nil (no comparator) or one of "lt"/"eq"/"gt"
56	    if c.from_box == nil then
57	        err(errors, "connection[" .. i .. "] missing 'from_box'")
58	    end
59	    if c.from_branch ~= nil
60	       and not valid_branches[c.from_branch]
61	       and not is_iterator_branch_name(c.from_branch) then
62	        err(errors, "connection[" .. i .. "] 'from_branch' must be nil, " ..
63	            "'lt'/'eq'/'gt' (comparator), or 'out_<n>' (iterator)")
64	    end
65	    if c.to_box == nil then
66	        err(errors, "connection[" .. i .. "] missing 'to_box'")
67	    end
68	    if c.to_input == nil then
69	        err(errors, "connection[" .. i .. "] missing 'to_input'")
70	    end
71	end
72	-- }}}
73	
74	-- {{{ validate_box
75	function M.validate_box(box)
76	    local errors = {}
77	    if type(box) ~= "table" then
78	        return { "box must be a table" }
79	    end
80	
81	    if box.id == nil or type(box.id) ~= "string" then
82	        err(errors, "missing or non-string 'id'")
83	    end
84	    if box.label == nil or type(box.label) ~= "string" then
85	        err(errors, "missing or non-string 'label'")
86	    end
87	    if box.kind == nil or not valid_kinds[box.kind] then
88	        err(errors, "missing or invalid 'kind' (must be 'call', 'read', or 'write')")
89	    end
90	
91	    if box.kind == "call" then
92	        -- Unified routing (issue 233). Every call box carries a
93	        -- `routing` field declaring how its single output reaches
94	        -- downstream wires. Routing kind also gates whether
95	        -- ref/fn are required: iterator is a pure routing
96	        -- primitive with no language function attached; plain
97	        -- and comparator boxes need a function to invoke.
98	        local r = box.routing
99	        local is_routing_primitive = false
100	        if r == nil then
101	            err(errors, "call box missing 'routing' field (issue 233)")
102	        elseif type(r) ~= "table" then
103	            err(errors, "'routing' must be a table")
104	        elseif type(r.kind) ~= "string" then
105	            err(errors, "'routing.kind' must be a string")
106	        elseif not valid_routing_kinds[r.kind] then
107	            err(errors, "'routing.kind' = '" .. r.kind ..
108	                "' is not one of 'plain'/'comparator'/'iterator' " ..
109	                "(other kinds belong to follow-on issues 240–243)")
110	        else
111	            if r.kind == "comparator" then
112	                if type(r.comparand) ~= "number" then
113	                    err(errors, "comparator routing requires numeric 'routing.comparand'")
114	                end
115	            elseif r.kind == "iterator" then
116	                is_routing_primitive = true
117	                if type(r.n_outputs) ~= "number"
118	                   or r.n_outputs < 1
119	                   or r.n_outputs ~= math.floor(r.n_outputs) then
120	                    err(errors, "iterator routing requires 'routing.n_outputs' to be a positive integer")
121	                end
122	            end
123	        end
124	
125	        -- Legacy fields are explicitly rejected (issue 233 ships
126	        -- no in-loader migration). The editor or a one-off script
127	        -- rewrites old maps to the new shape; reading the old
128	        -- shape with this schema is meant to fail loudly.
129	        if box.comparand ~= nil then
130	            err(errors, "'comparand' is a legacy field — use routing = " ..
131	                "{ kind = 'comparator', comparand = <number> } instead (issue 233)")
132	        end
133	        if box.iterator_outputs ~= nil then
134	            err(errors, "'iterator_outputs' is a legacy field — use routing = " ..
135	                "{ kind = 'iterator', n_outputs = <integer> } instead (issue 233)")
136	        end
137	
138	        if not is_routing_primitive then
139	            if box.ref == nil or type(box.ref) ~= "string" then
140	                err(errors, "box missing 'ref'")
141	            end
142	        end
143	        -- fn is optional for binary callers (shell scripts, binaries)
144	        if box.inputs ~= nil and type(box.inputs) ~= "table" then
145	            err(errors, "'inputs' must be an array")
146	        end
147	        -- variadic_inputs: optional list of base names; each name must
148	        -- correspond to a series of inputs named "<base>_<index>" in
149	        -- box.inputs (the editor maintains this; we only check the
150	        -- shape here). See issue 217 part B.
151	        if box.variadic_inputs ~= nil then
152	            if type(box.variadic_inputs) ~= "table" then
153	                err(errors, "'variadic_inputs' must be an array")
154	            else
155	                for i, name in ipairs(box.variadic_inputs) do
156	                    if type(name) ~= "string" then
157	                        err(errors, "'variadic_inputs[" .. i .. "]' must be a string")
158	                    end
159	                end
160	            end
161	        end
162	        -- has_output: optional; absence means "true" (default behavior).
163	        -- false marks a sink box whose function has no return values
164	        -- (issue 226); the runtime treats such boxes as terminal and the
165	        -- editor hides the output port and inspector output section.
166	        if box.has_output ~= nil and type(box.has_output) ~= "boolean" then
167	            err(errors, "'has_output' must be a boolean")
168	        end
169	        -- Per-port `optional` flag (issue 230). Absent means false: the
170	        -- port is required and must be either wired or carry a literal
171	        -- value. The wire/literal/optional triple-check happens at the
172	        -- graph level (validate-map.lua and the editor's compile path),
173	        -- not here — this only validates per-port shape.
174	        if box.inputs ~= nil and type(box.inputs) == "table" then
175	            for i, p in ipairs(box.inputs) do
176	                if type(p) == "table" and p.optional ~= nil and type(p.optional) ~= "boolean" then
177	                    err(errors, "'inputs[" .. i .. "].optional' must be a boolean")
178	                end
179	            end
180	        end
181	        if box.connections ~= nil then
182	            for i, c in ipairs(box.connections) do
183	                validate_connection(c, i, errors)
184	            end
185	        end
186	    end
187	
188	    -- read / write: dispatch-layer IO primitives (issue 229). Shape
189	    -- check is intentionally permissive — the graph loader does the
190	    -- "has a value or a path" semantic check.
191	    if box.kind == "read" or box.kind == "write" then
192	        if box.value ~= nil and type(box.value) ~= "string" then
193	            err(errors, "'value' must be a string")
194	        end
195	        if box.path ~= nil and type(box.path) ~= "string" then
196	            err(errors, "'path' must be a string")
197	        end
198	        if box.inputs ~= nil and type(box.inputs) ~= "table" then
199	            err(errors, "'inputs' must be an array")
200	        end
201	        if box.connections ~= nil then
202	            for i, c in ipairs(box.connections) do
203	                validate_connection(c, i, errors)
204	            end
205	        end
206	    end
207	
208	    if box.ui ~= nil then
209	        if type(box.ui) ~= "table" then
210	            err(errors, "'ui' must be a table")
211	        elseif box.ui.x == nil or box.ui.y == nil then
212	            err(errors, "'ui' must have 'x' and 'y' fields")
213	        end
214	    end
215	
216	    return errors
217	end
218	-- }}}
219	
220	-- {{{ check_input_bindings
221	-- Graph-level check from issue 230: every input port on every box
222	-- must be in one of three states by compile time —
223	--   1. a wire is connected to it
224	--   2. a literal `value` is set on it
225	--   3. it carries `optional: true`
226	-- Otherwise the box would silently receive a missing arg at runtime
227	-- and the bug would only surface where the function happens to
228	-- reference it. The check fails loud and points at the exact box +
229	-- port instead.
230	--
231	-- `boxes` is a table mapping box-id → box record (the shape the
232	-- editor cache and the phase 2 loader's graph use). Returns an
233	-- array of error strings; empty array means OK.
234	function M.check_input_bindings(boxes)
235	    local errors = {}
236	
237	    -- precompute: for each (to_box, to_input) → true if a wire targets it.
238	    -- Connections live on both endpoints (issue 228), so scanning every
239	    -- box's connection list overcounts but doesn't miss anything.
240	    local wired = {}
241	    for _, box in pairs(boxes) do
242	        for _, c in ipairs(box.connections or {}) do
243	            if c.to_box and c.to_input then
244	                wired[c.to_box .. "\0" .. c.to_input] = true
245	            end
246	        end
247	    end
248	
249	    -- stable per-box iteration for predictable error ordering
250	    local ids = {}
251	    for id, _ in pairs(boxes) do ids[#ids + 1] = id end
252	    table.sort(ids)
253	
254	    for _, id in ipairs(ids) do
255	        local box = boxes[id]
256	        for _, p in ipairs(box.inputs or {}) do
257	            local has_wire    = wired[id .. "\0" .. p.name] == true
258	            local has_literal = p.value ~= nil and p.value ~= ""
259	            local is_optional = p.optional == true
260	            if not (has_wire or has_literal or is_optional) then
261	                err(errors, "box '" .. id .. "': input '" .. tostring(p.name) ..
262	                    "' has no wire, no literal, and is not optional")
263	            end
264	        end
265	    end
266	
267	    return errors
268	end
269	-- }}}
270	
271	-- {{{ validate_meta
272	function M.validate_meta(meta)
273	    local errors = {}
274	    if type(meta) ~= "table" then
275	        return { "meta.json must be a table" }
276	    end
277	    if meta.name == nil or type(meta.name) ~= "string" then
278	        err(errors, "meta.json missing 'name'")
279	    end
280	    if meta.entry_box_id == nil or type(meta.entry_box_id) ~= "string" then
281	        err(errors, "meta.json missing 'entry_box_id'")
282	    end
283	    return errors
284	end
285	-- }}}
286	
287	-- {{{ validate_drivers
288	function M.validate_drivers(drivers)
289	    local errors = {}
290	    if type(drivers) ~= "table" then
291	        return { "drivers.json must be a table" }
292	    end
293	    for ext, path in pairs(drivers) do
294	        if type(ext) ~= "string" or ext:sub(1, 1) ~= "." then
295	            err(errors, "driver key '" .. tostring(ext) .. "' must be a dot-prefixed extension")
296	        end
297	        if type(path) ~= "string" then
298	            err(errors, "driver value for '" .. ext .. "' must be a string path")
299	        end
300	    end
301	    return errors
302	end
303	-- }}}
304	
305	return M
306	
```

All four 248 sub-tasks landed plus 315; only 319 left on the original todo. Five files touched for the editor slice:

- **`src/001-schema.lua`** — added `map` kind, the `external` block on read/write, and loosened `from_branch` to accept any non-empty string (encap output ports use it for port names). Spot-tested: every fixture shape passes, three deliberately-broken shapes get rejected with precise messages.
- **`assets/js/003-api.js`** — added `list_boxes_for(other_map_name)` for fetching sub-map shapes at encap time.
- **`assets/js/002-boxes.js`** — `map` gets a violet color, a `sub-map` default header that falls back to the ref basename, a multi-output port-positions branch driven by the declared `outputs` array, and a height calculation that respects the documented exception to single-output-per-box.
- **`assets/js/004-inspector.js`** — kind dropdown grows the `map` option; two new helpers wired into `show()`: `render_external_binding` (toggle + binding-kind dropdown + name/index field on read/write boxes) and `render_map_box` (ref input + editable inputs/outputs lists with +/− buttons).
- **`assets/js/005-app.js`** — `mk_map_row` grows an inline `encap` button; new `encapsulate_map(sub_name)` fetches the sub-map, derives ports from its externally-marked boxes, and drops a `kind:"map"` box at viewport center.

Suite stable at 23 / 4 (same 319 failures, unchanged).

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The encap button on the map-picker row is the **single editor surface that closes the loop on issue 248**: without it, the only way to create an encap box was to hand-edit JSON. Hand-edited boxes work but bypass every UI safety net. With this button, the user can click a map, get an encap box pre-populated with the right port shape derived from the sub-map's own external markings, and just wire it up. The "derive ports from the sub-map's own marked boxes" step is what makes the affordance trustworthy — no double-entry, no risk of the parent's encap declaring ports the sub-map doesn't have.
- Loosening `from_branch` to accept any non-empty string was the schema change with the most reach. Before: the field was restricted to lt/eq/gt/`out_<n>` because every routing kind that used it had a fixed vocabulary. After: encapsulated maps can use it freely for named output ports. The lexical schema gives up some precision, but the precision moves to the graph-load step where it actually belongs — the loader knows the producer's kind and can verify the port name exists. The schema's job is shape, not semantics; this change honours that boundary.
- I deliberately didn't auto-clear `ref` / `fn` / `routing` when a box flips from `call` to `map` (or vice versa). The user can edit them manually afterward, and stale fields get ignored by the kind-appropriate loader path. The alternative — implicit field clearing on kind-change — risks discarding work the user wanted to preserve when they were just exploring. The "fields ignored when the kind doesn't read them" rule is a quieter and more forgiving contract than "fields wiped on transition," and it composes naturally with issue 320's reconfigure path where every field can change at runtime anyway.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**Verification needs your browser.** The schema and JS parse cleanly, the suite is green, but the actual UI rendering needs you to run the dev server, open the editor, and try the four new affordances:

1. Click a map in the picker → the new `encap` button should appear next to its name.
2. Clicking `encap` should drop a violet box on the canvas, labelled with the sub-map's name, with the right number of input + output ports.
3. Selecting a `read` or `write` box in the inspector should show the new "externally-supplied / externally-consumed" toggle + binding controls.
4. Selecting a `map` box should show the specialized inspector with ref + inputs + outputs lists.

**Todo recap.** Four of five done. Last is 319 — still "open — planning stub" with several design questions you'd need to weigh in on before code lands. 1	# 319 — Built-in library for map self-construction
2	
3	## Status
4	open — planning stub. Several design questions need user resolution
5	before implementation can begin. See **Open design questions**
6	below.
7	
8	## Concept
9	
10	A map should be able to build more of itself while running.
11	Two built-in primitives, exposed by the runtime to every language
12	spec, are enough to bootstrap that capability:
13	
14	- **`create_box(filepath, function_name) -> box_handle`**
15	  Spawn a new box on the currently-running map. The first argument
16	  is the file holding the function the box will run; the second is
17	  the name of that function inside the file. The runtime does any
18	  build-pipeline work that's needed (compile the source, register
19	  the spec, allocate the box's input port slots) before returning
20	  a handle the caller can use to wire the box up.
21	
22	- **`connect(from_box, to_box_a, to_box_b, ...) -> bool`**
23	  Attach a wire from the single output of `from_box` to each of
24	  the destination boxes. Variadic on the destinations, since fan-out
25	  from a single producer is the common pattern. Returns true if
26	  every connection succeeded, false otherwise.
27	
28	Together these let a running map grow new sub-graphs in response
29	to runtime conditions: a planner box decides what sub-pipeline to
30	build, calls `create_box` for each node, calls `connect` to wire
31	them, and the dispatch layer picks up the new region on the next
32	push.
33	
34	## Why this shape works (and the parts that need to be checked)
35	
36	**Single-output-per-box is already the law.** Issue 218 collapsed
37	boxes to one output. Variadic destinations on `connect` is just
38	fan-out across that single output — no new concept on the wire
39	side. The variadic part of the API matches the data model.
40	
41	**`filepath + function_name` matches box JSON.** That's already how
42	language specs locate the code a box runs. The API takes the same
43	two strings the box JSON would hold.
44	
45	**Handle-as-return mirrors `data` boxes' encapsulation contract
46	(issue 248).** Encapsulated maps already expose typed handles
47	to externally-supplied inputs. A `create_box` handle is the same
48	kind of thing — a reference the caller uses to identify the box
49	in follow-up calls.
50	
51	## Open design questions
52	
53	These are real forks in the design. Each one changes what the
54	implementation looks like; none have a default answer that's
55	obviously right.
56	
57	### Q1 — When does the new box exist? — **RESOLVED: runtime growth, unified store**
58	
59	**Resolution.** The slot store grows at runtime. There is no
60	"static region" versus "dynamic region" distinction — every box
61	is a dynamic box, allocated through the same mechanism, whether
62	it was declared in `boxes/<id>.json` at graph load or created
63	by a `create_box` built-in call mid-run. Graph load becomes the
64	first user of the growth primitive rather than a separate code
65	path.
66	
67	**Why this is the right shape (not a compromise).**
68	
69	The slot store *already* needs dynamic memory at runtime for an
70	unrelated reason: a user may push 200 values into an input slot
71	before the consuming box has run even once. Ring buffer cells
72	have to be growable on the push path regardless of whether the
73	graph itself is growing. Once dynamic allocation is in the slot
74	store's hot path, gating new *box* allocation behind a separate
75	"static-only" pathway is artificial — we'd be solving the same
76	problem in two places.
77	
78	The encapsulated-map feature (248) and the same-language-merge
79	research (313) both want to *unzip* a `.map` file into the
80	runtime graph at the same level as ordinary boxes — the entire
81	point is that the runtime doesn't spawn a nested thread pool for
82	the inner graph. Unzipping requires growing the box population
83	at runtime. A unified growable store covers all three callers
84	(graph load, `create_box`, map unzipping) with one mechanism.
85	
86	**The structure: two-level chunked-append index table, no
87	static ceilings.**
88	
89	The slot store keeps a top-level array of "chunk pointers." Each
90	chunk is a fixed-size block of slot pointers. Slot bodies
91	themselves are allocated separately and pointed to from chunk
92	entries. Three layers of growth, each cheaper than the layer
93	above:
94	
95	- **Layer 1 — appending a slot inside a chunk** (most common).
96	  Atomic-increment the chunk's in-use counter; publish the slot
97	  pointer at that index. Lock-free, single-instruction-ish.
98	- **Layer 2 — adding a new chunk** (uncommon). Write a new chunk
99	  pointer into the top-level array at the next free top-level
100	  index; bump the atomic "chunks in use" counter. Lock-free.
101	- **Layer 3 — growing the top-level array** (rare; logarithmic in
102	  total slots across the run). When the top-level array itself
103	  fills, use the double-buffer-with-swap pattern: allocate a new
104	  top-level array of 2× size, copy existing chunk pointers
105	  (pointers only; chunks themselves stay put), atomically swap
106	  the top-level array pointer, defer-free the old array via
107	  refcount or epoch-based reclamation. Workers caching the old
108	  top-level pointer can finish their lookups against it — every
109	  chunk and every slot the old array references is still alive.
110	
111	**No static ceilings anywhere.** Layer 1's chunk capacity is a
112	tuning constant (cache-friendly size, e.g. 64), not a limit on
113	total slots. Layer 2's top-level capacity grows via layer 3.
114	Layer 3 has no upper bound. The user pays one extra indirection
115	on every slot access (top-level → chunk → slot), and a rare
116	double-buffer swap whose cost amortizes to zero across the run.
117	
118	**Same machinery serves three callers:** graph load (the first
119	batch of slots), `create_box` (one slot at a time during dispatch),
120	and `.map` unzipping for encapsulated maps (a burst of slots when
121	a sub-map is expanded into the runtime). All three look identical
122	to the slot store — append, append, append.
123	
124	The allocator-wide-lock-free property is preserved. Only the
125	in-use counters and the top-level swap use atomics; everything
126	on the hot read/write path stays per-slot.
127	
128	**Removal — refcount, not tombstone.** Issue 315 (compiled
129	artifact reference counting) is the safety mechanism. A box's
130	refcount goes to zero only when no other box references it as
131	producer or consumer; any worker about to use the box must hold
132	a reference that keeps the count positive. Therefore "refcount
133	reached zero" is a proof that no worker holds a stale pointer.
134	Slot indices freed at that moment are safe to reuse.
135	
136	No tombstoning required, no generation counters on handles, no
137	ABA hazard — 315's refcount discipline subsumes all three.
138	
139	**What this resolution does NOT decide:** the precise API of the
140	growth primitive on the slot store, the cache-line-aware chunk
141	size choice, and whether ring buffer *cell* growth uses
142	double-buffer-with-swap under the per-slot lock (the suggested
143	shape, since each slot already holds a lock during growth).
144	Those are implementation details for the slot store work itself,
145	not the `create_box` / `connect` design.
146	
147	### Prerequisite — remove the dispatch input cap before `create_box` ships
148	
149	Today `src/012-dispatch.c` allocates five parallel stack arrays
150	of size 16 (`bufs`, `buf_chunks`, `datas`, `sizes`,
151	`input_native`) inside the per-call invocation path. A box with
152	more than 16 inputs hits a hard error from the dispatcher. This
153	contradicts the "no static ceilings" principle resolved in Q1.
154	
155	**Fix:** convert the five arrays to VLAs (`char *bufs[n];` etc.,
156	C99). Cost is zero — VLAs adjust the stack pointer by
157	`n * 5 * sizeof(void*)` with no allocator call. Keep a sanity
158	guard at a generous ceiling (e.g. 4096 inputs) so a runaway
159	loader can't blow the stack; the existing error-return path
160	stays in place above that.
161	
162	**Related but lower priority:** the `branch[24]` stack buffers
163	at dispatch.c:629/647/678 hold a `snprintf("out_%u", ...)`
164	result. Worst-case formatted length is 15 bytes; 24 is
165	arbitrary-but-safe and `snprintf` truncates without overflowing.
166	Change to a named constant (`MAX_BRANCH_NAME = 16`) for hygiene
167	when the VLA work lands. Not a real bug.
168	
169	### Q1.5 — The shape of the `create_box` argument: box JSON schema as the contract
170	
171	`create_box`'s argument is **one structured value whose shape is
172	exactly the box JSON schema**. In Lua, a table; in C, either a
173	struct or a JSON string built by the caller; in Bash, a JSON
174	string. The runtime converts to JSON internally (same path as the
175	universal wire format), validates against the box schema, and
176	instantiates the box record. Anything you can write into
177	`boxes/<id>.json` on disk, you can pass to `create_box` at
178	runtime.
179	
180	**Why this shape (not a fat positional signature, not key/value
181	varargs, not a builder pattern):**
182	
183	- The box JSON schema **is** the source of truth on disk. Having
184	  `create_box` mirror that schema means there is no parallel
185	  "create_box parameter list" to maintain — adding a new schema
186	  field works in `create_box` automatically.
187	- New customization toggles (priority, debug-instrumentation
188	  flags, custom translation specs per port, emoji labels for tap
189	  mode, etc.) land in the schema and become available to
190	  `create_box` callers in the same change.
191	- Languages without rich native structured types (Bash) can use
192	  JSON strings; languages with rich types (Lua tables, C structs)
193	  can use native shapes that the spec converts.
194	
195	**Structural metadata vs runtime values — the split this design
196	enforces.** The argument carries **structural metadata** (id,
197	kind, lang, ref, fn, routing, inputs/outputs schema, position).
198	Per-invocation **runtime values** (the data flowing through
199	wires) keep flowing through input slots as before. They do not
200	mix. Asking "should priority arrive on an input slot?" is the
201	wrong question — priority is metadata, not a value flowing
202	through the dataflow. Mixing the two would make a box's *shape*
203	depend on runtime state, which the slot store and the dispatcher
204	both assume is fixed once the box exists.
205	
206	### Box customization surface — what `create_box` accepts (audit, 2026-05-23)
207	
208	Maintained list of every per-box customization that currently
209	exists or is on a known open issue. When a new toggle is added
210	anywhere in SoraMech, **append to this list** in the same change.
211	The list is a contract reminder: `create_box`'s structured
212	argument must cover all of these because they are all valid
213	fields in the box JSON schema.
214	
215	**Working today (in shipped box JSON):**
216	
217	- `id` — required, unique within the map.
218	- `kind` — call / read / data / write / comparator / iterator /
219	  randomizer / weighted / distributor / map (the encapsulated
220	  kind from 248).
221	- `lang` — lua / c / bash / map (issue 303 spec registry).
222	- `ref` — file path to the source containing the box's function.
223	- `fn` — function name within `ref`.
224	- `inputs[]` — per-port: `name`, `type`, `value` (default),
225	  `optional`.
226	- `value` (read-box literal source).
227	- `path` (data and write boxes — disk file).
228	- `comparand` (comparator boxes).
229	- `routing.kind` — plain / comparator / randomizer / weighted /
230	  iterator / distributor.
231	- `routing.weights` (weighted), `routing.n_outputs` (iterator,
232	  randomizer).
233	- `iterator_outputs[]` (iterator branch names).
234	- `output_capacity` (ring buffer cell size hint).
235	- `connections[]` — outgoing wires: `from_branch`, `to_box`,
236	  `to_input`. (May be omitted in `create_box` calls if the caller
237	  will follow up with `connect()`.)
238	- `ui.x`, `ui.y` (canvas position).
239	
240	**Coming from open issues (must be supported by `create_box`
241	when they land):**
242	
243	- `external` block on `data` boxes — issue 248 (externally-supplied).
244	- `external` block on `write` boxes — issue 248 amended (externally-consumed).
245	- `outputs[]` array — issue 248, encapsulated boxes only, exception
246	  to issue 218's single-output-per-box rule.
247	- `custom_translation_spec` per input port — issue 246.
248	- `encap_mode` (`inline` | `runtime`) — issue 248, on `kind: "map"` boxes.
249	- Four-emoji label for tap mode — issue 249.
250	- Debug instrumentation flags per box — issue 247.
251	- `priority` — not yet specced; would feed the pool's
252	  task-scheduling priority. Worth its own issue when introduced;
253	  goes into the schema and into this list.
254	
255	**Derived (NOT settable via `create_box`):**
256	
257	- Wire color — derived from producer/consumer language pairing
258	  (issue 245). The compiler colors wires; the user doesn't.
259	- Per-edge native flag — derived by the graph loader at compile
260	  time from input/output language pairs (issue 312). Not a
261	  user-set field.
262	
263	### Q2 — Which input port does `connect` target? — **RESOLVED: connection-entry shape from box JSON schema**
264	
265	**Resolution.** `connect`'s argument is **one (or many)
266	structured value(s) whose shape is exactly a connection entry
267	from the box JSON schema's `connections[]` array**:
268	
269	```
270	connect({from_box=A, from_branch=null, to_box=B, to_input="x"})
271	```
272	
273	Variadic for multiple connections at once:
274	
275	```
276	connect({from_box=A, from_branch=null, to_box=B, to_input="x"},
277	        {from_box=A, from_branch="gt",  to_box=C, to_input="value"},
278	        {from_box=A, from_branch="lt",  to_box=D, to_input="value"})
279	```
280	
281	The "which port" question is answered by **`to_input` being
282	explicit in every connection entry**. No implicit-first-free
283	magic, no pair-syntax that has to be remembered separately from
284	the JSON shape, no per-port sub-handles on the box handle. The
285	shape on disk and the shape in the API call are identical.
286	
287	**Why this shape (consistent with Q1.5).** The schema is the
288	API. Every place SoraMech needs a "way to describe a box" or a
289	"way to describe a wire," the same JSON shape we already have on
290	disk is what the API accepts. Two artifacts (the schema, the
291	API) collapse to one artifact, and every future schema change
292	updates the API for free.
293	
294	**Construction in each language — `native_to_json` is the answer.**
295	
296	Each language spec already implements `native_to_json` for the
297	dual-ring wire format (issue 312) — that's how a Lua box's
298	return value crosses into a C consumer. The *same callback*
299	converts the user's spec-side value into the JSON shape the
300	runtime ingests. No new spec contract; no new callback; adding
301	a new language gives self-construction for free.
302	
303	- **Lua:** table literal. Idiomatic, terse.
304	  ```lua
305	  soramech.connect({from_box = "a", from_branch = nil,
306	                    to_box = "b", to_input = "x"})
307	  ```
308	- **C:** designated-initializer struct (`connection_t c = {.from_box="a", ...};`)
309	  for the common case; varargs JSON-string helper for dynamic
310	  fields. The struct definition lives alongside the C spec's
311	  header.
312	- **Bash:** JSON string. Bash has no native dict; JSON strings
313	  are how it talks to everything anyway.
314	
315	**Benefits that stack from machinery reuse:**
316	
317	- No new callback on the language spec — `native_to_json` is
318	  already required for wire crossings.
319	- One validator in the runtime — the box JSON schema validator
320	  used for `boxes/<id>.json` files at graph load handles
321	  runtime-constructed connections as-is.
322	- Persistence is trivial — if `create_box` ever grows an "also
323	  write to disk" option, the JSON is already in hand.
324	- The connections inside a `create_box` call's structured value
325	  (the box's own `connections[]` field) and standalone `connect()`
326	  calls produce the same internal records.
327	
328	**What this resolution does NOT decide:** the precise validation
329	error policy when a `to_input` names a non-existent port (likely
330	hard-crash per Q3 territory), and whether `connect()` accepts
331	the `from_box` as a handle from `create_box`, as the box's
332	string id, or both (likely both, since both can be resolved to
333	the same internal record). These fall under Q3 and Q4
334	respectively.
335	
336	### Q3 — Bool return versus hard-crash — **RESOLVED: hard-crash with reason**
337	
338	**Resolution.** `connect` returns nothing (`void`). On any
339	failure it aborts the program with a plain-English message
340	naming the boxes, the attempted wire, and what went wrong:
341	
342	```
343	soramech: cannot connect 'a' → 'b'.in_x
344	  reason: 'b' has no input port named 'in_x'
345	  available ports: 'count', 'label'
346	```
347	
348	Matches the project-wide error policy in CLAUDE.md ("prefer
349	error messages and breaking functionality over fallbacks";
350	"nil checks are just asking for errors"). A bool return invites
351	silent ignoring — if the user is calling `connect` they
352	intend the wire to exist; any reason it doesn't is a bug worth
353	surfacing immediately, not a normal-flow result to branch on.
354	
355	The corresponding `create_box` rule: failure to instantiate a
356	box (missing file, malformed schema, unknown spec language,
357	duplicate id) is also a hard crash with reason. No box handle
358	is returned for a failed creation — the program aborts before
359	any caller has the chance to mis-use a null handle.
360	
361	### Q4 — What is the "box handle" actually? — **RESOLVED: auto-generated box_id string**
362	
363	**Resolution.** The handle returned by `create_box` is **a
364	string — the box's `id` field from the box JSON schema**. If
365	the caller's spec value supplied an explicit `id`, that string
366	is returned. If `id` was omitted, the runtime mints an
367	auto-generated UUID-style string (e.g.
368	`auto_8f3c2a1e9b4d`) and uses it as the box's id.
369	
370	The handle is therefore identical to the box_id used everywhere
371	else in the system: in `boxes/<id>.json` filenames, in the
372	`from_box` / `to_box` fields of connection entries, in dispatch
373	log lines, in the run-output JSONL. There is no separate handle
374	type, no fast in-process pointer that has to be unwrapped at
375	wire crossings, no struct carrying both an id and a pointer.
376	
377	**Why a string id (not an in-process pointer, not the function
378	name).**
379	
380	- *Not an in-process pointer*: the handle has to survive being
381	  passed to `connect()` from any worker, being persisted to
382	  `tmp/last-run.jsonl`, and potentially being carried as a value
383	  on a wire to another box. The cross-language wire format
384	  explicitly forbids handles that back-route to a specific spec
385	  (see `feedback_cross_language_pitfalls`). A string id has
386	  none of those problems.
387	- *Not the function name*: multiple boxes can run the same
388	  function with different wiring, different input slot widths,
389	  different external bindings. The id distinguishes them.
390	- *Why UUID-style auto-generation*: when a runtime caller
391	  constructs a box dynamically, they often don't have a
392	  meaningful name in mind. Auto-generation removes the need to
393	  invent one and removes the risk of collision with an
394	  existing id. Callers who *do* want a meaningful name (for
395	  log readability) can pass `id = "my_planner_step_3"`
396	  themselves.
397	
398	**Internal lookup cost.** The dispatcher resolves
399	box_id → box record via a hash table (already needed for the
400	existing static graph load path). One hash lookup per `connect`
401	call, amortized to ~zero for the steady-state wire-push hot
402	path (which holds a direct pointer cached at graph-build time).
403	Box destruction (315) removes the hash entry as part of the
404	refcount-zero teardown.
405	
406	### Q5 — Does `create_box` trigger the build pipeline? — **RESOLVED: both, via a compile cache in tmp/**
407	
408	**Resolution.** Both runtime and compile-time paths exist, and
409	the runner stays ignorant of the compiler's internals by treating
410	the compiler as an external shell-out tool (which it already is:
411	`scripts/soramech-compile.sh`).
412	
413	**The compile cache.** A directory under `tmp/` holds compiled
414	artifacts keyed by a content hash of (source file + spec
415	language + relevant compile flags). When `create_box` resolves
416	a `ref` + `fn`:
417	
418	1. Compute the cache key from the source's contents and the
419	   language spec.
420	2. Look up the key in the cache.
421	3. **Hit:** `dlopen` (or equivalent for the language) the cached
422	   artifact and proceed.
423	4. **Miss:** shell out to `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` with the
424	   source path and target artifact path; wait for completion;
425	   verify exit status; dlopen the freshly built artifact.
426	
427	The runner never links the compiler, never imports
428	compiler-internal modules, never duplicates compiler logic. It
429	only knows "if artifact X exists in the cache, use it; otherwise
430	run this script." The three-program separation in
431	`project_soramech` (server / runner / editor) extends cleanly to
432	"runner treats compiler as external tool, same as it treats
433	language-spec subprocess binaries."
434	
435	**Compile-time precompilation as optimization.** When the
436	compile pipeline can statically determine that some
437	`create_box(spec)` calls have constant `ref` + `fn` (e.g. the
438	spec is a literal table in the caller's source), it can
439	pre-populate the cache during the compile step. Runtime calls
440	to `create_box` with those refs hit the cache immediately, no
441	shell-out latency. This is purely an optimization — correctness
442	doesn't depend on it. Defer the analysis pass until profiling
443	shows the runtime compile-on-demand path is a bottleneck.
444	
445	**Cache invalidation.** Cache key includes source content hash,
446	so changing a source file naturally produces a new key (and the
447	old entry becomes garbage to be collected during run teardown).
448	No invalidation logic needed; content hashing is the
449	invalidation.
450	
451	**Why not pure runtime / pure compile-time:**
452	
453	- *Pure runtime*: every `create_box` call would pay shell-out
454	  latency even for code that hasn't changed since the previous
455	  run. Wasteful in tight loops or hot planner boxes.
456	- *Pure compile-time*: dynamic `create_box` calls (where `ref`
457	  comes from a runtime value, e.g. a planner box choosing what
458	  pipeline to construct based on LLM output) can't be analyzed
459	  ahead of time. Forbidding them gives up the use case that
460	  motivates self-construction in the first place.
461	
462	The cache makes both paths cheap when they apply and removes the
463	need to pick one.
464	
465	## Suggested implementation steps (after Q1–Q5 are resolved)
466	
467	1. Resolve the open design questions; update this issue with the
468	   chosen shape before any code is written.
469	2. Add the two built-ins to the language-spec contract
470	   (`lang_spec_t` — the runtime exposes them via the spec's
471	   built-in table; each language spec wraps them in its native
472	   calling convention).
473	3. Extend the slot store with the growth primitive Q1 selects
474	   (if Q1 picks (a) or (c)).
475	4. Add dispatch-layer logic for newly-created boxes — they need to
476	   participate in the same push-on-arrival mechanism as static
477	   boxes.
478	5. Tests under `tests/`: a small map whose first box uses
479	   `create_box` + `connect` to build a downstream pipeline, then
480	   runs end-to-end and validates outputs.
481	6. Update `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` to describe the
482	   self-construction contract and the slot-store growth shape.
483	7. Update phase-3-progress.md.
484	
485	## Related issues and documents
486	
487	- 248 — encapsulated map as box (the function-like abstraction
488	  these primitives could be used to construct ad-hoc).
489	- 302 — wire value slot store (the structure that needs the growth
490	  primitive in Q1).
491	- 218 — single output per box (justifies the variadic-on-destinations
492	  shape).
493	- 217–222 — compile pipeline (relevant to Q5).
494	- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — current threading model these
495	  primitives must fit inside.
496	
```

1976	/* {{{ Runtime mutation — box_add_connection() (issue 319d)
1977	 *
1978	 * Appends one connection to box `b`'s connections array via the
1979	 * same copy-and-publish discipline used for boxes: allocate a
1980	 * new connections[] sized current+1, copy the old in, append the
1981	 * new connection, atomic-store the new connections pointer, then
1982	 * atomic-store the new count. The old connections array is parked
1983	 * on stale_box_arrs (the list is generic, not box-specific) and
1984	 * freed at graph_destroy. */
1985	int box_add_connection(graph_t *g, box_t *b, connection_t conn)
1986	{
1987	    if (!g || !b) return -1;
1988	    pthread_mutex_lock(&g->graph_mu);
1989	
1990	    int n_old = atomic_load_explicit(&b->n_connections, memory_order_relaxed);
1991	    connection_t *old = atomic_load_explicit(&b->connections, memory_order_relaxed);
1992	
1993	    connection_t *new_conns = malloc((size_t)(n_old + 1) * sizeof(connection_t));
1994	    if (!new_conns) { pthread_mutex_unlock(&g->graph_mu); return -1; }
1995	    if (old && n_old > 0) {
1996	        memcpy(new_conns, old, (size_t)n_old * sizeof(connection_t));
1997	    }
1998	    new_conns[n_old] = conn;
1999	
2000	    if (old) {
2001	        struct stale_arr *st = malloc(sizeof *st);
2002	        if (!st) { free(new_conns); pthread_mutex_unlock(&g->graph_mu); return -1; }
2003	        st->ptr  = old;
2004	        st->next = g->stale_box_arrs;
2005	        g->stale_box_arrs = st;
2006	    }
2007	
2008	    atomic_store_explicit(&b->connections,   new_conns, memory_order_release);
2009	    atomic_store_explicit(&b->n_connections, n_old + 1, memory_order_release);
2010	
2011	    pthread_mutex_unlock(&g->graph_mu);
2012	    return 0;
2013	}

281	     * is stashed on the task itself so dispatch_action can release

283	    ua_t *heap = slot_store_allocator(ctx->slots);
284	    ua_chunk_t *chunk = ua_alloc(heap, sizeof(dispatch_task_t));
285	    if (!chunk) return;
286	    dispatch_task_t *t = (dispatch_task_t *)ua_data(chunk);
287	    t->chunk = chunk;
288	    t->live_wire_count = 0;
289	
290	    /* Assign task_id at submission so the same id correlates the
291	     * task_submit / task_start / task_end events. The next_task_id
292	     * counter is atomic so concurrent spawners don't collide. */
293	    dispatch_ctx_t *mctx = (dispatch_ctx_t *)ctx;
294	    t->task_id = atomic_fetch_add_explicit(&mctx->next_task_id, 1,
295	                                           memory_order_relaxed);
296	    t->box_id  = box_id;
297	    t->ctx     = ctx;
298	
299	    if (ctx->events) {
300	        const box_t *b = graph_box(ctx->graph, box_id);
301	        event_queue_task_submit(ctx->events, now_secs(),
302	            t->task_id, b ? b->id : "(unknown)", -1);
303	    }
304	    pool_spawn(ctx->pool, dispatch_action, t, priority);
305	}
306	/* }}} */
307	
308	/* {{{ dispatch_spawn_if_ready() */
309	void dispatch_spawn_if_ready(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, int box_id, int priority)
310	{
311	    if (!ctx) return;
312	    if (box_id < 0) return;
313	    if (!box_is_ready(ctx, box_id)) return;
314	
315	    const box_t *b = graph_box(ctx->graph, box_id);
316	    /* 244: read boxes are pull-on-demand value sources, not tasks.
317	     * They never enter the pool — their consumers read the cached
318	     * value directly when they fire. */
319	    if (b && b->kind == BOX_READ) return;
320	    if (b && b->multi_spawn) {
321	        /* Multi-spawn box (iterator or anything downstream of one).
322	         * The single-spawn guard doesn't apply: every push that
323	         * leaves the box ready spawns a new task, which will drain
324	         * one cell from each POP input. The iterator's own
325	         * dispatch_action also re-spawns itself while inputs remain
326	         * so a single push can wake the chain. */
327	        dispatch_spawn(ctx, box_id, priority);
328	        return;
329	    }
330	
331	    /* Single-spawn case: CAS the per-box guard. The first push that
332	     * finds the consumer ready wins; everyone else short-circuits.
333	     * The 1-cell peek model spawns each box at most once per run.
334	     * The chunk grows on demand so runtime-created boxes get a
335	     * slot without any pre-sized cap. */
336	    ctx_box_chunk_t *chunk = ctx_box_chunk(ctx, (unsigned int)box_id, 1);
337	    if (!chunk) return;
338	    int expected = 0;
339	    if (atomic_compare_exchange_strong(
340	            &chunk->spawned[(unsigned int)box_id % CTX_CHUNK_SIZE],
341	            &expected, 1)) {
342	        dispatch_spawn(ctx, box_id, priority);
343	    }
344	}
345	/* }}} */
346

349	{

351	        if (err) *err = err_fmt("dispatch_push_literals: NULL ctx");
352	        return -1;
353	    }

231	/* {{{ box_is_ready() — every required input has a value or fallback
232	 *
233	 * A port is satisfied when:
234	 *   - it is optional, OR
235	 *   - its slot currently holds a value, OR
236	 *   - it has at least one read-box predecessor (issue 244 — the
237	 *     consumer can pull the cached value at attempt time even
238	 *     though the slot is empty). */
239	static int box_is_ready(const dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, int box_id)
240	{
241	    const box_t *b = graph_box(ctx->graph, box_id);
242	    if (!b) return 0;
243	    if (b->n_inputs == 0) return 1;
244	    if (!b->input_slot_ids) return 0;        /* runtime not attached */
245	    for (int i = 0; i < b->n_inputs; i++) {
246	        if (b->inputs[i].optional) continue;
247	        if (slot_has_value(ctx->slots, b->input_slot_ids[i])) continue;
248	        if (b->n_read_predecessors && b->n_read_predecessors[i] > 0) continue;
249	        return 0;
250	    }
251	    return 1;
252	}
253	/* }}} */
254	
255	/* {{{ box_pop_ready() — every POP input has at least one cell */
256	/* For multi-spawn boxes, we want to re-spawn so long as every POP
257	 * input still has a queued value. PEEK inputs are always available
258	 * after their initial push, so they don't gate continuation. */
259	static int box_pop_ready(const dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, int box_id)
260	{
261	    const box_t *b = graph_box(ctx->graph, box_id);
262	    if (!b || !b->input_slot_modes) return 0;
263	    int saw_pop = 0;
264	    for (int i = 0; i < b->n_inputs; i++) {
265	        if (b->input_slot_modes[i] != SLOT_MODE_POP) continue;
266	        if (b->inputs[i].optional) continue;
267	        saw_pop = 1;
268	        if (!slot_has_value(ctx->slots, b->input_slot_ids[i])) return 0;
269	    }
270	    return saw_pop;
271	}
272	/* }}} */

1932	 *
1933	 * Appends a pre-built box to the graph's pointer index. The pointer
1934	 * array grows via copy-and-publish (allocate at 2x capacity, memcpy
1935	 * the old pointers in, atomic-store the new array, park the old on
1936	 * stale_box_arrs for destroy-time reclamation). The new box's count
1937	 * is published last with release semantics so a reader seeing
1938	 * count = N also sees box N-1 fully published into the index. */
1939	int graph_add_box(graph_t *g, box_t *box)
1940	{
1941	    if (!g || !box) return -1;
1942	    pthread_mutex_lock(&g->graph_mu);
1943	
1944	    uint32_t n   = atomic_load_explicit(&g->n_boxes,      memory_order_relaxed);
1945	    uint32_t cap = atomic_load_explicit(&g->box_capacity, memory_order_relaxed);
1946	
1947	    if (n + 1u > cap) {
1948	        uint32_t new_cap = cap == 0 ? 16u : cap * 2u;
1949	        box_t **new_boxes = calloc((size_t)new_cap, sizeof(box_t *));
1950	        if (!new_boxes) {
1951	            pthread_mutex_unlock(&g->graph_mu);
1952	            return -1;
1953	        }
1954	        box_t **old_boxes = atomic_load_explicit(&g->boxes, memory_order_relaxed);

1956	            memcpy(new_boxes, old_boxes, (size_t)n * sizeof(box_t *));
1957	        }
1958	        struct stale_arr *st = malloc(sizeof *st);
1959	        if (!st) { free(new_boxes); pthread_mutex_unlock(&g->graph_mu); return -1; }
1960	        st->ptr  = old_boxes;
1961	        st->next = g->stale_box_arrs;
1962	        g->stale_box_arrs = st;
1963	        atomic_store_explicit(&g->boxes,        new_boxes, memory_order_release);
1964	        atomic_store_explicit(&g->box_capacity, new_cap,   memory_order_release);

1970
