```json
{
  "content":"# SoraMech — Overview & quickstart\n\n## What SoraMech is\n\nSoraMech is a **visual dataflow runtime**. You build a *map* — a\ngraph of boxes connected by wires — in the browser-based editor.\nEach box runs a function (in Lua, C, or Bash). When you run the\nmap, the runtime fires boxes whose inputs are ready, threads the\noutputs along wires to downstream boxes, and keeps going until\nquiescence. Multiple boxes run in parallel across a thread pool.\n\nThe runtime is structural. It guarantees that wires deliver\nvalues from producers to consumers; that boxes fire when their\ninputs are ready; that values cross language boundaries cleanly.\nIt does not know what your boxes *do* — that's your code. The\nruntime is the apartment building's steel and concrete; box\nauthors and library authors design the rooms.\n\n## When to reach for it\n\nSoraMech fits well when:\n\n- The problem is naturally a dataflow: inputs flow through a\n  sequence of transformations to outputs.\n- You want to mix languages — a Lua planner driving C boxes that\n  feed a Bash post-processor.\n- You want to inspect the wiring visually instead of reading code.\n- The work is naturally parallel — independent boxes should fire\n  on different threads without you orchestrating threads yourself.\n- You want a **JSONL audit trail** of what happened during a run,\n  for debugging, replay, or feeding to a downstream tool.\n\nIt's less useful when the problem isn't dataflow-shaped (long\nsingle-threaded computations, tight tensor math, anything where\nthe box overhead would dominate the work).\n\n## Quickstart\n\n### Install\n\nSoraMech is a small set of C sources, shell scripts, and Lua /\nJavaScript assets. You build it from source.\n\nPrerequisites:\n\n- A C compiler with C11 support (`gcc` or `clang`)\n- `make`\n- `luajit` 2.1 (or compatible) with its headers\n- `bash`\n- `node` (for the editor's JavaScript tests; optional otherwise)\n\nBuild:\n\n```bash\nmake            # builds the pool runner + the three language specs\nmake test       # full ship-it suite (unit tests + integration fixtures)\nmake quicktest  # cheap iteration: just the C unit tests, no rebuild\n```\n\n### Your first map\n\nA map is a directory of JSON files. Boxes live in `boxes/`,\nsource code in `src/`, metadata in `meta.json`. The simplest\nmap is one Lua box wired to one read box.\n\n```\nmy-map/\n  meta.json\n  boxes/\n    seed.json\n    greet.json\n  src/\n    greet.lua\n```\n\n`meta.json`:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"name\": \"my-map\",\n  \"description\": \"Tiny example\",\n  \"entry_box_id\": \"seed\",\n  \"src_dirs\": [\"my-map/src\"]\n}\n```\n\n`boxes/seed.json` (a value source — emits the literal `\"world\"`):\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":    \"seed\",\n  \"kind\":  \"read\",\n  \"value\": \"world\",\n  \"connections\": [\n    { \"from_box\": \"seed\", \"to_box\": \"greet\", \"to_input\": \"name\" }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n`boxes/greet.json` (a Lua call box):\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":    \"greet\",\n  \"kind\":  \"call\",\n  \"lang\":  \"lua\",\n  \"ref\":   \"src/greet.lua\",\n  \"fn\":    \"greet\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"name\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n}\n```\n\n`src/greet.lua`:\n\n```lua\nlocal M = {}\nfunction M.greet(name)\n    return \"Hello, \" .. name .. \"!\"\nend\nreturn M\n```\n\nRun it:\n\n```bash\n./soramech-pool my-map\n```\n\nOutput:\n\n```\nsoramech-pool: 'my-map' — 2 box(es), entry seed, N worker(s)\nsoramech-pool: run log → /tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl\nsoramech-pool: run complete (1 task(s) in 234 µs).\nsoramech-pool: outputs:\n  greet → Hello, world!\n```\n\nThe seed box pushed `\"world\"` along its wire to `greet.name`.\nThe Lua function ran and returned `\"Hello, world!\"`, which is\nthe output captured for `greet`. The full per-event run log\nsits at `/tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl` — one JSON event per\nline, ready to feed to whatever downstream tool you like.\n\n### Editing in the browser\n\nFor anything more than a toy, you'll want the editor:\n\n```bash\n./scripts/start-server.sh\n# open http://localhost:7700/ in your browser\n```\n\nThe editor's a canvas-and-inspector view of the same map\ndirectory. Drag to create boxes, click-drag between port dots\nto wire them, click a box to edit its fields in the right\nsidebar. Saves go straight to the JSON files on disk; you can\nrun the map from another terminal at any time.\n\n## What's next\n\n- [`docs/002-map-model.md`](002-map-model.md) — the box kinds,\n  routing kinds, wire semantics, and how encapsulated sub-maps\n  let you compose larger graphs from smaller ones.\n- [`docs/003-editor.md`](003-editor.md) — the canvas + inspector\n  UI walkthrough.\n- [`docs/004-runtime.md`](004-runtime.md) — how runs work, what\n  the JSONL log contains, the compile pipeline, the\n  reference-counted artifact system.\n- [`docs/005-writing-boxes.md`](005-writing-boxes.md) — per-\n  language quickstarts for Lua, C, and Bash box authors.\n- [`docs/006-test-coverage-map.md`](006-test-coverage-map.md) —\n  the project's test inventory.\n",
  "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/001-overview.md"
}
```

```json
{
  "content":"# SoraMech — Map model\n\nA map is a directed graph of **boxes** connected by **wires**.\nBoxes have **input ports** (left side, where wires arrive) and a\nsingle **output side** (right side, where wires leave). Wires\ncarry values from one box's output to another box's input port.\n\n## Box kinds\n\nEvery box has a `kind` field that tells the runtime what it does.\n\n### `call` — runs a function\n\nThe general-purpose box. Names a function in some language\n(`lua` / `c` / `bash`) and runs it when the inputs are ready.\nThe function's return value becomes the value on the output wire.\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"double\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"lua\",\n  \"ref\":  \"src/math.lua\",\n  \"fn\":   \"double\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"x\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n}\n```\n\n### `read` — emits a value\n\nA pull-on-demand value source. Either a literal (`value` field)\nor the bytes of a file (`path` field). When a downstream box\nneeds a value, the read box's bytes get pulled in.\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":    \"config\",\n  \"kind\":  \"read\",\n  \"value\": \"production\",\n  \"connections\": [\n    { \"from_box\": \"config\", \"to_box\": \"router\", \"to_input\": \"env\" }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n### `write` — writes to disk\n\nThe sink for \"land this value on the filesystem.\" Reads its\n`value` input and writes it to the `path` input. By default\nemits the string `\"true\"` downstream as a success signal so\nlater boxes can chain off the write.\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"save\",\n  \"kind\": \"write\",\n  \"inputs\": [\n    { \"name\": \"path\",  \"value\": \"/tmp/result.txt\" },\n    { \"name\": \"value\", \"type\": \"string\" }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n### `map` — encapsulated sub-map\n\nAn entire sub-graph appearing as one box on the parent canvas.\nSee \"Encapsulation\" below for the full story.\n\n### `create_box` / `connect` — runtime self-construction\n\nA running box can spawn new boxes and wire them up mid-run. The\n`create_box` and `connect` kinds are the language-agnostic\ndispatch primitives; per-language wrappers like Lua's\n`soramech.create_box{...}` are convenience over the same path.\nSee [`docs/005-writing-boxes.md`](005-writing-boxes.md) for the\ncalling shape.\n\n## Wires (connections)\n\nA wire lives on the **producer** box's `connections[]` array. Each\nentry names a destination and (when the routing kind has named\nbranches) which branch the wire leaves from.\n\n```json\n{\n  \"from_box\":    \"router\",\n  \"from_branch\": \"lt\",          // optional; depends on routing kind\n  \"to_box\":      \"low_handler\",\n  \"to_input\":    \"value\"\n}\n```\n\nWhen a producer fires, the runtime pushes its output value into\nthe destination box's input slot. The destination fires when all\nits required input slots have values.\n\nA producer can fan out — multiple wires leaving the same output\nport deliver the same value to each consumer. The single-output-\nper-box rule (every kind except `map` has one output port)\nkeeps the wiring discipline simple.\n\n## Routing kinds\n\nThe `routing` field on a `call` box decides *where* the output\ngoes. Seven kinds ship:\n\n### `plain` — fan to every wire\n\nSingle output port (unnamed). Every wire on `connections[]`\nreceives the value. The default for new boxes.\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n```\n\n### `comparator` — pick by numeric threshold\n\nTwo flavours. The single-threshold form names three output\nbranches `lt` / `eq` / `gt` and picks the matching one based on\nthe producer's numeric output:\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"comparator\", \"comparand\": 5 }\n```\n\nThe multi-band form takes a non-decreasing `thresholds` array\nand carves the number line into N+1 named bands:\n`below_<t0>` / `between_<a>_<b>` / `above_<tN-1>`. Doubled\nadjacent thresholds carve zero-width equality bands named\n`eq_<t>`:\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"comparator\", \"thresholds\": [3, 7] }\n// → branches: below_3, between_3_7, above_7\n```\n\n### `iterator` — round-robin over N ports\n\nNo function attached — pure routing. Each fire rotates the\noutput among `n_outputs` ports named `out_0` ... `out_<n-1>`.\nMulti-spawn: a single arrival to an iterator's input slot drains\nqueued values one per fire.\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"iterator\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n```\n\n### `randomizer` — hashed pseudo-random pick\n\nSame `out_<i>` port shape as iterator. Each fire hashes the\nper-box counter and takes mod `n_outputs`, so consecutive fires\nspread across branches rather than going to consecutive indices.\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"randomizer\", \"n_outputs\": 4 }\n```\n\n### `weighted` — probability-weighted pick\n\nSame `out_<i>` ports. Each fire picks a branch by cumulative-\nband lookup over the user's `weights` array. The dispatch\nnormalises automatically — the weights don't have to sum to 1.0.\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"weighted\", \"weights\": [0.8, 0.2] }\n```\n\n### `distributor` — least-busy pick\n\nSame `out_<i>` ports. Each fire samples the downstream slot\nfill on every branch and picks the least-busy one. Ties resolve\nvia a per-box counter so a steady stream rotates across\nequally-empty branches.\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"distributor\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n```\n\n### `nonlinearity` — value-transforming auto-calibrated gate\n\nSingle output port. Reads the producer's numeric output,\nauto-calibrates bounds from a per-box ring buffer of the last\n`memory` observed values, normalises against those bounds,\napplies an S-curve, and emits `input × score` (gated linear\nunit shape) on the wire.\n\n```json\n\"routing\": {\n  \"kind\":   \"nonlinearity\",\n  \"range\":  \"signed\",   // \"signed\" → tanh, output [-1, 1]\n                        // \"unit\"   → sigmoid, output [0, 1]\n  \"memory\": 16,         // ring-buffer size for auto-calibration\n  \"k\":      1           // steepness\n}\n```\n\nUseful for decision-lattice composition: chain several into a\ndownstream aggregator and the soft-AND property of multiplying\nscored values bubbles up \"strong evidence reinforces, weak\nevidence stays weak\" behaviour.\n\n## Input port semantics\n\nA `call` box's `inputs[]` array declares its port set. Each port\nhas a name, an optional `type` (`\"string\"` is the convention),\nan optional inline `value` (a literal that supplies the port if\nno wire is attached), and an optional `optional` flag (when\ntrue, the box fires even if this port has no value).\n\nA port can be in one of three states at compile time:\n- **Wired** — a producer's `connections[]` entry targets it.\n- **Literal** — the port carries an inline `value`.\n- **Optional** — neither wired nor literal, but `optional: true`.\n\nAnything else is a hard error at graph load. SoraMech doesn't\nsilently fire a box with a missing required input.\n\n## Encapsulation — sub-maps as boxes\n\nA whole map can appear as a single box on another map's canvas.\nThis is `kind: \"map\"`. The parent's canvas sees one box; the\nruntime expands the sub-map at graph-load time into the parent's\nflat graph, with the sub-map's box ids prefix-renamed.\n\nHow the sub-map exposes ports:\n\n- A **read** box inside the sub-map marked with an `external`\n  block becomes one of the encap box's INPUT ports. Parent\n  wires landing on that port get spliced through to whatever\n  the read box was feeding inside the sub-map.\n\n```json\n{ \"id\": \"msg_in\", \"kind\": \"read\",\n  \"external\": { \"kind\": \"named\", \"name\": \"msg\" } }\n```\n\n- A **write** box marked externally-consumed becomes an OUTPUT\n  port on the encap box. The write still happens to its `path`\n  (when set); additionally the value gets surfaced back to the\n  parent on the wire.\n\nThe encap box itself declares the port shape:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"stats_pipeline\",\n  \"kind\": \"map\",\n  \"ref\":  \"../shared-maps/stats-pipeline\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"msg\",    \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"outputs\": [ { \"name\": \"result\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"connections\": [\n    { \"from_box\": \"stats_pipeline\", \"from_branch\": \"result\",\n      \"to_box\":   \"downstream\",     \"to_input\":    \"value\" }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\nEncapsulation is the documented exception to the single-output-\nper-box rule — an encap can declare any number of output ports\n(one per externally-consumed write box). The runtime treats them\nas independent value sources.\n\nEncaps nest. A sub-map can itself contain a `kind: \"map\"` box,\nand the load-time splice iterates until no encaps remain. Cycle\ndetection runs after the flattening.\n\n## What's next\n\n- [`docs/003-editor.md`](003-editor.md) — using the canvas to\n  build maps visually.\n- [`docs/004-runtime.md`](004-runtime.md) — how the runtime\n  executes maps, the JSONL transcript, the compile pipeline.\n- [`docs/005-writing-boxes.md`](005-writing-boxes.md) — per-\n  language box-author guides.\n",
  "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/002-map-model.md"
}
```

```json
{
  "content":"# SoraMech — Editor\n\nThe editor is a browser app. It loads a map directory, draws the\nboxes on a canvas, lets you wire them, and saves every change\nstraight to the JSON files on disk. The runner reads those same\nfiles — there's no \"save and rebuild\" step between editing and\nrunning.\n\n## Starting it\n\n```bash\n./scripts/start-server.sh\n# default: http://localhost:7700/\n```\n\nThe server is a small Lua HTTP server (`src/005-http-server.lua`)\nthat exposes the file CRUD endpoints the editor uses. It serves\nthe map directory you launched it against.\n\nYou can override the port or pick a different map root via\n`config/editor.json` or environment variables — see\n`scripts/start-server.sh` for the knobs.\n\n## The layout\n\nThree regions:\n\n- **Canvas** (centre) — boxes, wires, ports. Pan with click-drag\n  on empty space; zoom with the scroll wheel.\n- **Inspector** (right sidebar) — the selected box's editable\n  fields. Click a box to populate it; click empty canvas to hide.\n- **Map header** (top) — current map name (click to switch maps),\n  compile button, and run status.\n\n## Working with boxes\n\n**Create**: right-click an empty spot on the canvas and pick a\nkind from the menu. Or middle-click an existing box to\nduplicate it at the cursor position.\n\n**Move**: click-drag a box's body.\n\n**Inspect / edit**: click a box. The inspector fills with the\nbox's fields. Editing any field saves to disk on the next\nkeystroke (debounced) or on blur.\n\n**Delete**: click a box to select, then press the delete button\nat the top of the inspector. The wires attached to it get\ncleared automatically.\n\n## Working with wires\n\n**Draw**: click-drag from one box's port dot to another box's\nport dot. Source side is the right edge (an output port);\ndestination side is the left edge (an input port).\n\n**Delete**: click the wire (anywhere along its length) to select\nit, then press Delete.\n\n**Self-loops** route around the box body so they stay readable.\n\n## Inspector by box kind\n\nThe inspector shows only the fields that apply to the current\nbox's kind. The shared header (label, id, kind dropdown, delete\nbutton) is always there.\n\n### Call boxes\n\n- **kind**: dropdown lets you swap between `call` / `read` /\n  `write` / `map`. Changing kind clears the per-kind fields.\n- **routing**: dropdown picks the routing kind. Switching kinds\n  severs any outgoing wires whose port names would no longer\n  exist under the new kind.\n- **ref**: the source file. Click \"browse\" to pick from the\n  attached source directories.\n- **fn**: the function name within that file. Click \"fn\" to\n  pick from the parsed function list.\n- **inputs**: per-port editable rows. Name comes from the\n  parser; you supply the literal value (or leave blank for\n  wired input).\n- **per-routing-kind controls**: comparator gets a `comparand`\n  number input and a `thresholds` text input; iterator /\n  randomizer / distributor get an `n_outputs` number;\n  weighted gets a comma-separated `weights` text input;\n  nonlinearity gets the `range` toggle + `memory` + `k`.\n\n### Read boxes\n\n- **value**: literal text the box emits. When set, the `path`\n  input port hides on the canvas.\n- **external**: toggle to mark this read box as\n  externally-supplied (consumed by the encapsulating sub-map's\n  port shape). When on, a binding-kind selector lets you pick\n  `named` / `positional` / `numbered` plus the matching name or\n  index.\n\n### Write boxes\n\n- **inputs**: `path` (where to write) and `value` (what to\n  write). Either can be wired or carry a literal.\n- **external**: toggle to mark this write box as\n  externally-consumed (the value also surfaces as an output\n  port on the encapsulating sub-map). Same binding-kind shape\n  as read.\n\n### Map boxes (encapsulated sub-maps)\n\n- **ref**: path to the sub-map directory (relative to the\n  current map's directory, or absolute).\n- **inputs / outputs**: editable port lists. Each row is a\n  port name; +/− buttons add and remove rows. The names need to\n  match the externally-supplied read boxes and\n  externally-consumed write boxes inside the sub-map.\n\n## The file browser\n\nThe bottom of the inspector hosts the file browser when you\nclick \"browse\" or \"fn\" on a call box. It lists source files\nacross every attached source directory. Click a directory header\nto collapse / expand; right-click to hide a directory.\n\nThe \"+ library dir\" button at the top lets you attach an\narbitrary directory as another source root for the current map —\nuseful for sharing helpers across maps without copying files.\n\n## The map picker\n\nClick the map name in the header to open the map picker. It\nlists every map known to the current server, plus a recent-maps\nhistory. Selecting one switches the editor to that map.\n\nEach map row also has an **encap** button. Clicking it adds the\nselected map as a `kind: \"map\"` sub-map box on the\ncurrently-edited map's canvas. The new box's port shape is\nderived from the sub-map's externally-marked read and write\nboxes, so the wiring is ready as soon as the box appears.\n\n## Compile\n\nThe compile button at the top of the editor runs\n`scripts/soramech-compile.sh` against the current map. The\ncompiled artifact lands under `<map>/compiled/` and is portable\n— it bundles the language plugins, pre-compiles every C box,\nand includes the pool runner binary. Copy or symlink the\ndirectory anywhere on the same machine and it runs the map\nstandalone (no source tree required).\n\nSee [`docs/004-runtime.md`](004-runtime.md) for the runtime\nside of compilation, including the reference-counted artifacts\nsystem that keeps in-flight runs safe across rebuilds.\n\n## Keyboard shortcuts\n\n- **Delete**: delete the selected box or wire.\n- **Middle-click**: duplicate the box under the cursor at the\n  cursor position.\n- **Scroll**: zoom.\n- **Right-click**: context menu (new box, hide directory in the\n  file browser, etc.).\n",
  "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/003-editor.md"
}
```

```json
{
  "content":"# SoraMech — Runtime\n\nThis doc covers what happens when you run a map: how the runner\nloads the graph, fires boxes, threads values along wires, writes\nthe JSONL transcript, and tears down. Plus the compile pipeline\nand the reference-counted-artifact system that lets long-running\nprocesses hold onto a specific build of a map across rebuilds.\n\n## Running a map\n\n```bash\n./soramech-pool <map-dir>\n```\n\nThe runner reads `<map-dir>/meta.json` + `<map-dir>/boxes/*.json`,\nbuilds the in-memory graph, attaches the slot store (one slot\nper input port), starts a worker pool (one worker per CPU by\ndefault; override with `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`), and submits the\nentry boxes as initial tasks. Workers pick tasks off the pool\nqueue, run the box's spec function (Lua, C, or Bash), and push\nthe output along the producer's outgoing connections.\n\nWhen all consumers are satisfied and no tasks remain, the run\nhits quiescence and the runner exits. The stderr summary prints\neach box's most recent output.\n\n```\nsoramech-pool: 'hello' — 2 box(es), entry seed, 14 worker(s)\nsoramech-pool: run log → /tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl\nsoramech-pool: run complete (2 task(s) in 1245 µs).\nsoramech-pool: outputs:\n  seed → world\n  greet → Hello, world!\n```\n\n## The JSONL transcript\n\nEvery run writes a JSON-Lines transcript to\n`<map-dir>/tmp/last-run.jsonl` (or\n`/tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl` when the map directory has no\n`tmp/` symlink). One line per event, append-only as the run\nproceeds. The file is the authoritative record of what happened\n— the stderr summary is a quick glance; the transcript is the\naudit trail.\n\nDefault events (always emitted):\n\n| Event           | When |\n|-----------------|------|\n| `run_start`     | runner starts |\n| `task_submit`   | a box gets queued to fire |\n| `task_start`    | a worker picks it up |\n| `task_end`      | the box's function returns; carries duration_us, output_size |\n| `run_end`       | every task drained, no more queued |\n\nFor runtime graph mutations (issue 319 self-construction):\n\n| Event         | When |\n|---------------|------|\n| `box_create`  | `create_box` succeeds; records the new box's id + kind + lang + ref + fn |\n| `wire_add`    | `connect` succeeds; records the from→to wire |\n| `slot_alloc`  | a runtime-created box allocates an input slot |\n\nOpt-in verbosity, via env vars:\n\n- `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1` — adds `task_input` / `task_output`\n  events with the byte payloads (truncated to 4 KB per record).\n  Useful for inspecting what flowed where.\n- `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1` — adds the startup slot-layout\n  enumeration AND a per-push event (`push`) for every\n  dispatch-side wire push. The `push` event's `result` field\n  carries either `\"ok\"` or a short skip reason\n  (`\"input-slots-null\"`, `\"to-input-out-of-range\"`, etc.) — the\n  load-bearing diagnostic when a box fires but the value\n  doesn't seem to reach its consumer.\n\nSample (a runtime-create run with `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1`):\n\n```jsonl\n{\"event\":\"slot_alloc\",\"ts\":...,\"slot_id\":0,\"cell_capacity\":4,...,\"box\":\"trigger\",\"port\":\"input\"}\n{\"event\":\"run_start\",\"ts\":...,\"map\":\"runtime-planner\",\"n_workers\":14}\n{\"event\":\"task_submit\",\"ts\":...,\"task_id\":0,\"box_id\":\"trigger\",\"worker_idx\":-1}\n{\"event\":\"task_start\",\"ts\":...,\"task_id\":0,\"worker_idx\":3}\n{\"event\":\"slot_alloc\",\"ts\":...,\"slot_id\":1,\"box\":\"auto_00000000\",\"port\":\"x\"}\n{\"event\":\"box_create\",\"ts\":...,\"box_id\":\"auto_00000000\",\"kind\":\"call\",\"lang\":\"lua\",...}\n{\"event\":\"wire_add\",\"ts\":...,\"from_box\":\"trigger\",\"to_box\":\"auto_00000000\",\"to_input\":\"x\"}\n{\"event\":\"push\",\"ts\":...,\"from_box\":\"trigger\",\"to_box\":\"auto_00000000\",\"slot_id\":1,\"result\":\"ok\"}\n{\"event\":\"task_end\",\"ts\":...,\"task_id\":0,\"duration_us\":418,\"output_size\":46}\n{\"event\":\"task_start\",\"ts\":...,\"task_id\":1,\"worker_idx\":11}\n{\"event\":\"task_end\",\"ts\":...,\"task_id\":1,\"duration_us\":78,\"output_size\":64}\n{\"event\":\"run_end\",\"ts\":...,\"duration_us\":3820,\"n_tasks\":2}\n```\n\nThe transcript is line-oriented and JSON-shaped, so any tool\nthat handles JSON Lines (jq, log aggregators, your own parser)\ningests it directly. The line-per-event shape also means a\ncrash mid-run leaves a recoverable file — the writer just stops\nappending; existing lines are intact.\n\n## The compile pipeline\n\n`scripts/soramech-compile.sh` bundles a map into a portable\nartifact:\n\n```bash\n./scripts/soramech-compile.sh <map-dir>\n```\n\nThe artifact lives at `<map-dir>/compiled/` and contains:\n\n- `meta.json`, `boxes/`, `src/`, `data/` — verbatim copies of\n  the map source\n- `langs/<lang>/spec.so` — the language plugins the map needs\n- `bin/<box>.so` — pre-compiled C boxes (informational; the\n  runner still lazy-compiles from `src/` if a `.so` is missing)\n- `pool-runner` — a copy of `soramech-pool` (a real copy, not a\n  symlink, so the binary discovers its sibling `langs/` via\n  `/proc/self/exe`)\n- `manifest.json` — compile stats and provenance\n\nRun the compiled artifact like the source map:\n\n```bash\n./<map-dir>/compiled/pool-runner <map-dir>/compiled\n```\n\nThe artifact is self-contained — copy or symlink the directory\nanywhere on the same machine and it runs without the source\ntree, the project's `langs/`, or the project's build environment.\n\n## Reference-counted artifacts\n\nA compiled directory carries its own reference log (`.refs`).\nOther programs that hold onto a build of a map across time\n(long-running runners, sibling tools that opened the artifact\nyesterday) **acquire** a reference on startup and **release** on\nshutdown. The compile pipeline checks the log before rebuilding:\n\n- If `compiled/` doesn't exist → build there fresh.\n- If `compiled/` exists with zero live references → wipe and\n  rebuild in place (the destructive case).\n- If `compiled/` exists with **one or more** live references →\n  fork to the next `compiled.N` sibling. The original stays\n  intact for its holders.\n\nEach fork's manifest carries a `forked_from` field naming its\nparent generation, so the lineage is recoverable.\n\nHelper:\n\n```bash\n# acquire a reference (prints the assigned id to stdout)\n./scripts/soramech-ref.sh acquire <compiled-dir>\n\n# release when you're done\n./scripts/soramech-ref.sh release <compiled-dir> --id <id>\n\n# count live references\n./scripts/soramech-ref.sh count <compiled-dir>\n\n# inspect — JSON array with per-entry validity\n./scripts/soramech-ref.sh list <compiled-dir>\n\n# garbage-collect dead entries (stale PIDs, missing marker files)\n./scripts/soramech-ref.sh reap <compiled-dir>\n```\n\nThe back pointer is PID + `/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22 (start\ntime in clock ticks). PID alone isn't enough — PIDs recycle —\nso the start-time match is what distinguishes \"the original\nholder is still alive\" from \"a different process has the same\nPID now.\" An optional marker file path supplies a second\nliveness signal.\n\nThe reference count is **expected to be unreliable** by design:\na crashing holder doesn't get to release. The back pointer is\nwhat lets `list` and `reap` independently verify whether any\ngiven entry is still meaningful.\n\n## Parallelism\n\nThe runner's thread pool fires independent boxes on different\nworkers. Two boxes whose inputs both become ready at the same\nmoment will run concurrently — there's no global lock on the\ngraph.\n\nSame-box concurrent fires are gated. A box that has been\nspawned but not yet completed won't get spawned again until it\nfinishes (single-spawn invariant). The exception is iterator\nrouting and any box downstream of an iterator: those boxes are\nmarked multi-spawn, and the dispatch re-fires them while their\ninput slots have queued values to drain.\n\nCross-language wires are atomic at the value level. The slot\nstore carries values as native bytes (when both sides share a\nlanguage) or JSON (when the sides differ); the dispatch picks\nthe right format per-wire. Each consumer sees a consistent\nsnapshot of the value, never a partial one.\n\n## Quiescence\n\nThe runner exits when the work queue is empty AND every\nin-flight task has completed AND no boxes have queued values\nwaiting to fire. Long-running maps (e.g., the timer-box design\nin issue 251) prevent quiescence by re-arming after each fire —\nthe runner stays up until you Ctrl-C.\n\n## Running tests\n\n- `make test` — full ship-it suite: builds + runs the C unit\n  tests, then runs the integration fixtures.\n- `make quicktest` — cheap iteration loop: runs only the\n  already-built C unit binaries. Add `ARGS=009` to filter to\n  binaries whose names start with `009`.\n\nSee [`docs/006-test-coverage-map.md`](006-test-coverage-map.md)\nfor the test inventory.\n",
  "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/004-runtime.md"
}
```

```json
{
  "content":"# SoraMech — Writing boxes\n\nThree languages ship with first-class support: Lua, C, and Bash.\nEach follows the same dataflow contract — a box function takes\ninput values, returns one output value — but the calling shape\ndiffers per language. This doc covers each language's\nquickstart plus the runtime self-construction API every spec\nexposes.\n\n## The contract, in plain english\n\nA box function receives values for each declared input port and\nmust produce exactly one output value. The output gets pushed to\nthe box's outgoing wires by the runtime — your function doesn't\npush or fan out anything itself; you just return.\n\nInput port names are declared on the box's JSON. Input order\nmatches the JSON's `inputs[]` order. The runtime delivers values\nin that order to your function.\n\n## Lua\n\n```lua\n-- src/greeter.lua\nlocal M = {}\n\n-- A box function: receives one string, returns one string.\nfunction M.greet(name)\n    return \"Hello, \" .. name .. \"!\"\nend\n\nreturn M\n```\n\nWired up via the box JSON:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"greet\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"lua\",\n  \"ref\":  \"src/greeter.lua\",\n  \"fn\":   \"greet\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"name\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n}\n```\n\nThe Lua spec keeps a `lua_State` per worker, so consecutive\nfires of the same box reuse the same Lua state — module\nimports and closures persist across calls within a run.\n\n### Lua's runtime self-construction\n\nInside a Lua box's function, you can spawn new boxes and wire\nthem on the fly:\n\n```lua\nfunction M.planner(seed)\n    local id = soramech.create_box{\n        kind = \"call\",\n        lang = \"lua\",\n        ref  = \"src/worker.lua\",\n        fn   = \"process\",\n        inputs = { { name = \"x\", type = \"string\" } }\n    }\n    soramech.connect{\n        from_box = \"planner\",\n        to_box   = id,\n        to_input = \"x\"\n    }\n    return seed   -- the dispatch fans this to the new wire\nend\n```\n\nThe freshly-created box fires after the planner's return value\nhits its newly-attached connection. The new box's id (returned\nby `create_box`) is auto-generated unless you pass an explicit\n`id` field in the spec.\n\n### Lua values across wires\n\nThe Lua spec serialises return values to bytes for the wire.\nStrings pass through unchanged; numbers format as their JSON\nrepresentation; tables serialise to JSON; functions become a\n`$lang_opaque` sentinel that consumer Lua workers can\nreconstruct in their own state.\n\n## C\n\n```c\n// src/sqr.c\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n\nint square(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n_inputs,\n           void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)\n{\n    (void)n_inputs; (void)out_capacity;\n    // First input is a string-encoded number.\n    char tmp[64];\n    int n = sizes[0] < 63 ? sizes[0] : 63;\n    memcpy(tmp, inputs[0], n);\n    tmp[n] = '\\0';\n    long x = strtol(tmp, NULL, 10);\n    long r = x * x;\n    int written = snprintf(out_buf, out_capacity, \"%ld\", r);\n    if (written < 0 || written >= out_capacity) return -1;\n    *out_size = written;\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\nWired up:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"sqr\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"c\",\n  \"ref\":  \"src/sqr.c\",\n  \"fn\":   \"square\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"x\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n}\n```\n\nThe C spec compiles `src/sqr.c` to `<map>/bin/sqr.so` at\ncompile-pipeline time (or to a `/tmp` artifact at first dispatch\nwhen no compile pipeline has run), then `dlopen`s it.\n\n### Compile hints per box\n\nTwo optional fields on the box JSON let you tune the build:\n\n```json\n{\n  ...\n  \"cflags\":    \"-O3 -DDEBUG_FLAG=1\",\n  \"link_libs\": [\"m\", \"crypto\"]\n}\n```\n\n`cflags` strings are split on whitespace and passed as\nindividual argv entries to gcc. `link_libs` produces `-l<name>`\nentries.\n\n### C's runtime self-construction\n\nC boxes can use the same `create_box` / `connect` primitives via\nthe bindings in `langs/c/soramech.h`:\n\n```c\n#include \"soramech.h\"\n\nint planner(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n            void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)\n{\n    char id_buf[SORAMECH_BOX_ID_BUF_SIZE];\n    soramech_create_box(\n        \"{ \\\"kind\\\":\\\"call\\\", \\\"lang\\\":\\\"c\\\", \"\n        \"  \\\"ref\\\":\\\"src/worker.c\\\", \\\"fn\\\":\\\"process\\\",\"\n        \"  \\\"inputs\\\":[{\\\"name\\\":\\\"x\\\",\\\"type\\\":\\\"string\\\"}] }\",\n        id_buf, sizeof id_buf);\n    char conn[256];\n    snprintf(conn, sizeof conn,\n        \"{\\\"from_box\\\":\\\"planner\\\",\\\"to_box\\\":\\\"%s\\\",\\\"to_input\\\":\\\"x\\\"}\",\n        id_buf);\n    soramech_connect(conn);\n    /* return the seed; the dispatch fans it to the new wire */\n    memcpy(out_buf, inputs[0], sizes[0]);\n    *out_size = sizes[0];\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\n## Bash\n\n```bash\n# src/greet.sh\ngreet() {\n    local name=\"$1\"\n    echo \"Hello, $name!\"\n}\n```\n\nWired up:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\":   \"greet\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"bash\",\n  \"ref\":  \"src/greet.sh\",\n  \"fn\":   \"greet\",\n  \"inputs\":  [ { \"name\": \"name\", \"type\": \"string\" } ],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n}\n```\n\nThe Bash spec runs a persistent helper bash process per worker\nand dispatches invocations over a socketpair using a small line\nprotocol. The function reads its inputs as positional args and\nwrites its output to stdout. Function source is loaded into the\nhelper's environment once per worker; subsequent invocations\nreuse the same helper.\n\nBash doesn't have a native dict, so the runtime\nself-construction API uses JSON-string arguments (same shape as\nthe C bindings):\n\n```bash\nplanner() {\n    local id=$(soramech_create_box \\\n        '{\"kind\":\"call\",\"lang\":\"bash\",\"ref\":\"src/worker.sh\",\n          \"fn\":\"process\",\"inputs\":[{\"name\":\"x\",\"type\":\"string\"}]}')\n    soramech_connect \\\n        \"{\\\"from_box\\\":\\\"planner\\\",\\\"to_box\\\":\\\"$id\\\",\\\"to_input\\\":\\\"x\\\"}\"\n    echo \"$1\"\n}\n```\n\n(The `soramech_create_box` and `soramech_connect` bash\nfunctions get pre-defined in every worker's helper environment\nby the spec.)\n\n## Choosing a language\n\n- **Lua** — easiest, fastest iteration. Source changes pick up\n  on the next worker init. Best for planner / glue logic and\n  anything where the box body is short.\n- **C** — fastest steady-state execution. Pays a compile on the\n  first dispatch (cached after); the compile pipeline can\n  precompile every C box so the runtime doesn't pay that cost.\n  Best for tight inner loops and anything you'd write in C\n  anyway.\n- **Bash** — for boxes that wrap external CLI tools. The\n  per-call overhead is real (process IPC), so don't use it for\n  hot inner work.\n\n## Cross-language wires\n\nA wire between two boxes of the same language carries values in\nthat language's native representation. A wire between two boxes\nof different languages crosses via JSON: the producer's spec\nserialises to JSON on the way out, the consumer's spec\ndeserialises on the way in. The dispatch handles the bookkeeping;\nyour box function never sees the boundary.\n\nThe slot store carries values dual-ring per wire — native and\nJSON cells side-by-side, with a per-cell tag picking which the\nconsumer reads. This is what makes a Lua function value sent on\na Lua → Lua wire survive as a callable function on the\nconsumer's side, while the same value sent on a Lua → C wire\narrives as a JSON sentinel the C side can pass back to Lua\nunchanged.\n\n## Adding a language\n\nIf you need a fourth language (Python, JavaScript, …), the\ncontract is the `lang_spec_t` struct in `langs/lang-spec.h`:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;\n    const char *file_ext;\n    int  (*init)(int worker_idx);\n    int  (*invoke)(void *handle, ...);\n    void (*teardown)(void *handle);\n    int  (*compile)(const char *src, const char *out, const box_t *box);\n    int  (*native_to_json)(const void *handle, const void *bytes, int size,\n                           char *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size);\n    int  (*json_to_native)(const void *handle, const void *bytes, int size,\n                           char *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size);\n    /* ... see the header for the full surface */\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\nShip a `langs/<name>/spec.so` that exports a `lang_spec_t` plus\nthe registration entrypoint, and the spec registry picks it up\non startup. The Lua / C / Bash specs are working references —\n`langs/lua/spec.c` is the most heavily-commented and the easiest\nstarting point.\n",
  "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/005-writing-boxes.md"
}
```

**307 fix:** distinct `.so` paths per build, stamped with both PID + timestamp; mirrors the production discipline of unique-per-box artifact paths. 179/179 unit, 33/33 integration, three consecutive 307 runs stable.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The 307 failure was a **test bug, not a runtime bug**. The C spec was correctly passing cflags through to gcc, the build was producing genuinely different `.so` files on disk, but `dlopen`'s same-path cache kept returning the previously-loaded mapping. Production code dodges this by deriving `.so` paths from box ids (each box gets a unique path), so the cache never returns wrong content. The test was the only place where two builds raced for one path. Fixing the test rather than the spec was the right call — the spec's behaviour is correct under the assumption production gives it, and changing the spec to defensively re-`dlopen` on every invoke would slow every dispatch for a hazard no real workflow hits.
- The docs rewrite **deleted 5 files totalling ~1500 lines and replaced them with 5 files totalling ~750 lines**. The compression isn't because content was redundant — it's because the old docs were oriented around the project's development timeline (what each phase added, how features evolved). A user reading "Phase 2 used driver scripts; Phase 3 uses language specs" has to mentally compute "so what do *I* use?" The new docs answer that directly. The development-history information lives more honestly in the `issues/phase-*-progress.md` files where someone actually researching how the project got here would look.
- The big risk in this kind of doc rewrite is **losing institutional context** — the "structural shell" / apartment-building framing was a load-bearing way to think about why the runtime is shaped the way it is. I preserved a compressed version of it in the overview rather than throwing it out, because it answers the "why is X someone-else's-problem" questions that any user eventually hits. The full philosophy can live in `notes/vision`, which the ToC still points at.

17	it's running" — issue 319's `create_box` / `connect` primitives,
18	and issue 248's load-time encapsulation splice — both **add** to
19	the graph; they never **rewrite** a box that already exists. A
20	box is the box it was born as.
21	
22	This issue introduces the third path: a running box can be
23	**reconfigured** mid-run. A new configuration arrives as a
24	JSON-shaped message inside the normal input stream, on any input
25	port; the worker that's gathering inputs for the next fire
26	encounters the reconfigure tag, applies it, and continues
27	gathering under the new config before firing.
28	
29	## Concept
30	
31	Every input slot grows a **third ring** alongside the native +
32	JSON pair from issue 312. The third ring carries one kind of
33	message only — a JSON object **exactly matching the box's own
34	JSON schema**, the same shape a `boxes/<id>.json` file holds at
35	load. Any input port can carry reconfigure messages; producers
36	push to whichever port makes sense for their fan-in topology, and
37	the dispatch layer treats reconfigure cells as a peer to native
38	and JSON cells.
39	
40	The per-cell **ring-selector tag** (the bookkeeping that already
41	tells the consumer "this cell came in on the native ring, or the
42	JSON ring" — issue 312's dual-ring `which_ring` flag, extended
43	through issue 318a's per-call ordering) grows a third value:
44	**reconfigure**. When the consumer's input-gathering walks a port
45	and sees the next cell tagged `reconfigure`, it doesn't push the
46	bytes into an input buffer for the box function; it interprets
47	them as a re-parse of the box's own JSON.
48	
49	### The mixed-stream scenario
50	
51	Imagine a box with three input ports under the old config. The
52	dispatch begins gathering inputs for the next fire and pops cells
53	in turn:
54	
55	```
56	port_a → native value (popped, retained)
57	port_b → JSON value   (popped, retained)
58	port_a → native value (popped, retained — second value on a)
59	port_c → RECONFIGURE
60	```
61	
62	-- this actually will never happen. We only pop one value from each slot per box
63	   execution cycle. We should do a quick audit to ensure the design reflects this,
64	   updating current or re-opening closed issues if necessary.
65	
66	The worker:
67	
68	1. Sees the `reconfigure` tag on `port_c`'s next cell.
69	2. **Keeps every already-popped value** for ports a / b / a-second
70	   in worker-local stack buffers.
71	3. Acquires the YARQ barrier (see below). If acquisition fails
72	   because another worker is already inside the box, this worker
73	   re-submits its task to the tail of the pool queue and exits;
74	   the re-submission picks up later, after the contended box is
75	   done.
76	4. Pops the reconfigure-tagged cell, runs the JSON through the
77	   same `parse_box_file` machinery (operating on the in-memory
78	   buffer instead of a path), and rewrites the box record in
79	   place.
80	5. Releases the YARQ barrier.
81	6. Resumes input-gathering for the SAME fire — pops once more
82	   from the same port (or the next one per the new config's port
83	   shape) and continues until every required input is satisfied.
84	7. Fires the box under the new config, passing the retained
85	   already-popped values plus the new pops in the order the
86	   new config expects.
87	
88	The fire that triggered the gather still happens. The reconfigure
89	is a side-effect that lands between the start of input-gathering
90	and the function call itself, not a separate scheduling unit.
91	
92	### What about the values popped before the reconfigure?
93	
94	The retained values were popped under the OLD port shape. If the
95	new config keeps every original port (rename allowed, add allowed,
96	remove disallowed in this slice → see open questions), the
97	retained values still map by port name. If the new config renames
98	a port that has a retained value, the retained value follows the
99	rename via the port's previous-name → new-name correspondence
100	recorded during reconfigure. If a future slice allows port
101	removal mid-gather, the retained values for the removed port get
102	dropped on the floor and a JSONL event records the discard.
103	
104	## YARQ — the yield-and-requeue barrier
105	
106	A reconfigure has to be atomic with respect to other workers
107	firing the same box. While one worker is rewriting the record,
108	no other worker may read inconsistent state — half the new
109	`inputs[]` array with the old `routing.kind`, for example.
110	
111	A spinlock would work but burns a worker. The user's phrasing
112	captures the intended shape exactly:
113	
114	> "it's essentially 'hey we're not ready yet, put yourself back
115	> at the beginning of the queue please'"
116	
117	**YARQ** — yield-and-requeue — is the project name for this
118	primitive. Mechanism:
119	
120	- One atomic word on the box record (`box->yarq`, or similar).
121	- **Acquire**: CAS from 0 to 1. On success, the worker owns the
122	  box for the duration of the rewrite. On failure, the worker
123	  re-submits its current task to the **tail** of the pool queue
124	  and returns — no busy-wait, no parking, no priority inversion.
125	  The tail (rather than the head) is the **longest distance from
126	  re-running**: the contended worker doesn't immediately
127	  re-collide with whoever is currently inside the barrier; other
128	  pending work runs first.
129	- **Release**: atomic store of 0.
130	
131	The cost is one extra trip through the scheduler for each
132	contended worker. The benefit is that the synchronization
133	primitive is *cooperative with the scheduler* rather than
134	*adversarial to it* — the scheduler keeps doing what it does
135	best (managing many small units of work fairly), and the barrier
136	just nudges contended workers to circle back later.
137	
138	The YARQ barrier is acquired by **every** path that mutates the
139	box record — not just reconfigure but also `connect` (issue
140	319d's runtime wire attachment, which already does its own
141	copy-and-publish atomic dance on the connections array). Folding
142	those into the same barrier means the two mutation paths can't
143	interleave dangerously when both fire at once.
144	
145	-- workers who are just executing the box function should not claim the yarq.
146	   they don't need it - they're just reading values, not mutating them.
147	
148	## Schema for the third-ring message
149	
150	A message on the third ring is a JSON object identical in shape
151	to what `parse_box_file` parses today:
152	
153	```json
154	{
155	    "id":      "my_box",          // must match the target box
156	    "kind":    "call",            // any kind, including a kind change
157	    "lang":    "lua",
158	    "ref":     "lib/new_impl.lua",
159	    "fn":      "new_handler",
160	    "routing": { "kind": "plain" },
161	    "inputs":  [
162	        { "name": "x", "type": "string" },
163	        { "name": "y", "type": "string", "optional": true }
164	    ],
165	    "connections": [
166	        { "to_box": "next", "to_input": "value" }
167	    ]
168	}
169	```
170	
171	The `id` field MUST match the target box (a safety check; mixed
172	ids hard-error). Every other field is the new state. Fields
173	absent get default treatment (same as a freshly-parsed box file).
174	The schema validator runs in full — a malformed reconfigure
175	can't half-apply.
176	
177	## Reconfigure semantics — what changes
178	
179	**Slice 1 supports every field comprehensively.** No "cheap vs
180	medium vs expensive" split; the same machinery that parses a box
181	at load time runs against the in-memory reconfigure buffer and
182	applies the result wholesale. Splitting the work into easy /
183	hard tiers means coming back later to finish, and round-trips
184	are where details get forgotten.
185	
186	That means slice 1 has to handle, in one pass:
187	
188	- **Cheap-field rewrites** (lang / ref / fn / routing.kind /
189	  routing.comparand / routing.weights / output_capacity /
190	  returns / cflags / link_libs / headers) — pointer assignments
191	  on the live record. The arena holds the strings; the rewrite
192	  swaps pointers.
193	- **Connections array swap** — uses the same copy-and-publish
194	  pattern issue 319d established for `box_add_connection`,
195	  except wholesale-replace instead of append. Old array goes to
196	  the graph's stale list and is freed at graph_destroy.
197	- **Input port shape changes** — adding, removing, renaming
198	  ports. Triggers:
199	  - Slot-store growth or shrink (issue 319b's slot growth in
200	    the additive case; symmetric drain-and-release in the
201	    removal case).
202	  - Re-resolution of every producer's connection
203	    `to_input_idx` against the new port names.
204	  - Rebinding of retained pre-pop values via the old-name →
205	    new-name correspondence (rename allowed; removal of a
206	    retained port drops its values to the JSONL transcript).
207	- **Kind changes** (BOX_CALL ↔ BOX_WRITE, etc.) — the dispatch
208	  table is already keyed off kind; flipping the field flips
209	  which branch runs next. BOX_MAP is the special case (would
210	  re-trigger the encapsulation pass) — see open questions.
211	
212	A reconfigure that hands in an invalid spec is a hard error: the
213	box dies, the JSONL transcript records the failure with the
214	offending JSON, the run terminates. No silent reject-and-continue
215	— matches the project's "errors over fallbacks" rule.
216	
217	## How the third ring gets fed
218	
219	Two complementary mechanisms, symmetric with issue 319's
220	create_box / connect:
221	
222	1. **A `reconfigure` box kind** — one input port `spec` carries
223	   the box-JSON, one field (or a second input port) names the
224	   target box id and the target's input port to push the message
225	   onto. On fire, the box pushes the reconfigure-tagged cell onto
226	   the target slot's third ring.
227	
228	2. **A runtime API** —
229	   `runtime_reconfigure(target_id, target_port, json, size, err)`
230	   — that any language spec's invoke can call. Same shape as
231	   `runtime_create_box` and `runtime_connect` from issue 319d.
232	
233	A box can reconfigure itself by pushing onto its own third ring;
234	the next time the dispatch gathers inputs for this box, the
235	reconfigure lands.
236	
237	## Suggested implementation steps
238	
239	1. **Extend the per-cell ring-selector tag** in
240	   `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}`. The dual-ring slot's `which_ring`
241	   field grows a third value (`RING_RECONFIGURE`).
242	2. **Add the third ring to every input slot.** Same shape as the
243	   JSON ring (variable-size cells, large-value-heap backed). Cell
244	   capacity per slot is small (8? 16?) — reconfigures shouldn't
245	   pile up faster than the box can apply them.
246	3. **Add the YARQ barrier field** to `box_t`
247	   (`src/010-graph-loader.h`). One `_Atomic int`;
248	   acquire / release / yield-and-requeue helpers in
249	   `src/012-dispatch.c`.
250	4. **Fold issue 319d's `box_add_connection` into YARQ.** Today
251	   it has its own copy-and-publish atomic dance; sharing the
252	   barrier keeps mutation paths from racing.
253	5. **Refactor `parse_box_file`** so the JSON-parsing core
254	   accepts an in-memory buffer (not just a file path). The
255	   reconfigure path uses the same parser; one schema, one
256	   validator, two entry points.
257	6. **Add a `reconfigure_apply` function** in
258	   `src/010-graph-loader.c` that takes a parsed box record and
259	   merges it into a live box, handling port-rename via name
260	   correspondence, slot growth / shrink, connection array swap,
261	   and producer re-resolution.
262	7. **Teach the dispatch's input-gather loop** to peek the
263	   ring-selector tag and, on `RING_RECONFIGURE`, acquire YARQ,
264	   retain pre-popped values, apply the reconfigure, release
265	   YARQ, then resume gathering under the new shape.
266	8. **Implement the `reconfigure` box kind** in
267	   `src/012-dispatch.c` and add parse-side support in
268	   `src/010-graph-loader.c`.
269	9. **Add `runtime_reconfigure`** to
270	   `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}`.
271	10. **JSONL event** for every reconfigure: full before / after
272	    (or at least the changed fields), task id, worker id.
273	    Reconfigures change behaviour mid-run; the audit log must
274	    show them.
275	11. **Fixtures**:
276	    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-routing/` — comparator routing
277	      flipped to iterator routing mid-run; downstream
278	      connections fire on the new branches.
279	    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-fn/` — same box, different
280	      function on the same lang; output changes mid-stream.
281	    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-port-shape/` — input port
282	      added (slot store growth) and renamed (producer
283	      re-resolution); pre-popped retained values still land on
284	      the right inputs.
285	    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-kind/` — BOX_CALL flipped to
286	      BOX_WRITE; subsequent fires write to disk instead of
287	      invoking a function.
288	    - `tests/maps/320-yarq-contended/` — two reconfigure-feeders
289	      race on the same target; both reconfigures land, neither
290	      is lost, the box behaves correctly after both apply.
291	
292	## Relevant files
293	
294	- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — ring-selector tag, third ring
295	  storage per slot.
296	- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — `parse_box_file` refactor,
297	  `reconfigure_apply`, YARQ field on box_t.
298	- `src/012-dispatch.c` — dispatch input-gather changes, YARQ
299	  acquire / release / yield-and-requeue, `reconfigure` box kind.
300	- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — `runtime_reconfigure` entry
301	  point for language specs.
302	- `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` — reconfigure event emission.
303	- `issues/319-builtin-library-for-map-self-construction.md` —
304	  sister issue: create_box / connect are the additive
305	  primitives, this is the mutative primitive.
306	- `issues/318a-per-call-output-format-threads-to-push.md` and
307	  `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — the per-cell
308	  ring-selector mechanism the third ring extends.
309	- `issues/319b-slot-store-growth.md` — slot growth in the
310	  additive port-add direction; symmetric shrink is new.
311	
312	## Open questions
313	
314	- **Scheduler ordering between value-pops and reconfigure-pops.**
315	  The mixed-stream scenario above shows reconfigure cells
316	  interleaved with value cells on the same input port; the
317	  consumer encounters them in producer-push order. Is that
318	  ordering strict per port, or strict across all ports of the
319	  box (so a reconfigure on port A blocks pops from port B until
320	  it's applied)? The cleanest reading of "ordered same as all
321	  the other inputs" is **strict per port**, with the consumer
322	  applying reconfigures as it hits them. Across-port ordering
323	  would need a per-box sequence number on every cell, which is
324	  more bookkeeping than the user described.
325	- **Slot growth and shrink for input port changes.** Issue 319b
326	  defined slot growth in the create_box direction; this issue
327	  extends it to the within-a-box direction (adding a new port
328	  to an existing box). Shrink — releasing a slot when a port
329	  goes away — is genuinely new and needs an issue of its own,
330	  or rolled in here as part of slice 1.
331	- **Port-rename correspondence.** When a reconfigure renames
332	  port `x` to `y`, the rename is unambiguous if both
333	  configurations declare the same number of ports in the same
334	  position-order. When the port count or order changes too,
335	  the correspondence isn't obvious — fall back to name match
336	  (ports keeping their names get rebound by name; ports
337	  whose names no longer exist get dropped). Worth documenting
338	  precisely so the implementation behaves consistently.
339	- **Recursive reconfigure / loop guard.** A box reconfigures
340	  itself, the new config includes a producer that pushes
341	  another reconfigure, etc. Cap per-box reconfigure depth per
342	  run? Or trust the user and rely on integration tests to
343	  surface infinite loops?
344	- **BOX_MAP as a reconfigure target / source.** Changing a
345	  BOX_CALL to a BOX_MAP would require re-running the
346	  encapsulation pass on just this one box. The load-time pass
347	  assumes single-pass flat-graph construction; running it
348	  per-box at runtime is structurally awkward. Probably
349	  out-of-scope unless a clear use case appears. Hard-error
350	  the BOX_MAP transition in slice 1.
351	- **Reconfigure visible in the compile artifact.** Issue 309's
352	  compile pipeline bakes the box JSONs into the built program.
353	  Reconfigure machinery is runtime-only by nature, but the
354	  compile artifact needs to keep the YARQ barrier field, the
355	  third ring per slot, and the in-memory parser path linked in
356	  regardless. Probably means slice 1 ships always-on; the
357	  per-box opt-out flag (`reconfigurable: false`) is a future
358	  refinement if anyone needs the slot-store savings.
359	- **JSONL event shape.** Full before/after JSON is the most
360	  faithful audit trail; diff-only is smaller; "just record
361	  the new state" loses the before. Default: full before/after
362	  so the transcript is self-describing without cross-event
363	  reasoning.
364	- **Pre-popped retained values that don't fit the new schema.**
365	  Reconfigure renames port `x` → `y` and adds port `z`; the
366	  worker had already popped a value for `x` before hitting
367	  the reconfigure cell. Rebind by name correspondence? If
368	  the new config has no port `y` after a removal-rename
369	  (effectively a delete), the retained value goes to the
370	  JSONL transcript as a discard event and the box still fires
371	  with whatever the new shape requires.
372	
373	## Design history
374	
375	The shape of this issue evolved across two passes. The first
376	draft (now discarded) proposed a per-box config inbox treated as
377	a separate scheduling unit — i.e. reconfigure as its own task,
378	distinct from any fire. The user redirected to **per-port**
379	placement, with reconfigure cells riding the same ring-selector
380	tag mechanism that already distinguishes native from JSON cells
381	on each port. The mixed-stream scenario described in the
382	"Concept" section is the user's clarifying example.
383	
384	The YARQ name landed in the same conversation. The user's
385	phrasing:
386	
387	> "yield and requeue works. yarq for short. YARQ what a weird
388	> name!! I want to name my dog yarq. BARK BARK says yarq, haha
389	> what a cute puppy ^_^"
390	
391	So: YARQ in the code, YARQ in the docs, and somewhere out there
392	a dog who answers to the same name. Both kinds of YARQ go where
393	the scheduler tells them — that's the joke and that's the
394	mechanism.
395	
396	On the YARQ requeue target (tail vs head of the pool queue),
397	the user's instruction was:
398	
399	> "put it at the part of the queue that has the longest time
400	> until running again. I think that's the end of the queue, but
401	> you can decide. The tip of the tail maybe? snakes move
402	> forward after all..."
403	
404	End-of-queue (the "tip of the tail") is the chosen default.
405	The contended worker won't immediately re-collide with whoever
406	is inside the barrier; the scheduler gets a chance to drain
407	other pending work first.
408	
409	On scoping, the user's direction was decisive:
410	
411	> "they should all be configurable with the same interface,
412	> so... don't split up the work in that way. Just do it
413	> comprehensively the first time so we don't forget anything
414	> on the return trip."
415	
416	Slice 1 covers every reconfigurable field — including the
417	port-shape changes that require slot store growth / shrink and
418	producer re-resolution. No tiered "cheap then medium then
419	expensive" split; one comprehensive pass.
420	
```

54	
55	The phase 2 single-document format does not work when the runner is

57	JSON object per line, each line is one event, the file grows
58	monotonically as the run proceeds.

117	extension reflects the format change). Overwritten on every run.
118	
119	A rotated archive (`last-run.jsonl.1`, `.2`, …) is out of scope.
120	Users who want history copy the file before re-running.
121	
122	## Part B — Integration tests
123	
124	### Scope
125	
126	End-to-end tests of the pool runner against real map directories.
127	Each test is:
128	
129	1. A map directory under `tests/maps/<name>/`
130	2. An expected `last-run.jsonl` (or a comparison spec) under
131	   `tests/expected/<name>.jsonl`
132	3. A test driver script that runs the map and diffs
133	
134	The test driver is `scripts/run-tests.sh`. It iterates
135	`tests/maps/`, runs each, diffs against expected (with a normalizer
136	that drops timestamps, durations, worker indices — anything non-
137	deterministic), and reports pass/fail.
138	
139	### Test maps
140	
141	Coverage targets:
142	
143	| Test map                  | What it exercises                                    |
144	|---------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
145	| `hello`                   | Single Lua box, one input, one output                |
146	| `data-only`               | Data box → call box. No inputs, just stored values   |
147	| `fan-out-3`               | One output → three consumer boxes (peek, refcount)   |
148	| `fan-in-iterator`         | Three producers → iterator with queued input         |
149	| `comparator-routing`      | Comparator with all three branches (lt/eq/gt)        |
150	| `iterator-100`            | Iterator with 100 input values, round-robin to 3 paths |
151	| `multilang`               | One Lua box, one C box, one Bash box, all wired      |
152	| `large-output`            | Box producing a 1 MB string (variable-size heap)     |
153	| `cycle-detector-fail`     | Non-iterator cycle — load must abort                 |
154	| `missing-input-fail`      | Connection references a nonexistent box — load aborts|
155	| `box-error-fail`          | Box function returns nonzero — runner aborts         |
156	
157	The `*-fail` tests verify error behavior — the runner is expected
158	to exit nonzero with a precise error message. The driver matches
159	exit code and stderr against expected.
160	
161	### Test driver
162	
163	```bash
164	# scripts/run-tests.sh
165	for test_dir in tests/maps/*/; do
166	    name=$(basename "${test_dir}")
167	    expected="tests/expected/${name}.jsonl"
168	
169	    actual=$( "${SOURCE_DIR}/soramech-pool" "${test_dir}" )
170	    rc=$?
171	
172	    if [ -f "${expected}.exit" ]; then
173	        # *-fail tests: assert exit code and stderr substring
174	        check_failure "${name}" "${rc}" "${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl"
175	    else
176	        # success tests: diff normalized last-run.jsonl
177	        check_success "${name}" "${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl" "${expected}"
178	    fi
179	done
180	```
181	
182	`normalize_jsonl` strips timestamps, durations, worker indices,
183	slot ids, and task ids (all non-deterministic) and sorts events by
184	event type. The result should be deterministic across runs.
185	
186	### Phase 3 demo map
187	
188	A single map under `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/` that
189	demonstrates everything working together:
190	
191	- Multiple entry-point data boxes
192	- Lua, C, and Bash boxes all wired together
193	- An iterator with a queued input
194	- A comparator routing into different downstream paths
195	- A large-output box (variable-size heap)
196	- Non-trivial graph topology (≥ 10 boxes)
197	
198	Run with `./run.sh` from the demo directory. Prints a short summary
199	of what happened (parsing the `last-run.jsonl`) so the demo is
200	visible without a viewer utility.
201	
202	This satisfies the standing project rule (CLAUDE.md) that each
203	phase produces a runnable demo in `issues/completed/demos/`.
204	
205	### Test infrastructure constraints
206	
207	- Tests must not depend on the editor or any HTTP server
208	- Tests must not depend on internet access
209	- Tests must run in under 60 seconds total on a developer machine
210	- Tests must be deterministic when normalized (any
211	  non-determinism is normalized out, not papered over with retries)
212	
213	## Open questions
214	
215	- Whether to log inputs/outputs by default. Useful for development,
216	  noisy for production. Current decision: opt-in via env var,
217	  default off.
218	- Slot-event logging: also opt-in. Useful for diagnosing memory
219	  issues. Off by default.
220	- File format: JSON Lines is the choice. An alternative was a
221	  protobuf or msgpack binary log, which is faster to write but
222	  harder to inspect by hand. JSONL wins on inspectability.
223	- Whether to keep timestamps as Unix epoch floats or ISO 8601
224	  strings. Epoch floats are smaller and easier to diff. Stick with
225	  floats.
226	
227	## Suggested implementation sequence
228	
229	### Run output (Part A)
230	1. Define the event struct and JSONL line format. Start with
231	   `run_start`, `task_start`, `task_end`, `run_end`.
232	2. Implement the MPSC ring buffer for events.
233	3. Implement the writer thread: pulls from ring, serializes,
234	   appends a line to the output file.
235	4. Wire event emission into the pool runner: `run_start` at
236	   startup, `task_start` and `task_end` in the dispatch action,
237	   `run_end` after quiescence.
238	5. Add the verbosity env vars and the optional event types.
239	
240	### Tests (Part B)
241	6. Create `tests/maps/` and `tests/expected/` directory structure.
242	7. Write the `hello` test as the first end-to-end smoke check.
243	8. Write the test driver `scripts/run-tests.sh` and the JSONL
244	   normalizer.
245	9. Add tests one at a time as each runtime feature lands. The
246	   `*-fail` tests can land before their corresponding successful
247	   tests if the failure path is implemented first.
248	10. Build the phase 3 demo map under `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/`
249	    once the rest of phase 3 is implemented.
250	
251	## Relevant files
252	
253	- `scripts/run-tests.sh` — test driver (to be written)
254	- `tests/maps/`, `tests/expected/` — test fixtures (to be created)
255	- `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/` — phase 3 demo (to be built)
256	- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — emits run_start / run_end
257	- `src/dispatch.c` — emits task_start / task_end
258	- `src/slot-store.c` — emits slot_alloc / slot_free (verbose mode)
259	- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle
260	- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot events
261	- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task lifecycle events
262	- `issues/305-c-graph-loader.md` — load-time errors
263	- `issues/309-build-system.md` — `make test` invokes this
264	- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — blocking semantics relevant to
265	  test design
266	
267	## Implementation log
268	
269	### JSON writer half — 2026-05-12
270	
271	`libs/json/json.c` had stub writer bodies left over from 314's
272	parser milestone; this pass filled them in. The writer maintains
273	a small depth stack (capped at 16) where each entry packs two
274	booleans — "next element is first" and "this level is an
275	object." That's enough to handle comma placement and pick the
276	right close bracket. Overflow of the caller-supplied buffer is
277	sticky on `w->err`; `json_writer_finish` reports it.
278	
279	Eight new writer tests in `tests/314-json-test.c` cover the
280	primitives, escape encoding, empty and non-empty containers,
281	nesting depth, overflow detection, and a round-trip where the
282	writer emits an object that the parser then decodes and the test
283	verifies via the accessor API.
284	
285	Still ahead for 311: the JSONL event writer (a thin wrapper that
286	serializes `task_start` / `task_end` / `run_start` / `run_end`
287	records using this writer), the MPSC ring buffer the worker
288	threads push events into, and the dedicated writer thread that
289	drains them.
290	
291	### Event emitters — 2026-05-12
292	
293	`src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` ships the per-event emit functions
294	on top of issue 314's bounded writer:
295	
296	- `jsonl_emit_run_start(w, ts, map, n_workers)`
297	- `jsonl_emit_task_submit(w, ts, task_id, box_id, worker_idx)`
298	- `jsonl_emit_task_start(w, ts, task_id, worker_idx)`
299	- `jsonl_emit_task_end(w, ts, task_id, worker_idx, duration_us, output_size)`
300	- `jsonl_emit_run_end(w, ts, duration_us, n_tasks)`
301	
302	Each emit serializes into a fixed 512-byte buffer, appends a
303	newline, and writes to a `FILE *` under a per-writer mutex. The
304	MPSC ring + dedicated writer thread aren't there yet — the mutex
305	is a placeholder until dispatch is producing events fast enough
306	to justify the contention.
307	
308	`tests/013-jsonl-events-test.c` writes a full sequence, slurps
309	the file back, and parses each line through 314's JSON parser to
310	verify the event shape. A concurrent-emit test runs 8 producer
311	threads each emitting 200 events into the same writer and
312	verifies every line round-trips.
313	
314	Still ahead inside 311: slot-event opt-in
315	(`SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1`), inputs/outputs opt-in
316	(`SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1`), the MPSC ring + writer thread, and
317	the integration-test harness map fixtures.
318	
319	### Multi-producer event queue + writer thread — 2026-05-12
320	
321	`src/014-event-queue.{c,h}` ships the producer-side queue and the
322	dedicated writer thread. Producers (worker threads + the main
323	thread) call `event_queue_run_start` / `task_submit` / `task_start`
324	/ `task_end` / `run_end`; each emit appends a small fixed-size
325	event record under a brief mutex and signals a CV. The writer
326	thread sleeps on the CV, snapshots the queue head into a local
327	batch under the lock, then drains the batch outside the lock —
328	JSON encoding + fwrite happen with zero producer contention.
329	
330	Four unit tests in `tests/014-event-queue-test.c` cover single
331	producer / multi-thread burst (8 producers × 250 events each =
332	2000 lines, all round-trip through the JSON parser) / shutdown-
333	drain / pending-count.
334	
335	The dispatch action (issue 304) opt-in emits task_start and
336	task_end events with monotonic-clock durations via the queue;
337	the pool runner emits run_start and run_end. `soramech-pool`
338	writes to `map_dir/tmp/last-run.jsonl` when that directory
339	exists, falling back to `/tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl`.
340	
341	What's still ahead inside 311:
342	- Lock-free Vyukov MPSC ring with sequence numbers — the
343	  architecture doc's preferred design. The mutex queue is a
344	  placeholder; upgrade once contention shows up.
345	- Opt-in slot events and per-task input/output dumps.
346	
347	### Integration test runner — 2026-05-12
348	
349	`scripts/run-tests.sh` runs every fixture map under `tests/maps/`
350	through `soramech-pool` and asserts the expected box-output
351	substrings show up in stderr. `make test` invokes the script
352	after the unit tests so a full `make test` covers everything
353	from slot operations all the way through end-to-end Lua / C /
354	Bash dispatch via JSONL logging.
355	
356	Six fixture checks at the moment:
357	- `calc`            — single Lua `add → 42`
358	- `hello`           — data → Lua, `greet → "Hello, World!"`
359	- `comparator`      — `high` fires, `low` / `mid` don't
360	- `iter-route`      — single-fire iterator picks `out_0` → `a`
361	- `pipeline`        — five-box multilang chain
362	- `pipeline file`   — verifies the file_write sink wrote
363	  `"11!"` to `/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt`
364	
365	### Runtime-mutation and per-push events — 2026-05-24
366	
367	Three new events extend the JSONL transcript to cover the
368	runtime self-construction path from issue 319, which previously
369	left no trace in the log even with `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1`
370	because the events fire from inside a spec's invoke rather than
371	from the dispatch's task lifecycle.
372	
373	- **`box_create`** — fires from `runtime_create_box` after the
374	  new box is published into the graph. Records id, kind, lang,
375	  ref, fn. Always emits when an event queue is open (rare and
376	  load-bearing — no verbosity gate).
377	- **`wire_add`** — fires from `runtime_connect` after the
378	  connection is appended to the producer's array. Records
379	  from_box, from_branch, to_box, to_input. Always emits.
380	- **`slot_alloc`** (runtime variant) — fires from
381	  `runtime_create_box`'s per-input-port slot allocation loop.
382	  Same shape as the startup slot enumeration but for the
383	  runtime path. Always emits.
384	- **`push`** — fires from `push_one_connection` on every
385	  attempt, with a `result` field carrying either `"ok"` or a
386	  short skip reason (`no-to-box-idx`, `dst-null`,
387	  `input-slots-null`, `to-input-out-of-range`, `push-failed`).
388	  Opt-in via `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1` — would be too noisy by
389	  default. Crucial for diagnosing the latent visibility race
390	  noted on 319's completed status: a `push` event with
391	  `result=input-slots-null` is the immediately-recognisable
392	  signature.
393	
394	The runtime context that `dispatch_action` publishes via TLS
395	grew an `event_queue *` slot so the runtime builtins reach the
396	same writer the dispatch uses. The pool runner reads
397	`SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS` into a `ctx->log_slots` flag that gates
398	both the startup slot enumeration AND the per-push events —
399	one env var, one slot-level verbosity story.
400	
401	End-to-end check: running `319d-runtime-create` with
402	`SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1` produces a transcript where the
403	mutation timeline is fully visible — `task_start →
404	slot_alloc → box_create → wire_add → push(result=ok) →
405	task_submit → task_end → task_start → task_end`. If the
406	visibility race resurfaces under some build layout, the push
407	event flips to `result=input-slots-null` and the diagnosis is
408	in the log without a rebuild.
409	
410	What's still ahead inside 311:
411	- Lock-free Vyukov MPSC ring with sequence numbers — the
412	  architecture doc's preferred design. The mutex queue is a
413	  placeholder; upgrade once contention shows up.
414	- JSONL normalizer for diff-based test verification (currently
415	  the test harness uses substring matching against stderr).
416	
417	### Phase-3 demo — 2026-05-24
418	
419	`issues/completed/demos/phase-3-runtime-planner/` is the phase-3
420	deliverable: a Lua planner box receives a seed string and uses
421	`soramech.create_box` + `soramech.connect` inside its invoke to
422	spawn three downstream worker boxes mid-run (each running a
423	different transformation function from `src/worker.lua`), then
424	fans the seed value into all three. The accompanying `run.sh`
425	runs the map with `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES` and `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS`
426	on and extracts the story from the JSONL transcript: the seed
427	value, the boxes that got created mid-run, the wires that got
428	added, each worker's distinct output, and a small statistics
429	block (tasks fired, runtime slots, runtime boxes, runtime wires,
430	total duration).
431	
432	Top-level `demo.sh 3` invokes the demo's own `run.sh`, matching
433	the existing phase-1 pattern. The new demo proves end-to-end
434	that the C thread pool runner (301), the slot store (302), the
435	Lua spec (306), the dispatch (304), the runtime self-construction
436	primitives (319), and the JSONL transcript with the new
437	runtime-mutation events all work together on a single map.
438	
```

```
1	# 009-slot-store.c — public surface
2	
3	Per-input-port slot store. Allocated once at graph load; each box
4	input port owns one slot, freed when the run ends. The dispatch
5	layer reads and writes through this API; language specs never see
6	slot IDs (issue 303 keeps that boundary clean).
7	
8	## Lifecycle
9	
10	- `slot_store_t *slot_store_create(void)` — empty store; NULL on OOM.
11	- `void slot_store_destroy(slot_store_t *s)` — frees every slot.
12	
13	## Allocation
14	
15	- `slot_id_t slot_alloc(store, cell_capacity, n_cells, flags)`
16	  - Returns `SLOT_INVALID` on bad args / OOM.
17	  - Flags: `SLOT_FLAG_NONE`, `SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED`, `SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER`.
18	  - `cell_capacity` and `n_cells` are ignored for atomic-counter slots.
19	
20	## Ring-buffer ops (push / peek / pop / has_value / fill_count)
21	
22	- `int slot_push(store, id, data, size, tag)` — 0 on success, -1 on
23	  full / wrong type / size too big.
24	- `int32_t slot_peek(store, id, buf, buf_size)` — returns the cell's
25	  filled_size on success; -1 on empty / wrong type / buf too small.
26	  Does not advance head. Used for 1-cell peek slots.
27	- `int32_t slot_pop(store, id, buf, buf_size)` — drains. Untagged
28	  pops head FIFO; tagged pops the lowest-tag filled cell.
29	- `int slot_has_value(store, id)` — 1 if a value is available.
30	- `int32_t slot_fill_count(store, id)` — number of filled cells.
31	
32	## Atomic-counter slot
33	
34	- `uint32_t slot_read_inc(store, id, mod)` — fetch-and-add. Returns
35	  the pre-increment counter value mod the supplied bound.
36	  `UINT32_MAX` on wrong type or `mod == 0`.
37	
38	## Thread safety
39	
40	- The atomic-counter slot uses `atomic_fetch_add_explicit`; no lock.
41	- Ring-buffer slots use a per-slot `atomic_flag` spinlock around
42	  header + cell mutations.
43	- The store itself is single-threaded for allocation (graph-load
44	  phase); after that, the slot array is read-only and per-slot
45	  operations run concurrently.
46	
47	## Variable-size payloads
48	
49	Slots allocated with `SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE` store payload bytes in
50	the unified allocator (016) and keep only an opaque chunk handle in
51	the cell. Push acquires a chunk (refcount 1, owned by the slot);
52	pop copies the bytes into the caller's buffer and drops the
53	reference, returning the chunk to the allocator's free-lists with
54	an eager neighbor-merge. The reclamation test
55	(`tests/009-slot-store-test.c::large_value_reclamation`) is the
56	regression guard for the previous monotonic-growth path.
57	
58	`slot_store_large_value_bytes_in_use` exposes the allocator's
59	"in use" total for the regression test and for future telemetry.
60	
61	## What's NOT here (deferred)
62	
63	- Size-class free lists for the fixed-size cell arrays themselves —
64	  plain `malloc` per slot for now. Allocator-driven cell allocation
65	  is the next step in issue 302.
66	- Producer-declared output sizes are not yet piped through to
67	  `ua_create`, so the allocator starts with no pre-warmed classes
68	  and learns them by accretion. The graph loader integration is
69	  the follow-on.
70	
71	## Related
72	
73	- Issue 302 — design.
74	- Issue 304 — the dispatch layer that calls this API.
75	- Issue 301 — the pool whose workers contend on these slots.
76	
```
