You're catching a really deep problem and proposing a really clever solution. Let me work through both halves separately.

## On garbage collection paranoia

You've hit on something fundamental: **in a system that allows runtime creation and reconfiguration, you genuinely cannot prove a box will never run again.** Any currently-running box could call create_box-with-connection-to-Y, or reconfigure-some-existing-box-to-connect-to-Y. There's no finite analysis that says "this box is unreachable forever."

This is the same problem Java's GC solves with mark-and-sweep, and it's the same problem the Linux kernel deals with via epoch-based reclamation. The general lesson: **you can't reason locally about reachability in a system that allows arbitrary mutation.** You either need a global walk (expensive) or you accept the leak.

For this codebase, I'd actually argue the right answer is: **don't try to GC live boxes at all.** Here's the reasoning chain:

- The refcount system handles SUPERSEDED boxes (the reconfigure cleanup case). That's the only "lifetime ends mid-run" we genuinely need.
- For boxes that just sit idle with no incoming values — they're not freed, they're just dormant. They consume metadata-sized memory (one box record + slot ids), which is tiny. The values that would otherwise pile up in their slot ring buffers aren't there, because no producer is feeding them.
- For the case where a user genuinely wants a box destroyed during a run: add an explicit `runtime_destroy_box(id)` API. The user knows when their planner box is done planning. Trust them.
- Runs are bounded. When the run ends (quiescence), everything gets cleaned up by graph_destroy.

The leak you're worried about — "what if we have too many boxes cluttering up memory" — would only show up in extremely long-running maps that constantly create new boxes without destroying old ones. Each box is ~200 bytes plus its slots. You'd need to create literally millions of boxes for this to matter on a workstation. Maps that long would have other architectural concerns anyway.

**My proposal:** refcount handles superseded-box reclamation (automatic, transparent). Explicit destroy handles user-requested-destruction (rare, opt-in). Nothing tries to be clever about reachability. The leak case is real but practically negligible.

## On the multi-reconfigure question

OK so let me try to simplify what you described, because I think there's a cleaner shape hiding inside your description, and the cleaner shape eliminates the "what if values for first but not second" edge case entirely.

You're absolutely right that **peeking the ordering messages first (without popping any values) is the right move.** That part is the key insight. Let me re-state it in your terms: every input ring has, riding alongside the native and json rings, a third ring that's the **ordering ring** — it stores tags saying "the next value on this slot is in the native ring" or "...is in the json ring" or "this is a reconfigure message, not a value." The ordering ring's head tells you what kind of thing is up next, without committing to consume the actual value or message yet.

So the worker's hot path becomes:

```
worker arrives at box:
   1. for each input port, peek the head of its ordering ring (just the tag, no consume).
   2. branch on what you saw:
        no reconfigures anywhere AND all ports have a value waiting:
           → pop one ordering tag from each port,
             follow each tag to its native/json ring,
             pop the value,
             fire the box.

        at least one port shows RECONFIGURE at its head:
           → try CAS to become the mutator. yield if you lose.

        no reconfigures, but some ports are empty:
           → don't pop anything. nothing to fire yet. exit; the pool
             will re-spawn this box when more values arrive.
```

Now for the multi-reconfigure case — here's where I want to push back on the "build multiple tasks for multiple epochs" idea. **I don't think we need it.** Let me show why with your scenario.

### Walking through your hard case

Setup: port X has `[R1, v1]`. Port Y has `[R2, v3]`. Two reconfigures (one per port), one fire's worth of values.

Worker arrives. Peeks X → R1. Peeks Y → R2. Both reconfigures visible. Worker becomes mutator. What now?

The thing to notice: **R1 and R2 are on DIFFERENT ports.** They're not temporally ordered with respect to each other. The producer that pushed R1 onto X did so at some wall-clock moment; the producer that pushed R2 onto Y did so at some other wall-clock moment; the ring buffer system doesn't preserve cross-port ordering. So there's no "right" order for R1 vs R2 — apply them in any order, doesn't matter.

Mutator pops R1, applies it. Now the box has shape-after-R1. Mutator pops R2, applies it. Now the box has shape-after-R1-and-R2. Mutator releases.

Next worker arrives. Peeks X → v1 (head of X now). Peeks Y → v3 (head of Y now). Both are values. Pops both, fires the box with v1 and v3 under the shape-after-R1-and-R2.

**There's only one fire, and it happens after both reconfigures are applied.** The "different epochs" framing doesn't apply because the values v1 and v3 were queued BEHIND the reconfigure messages on their respective ports. So they were always meant for the post-reconfigure shape — that's what the producer signaled by ordering them that way on the ring.

If the producer had wanted v1 consumed under the pre-reconfigure shape, they would have pushed v1 FIRST, then R1. The ring would be `[v1, R1]`. Peek would show v1; a fire would happen with v1 under OLD shape; then peek would show R1; reconfigure applies; the next fire would be under NEW.

### Now the harder case — back-to-back reconfigures

Setup: port X has `[R1, R2, v1]`. Port Y has `[v3]`.

Worker peeks X → R1. Peeks Y → v3. Has a reconfigure pending. Becomes mutator.

The mutator's loop:
- Pop R1 from X. Apply it.
- Peek X again. Head is now R2 (because R1 got popped). 
- Pop R2. Apply it.
- Peek X again. Head is now v1. Not a reconfigure.
- Release mutator role. Don't fire here; let a worker do that.

Next worker arrives. Peeks X → v1, peeks Y → v3. Both values. Pop, fire.

**One fire, after both R1 and R2 are applied.** No multi-task batching.

### And the case you specifically asked about

Setup: port X has `[R1, R2]`. Port Y has `[v3]`. Two reconfigures, only one port has a value.

Worker peeks X → R1. Becomes mutator. Pops R1, applies. Peeks X → R2. Pops R2, applies. Peeks X → empty. Releases.

Next worker arrives. Peeks X → empty. Peeks Y → v3. Mixed — some ports have values, some don't. Worker can't fire. Doesn't pop anything. Exits.

The next time someone pushes a value to X, the pool will spawn a task for the box. Next worker arrives, peeks X → (whatever's there now). If it's a value AND Y still has v3, fires. Otherwise waits.

**No edge case to handle.** The "we have enough values for the first reconfigure but not the second" scenario doesn't actually exist, because reconfigures are NOT consumers of values. They're sideband messages that modify the box. Values are consumed by FIRES, and fires only happen when every required port has a value ready.

### Why I think the multi-task batching isn't needed

Your design described the mutator preparing multiple tasks for different box epochs. But under the simpler "do one thing per worker visit" model:

- Reconfigure messages get drained (in batches if multiple are visible at peek time, but only one batch per mutator visit).
- Fires happen separately, each one under the box's current shape at fire time.
- A worker either fires once OR mutates once per visit; never both, never multiple of either.

The pool's natural re-spawning handles the back-and-forth. If there are 5 reconfigures and 5 fires worth of values queued, the workflow is:
- Worker 1 visits: drains all visible reconfigures, releases.
- Worker 2 visits: drains any reconfigures that became visible after the first batch (because they were behind the first batch on the rings), or fires if values are next up.
- ...
- Eventually all reconfigures are drained and fires proceed normally.

This is slightly more pool-queue traffic than the "do everything in one mutator visit" design, but each pool round-trip is cheap (microseconds). The complexity savings are large — no multi-task batching, no epoch tracking, no "store this task pointing at the OLD box, submit it, store another pointing at NEW, submit that."

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **The "you can't prove a box won't run again" realisation is the same as the halting problem in disguise.** In a Turing-complete dataflow system (which is what we are, since boxes can create boxes and connect them dynamically), you can't statically determine reachability. The Java GC people solved this with mark-sweep; Linux kernel people solved it with epoch-based reclamation; everybody else solves it with explicit destroy. Your project's vision is closer to "explicit destroy" because runs are bounded — when the run ends, everything frees. The leak you were worried about doesn't actually accumulate across runs, just within a single run, which is bounded.
- **The "epoch tasks" idea is reinventing event sourcing.** Your instinct was: instead of mutating state and losing the history, capture the history (each reconfigure is an event) and replay tasks against each state in the history. That's exactly what event sourcing does in distributed systems. It's powerful but adds significant complexity. For this codebase, the "ring buffer ordering IS the history" framing is sufficient — values queued behind a reconfigure are implicitly "for the post-reconfigure shape." The implicit ordering replaces explicit epoch tracking.
- **The peek-don't-pop discipline solves the push-back problem entirely.** You arrived at this independently and correctly: if you commit nothing until you've inspected everything, there's nothing to put back if you bail. The same pattern shows up in database transactions (read-then-decide-then-commit), in optimistic concurrency control, and in modern parser combinators (peek-don't-consume until you know the production matches). It's a strong general pattern: in any concurrent system, prefer "look first, commit later" over "commit first, undo if wrong."
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Questions back

1. **Do you buy the "no multi-task batching, do one thing per worker visit" simplification?** It dramatically simplifies the mutator's logic and eliminates the edge case you were worried about. The cost is more pool round-trips when many reconfigures are queued — but that cost is small.

2. **Are you OK with "no GC of live boxes, only superseded ones"?** Plus an explicit `runtime_destroy_box(id)` API for users who want to actively clean up? That sidesteps the unreachability halting problem cleanly.

3. **One subtle thing about the mutator's "drain multiple visible reconfigures in one go" loop** — should there be a cap on how many it'll drain before releasing? If a malicious or buggy producer keeps pushing reconfigures faster than the mutator can apply them, the mutator could be stuck draining forever. A cap (say, 100 reconfigures per mutator visit, then release and let someone else continue) would be a safety valve. Worth adding, or YAGNI?

Once you've signed off on these, I'll update 320's issue file with the consolidated design and start implementing.

You found a genuine race, and it's the deepest problem we've hit yet. Let me think through it carefully because the answer reshapes some of what we've decided.

## Walking through what you just identified

Let me restate to make sure I understand: two workers, A and B, both arrive at the same box at roughly the same time. Both peek every input port's head. Both see `[v1, v2, v3]`. Both decide "no reconfigures, proceed to pop." A wins the pop race and gets `[v1, v2, v3]`. B's pops return `[v4, v5, R1]` — because v1, v2, v3 are gone, what B actually gets is whatever is NOW at the head of each ring.

B has popped a reconfigure message it never saw during peek. B's choice is now: apply the reconfigure (but it already popped v4 and v5, which were meant for who?), or somehow undo. Both are bad.

**Your three suggestions, evaluated:**

- *Should peeking be atomic?* Atomic across what? Atomic peek of a single ring is already true. Atomic peek across THREE rings simultaneously is the hard part — it would essentially require locking all three rings at once, which is the very serialization we wanted to avoid.

- *Should peek return a pointer and advance the index?* This is "soft pop" — reserve but don't release. The problem: if B bails (because it sees a reconfigure in its reserved set), the reservation has to be released. And once released, A might already have pop-committed past the reserved spot. We're in the same push-back problem we tried to avoid, just dressed up in different clothes.

The honest answer: **peek-then-pop cannot be made race-free across multiple rings without serializing the workers somewhere.** The race is inherent to "two workers reading different rings at the same time."

## When this race can actually happen

Here's a saving grace: **the race only exists for boxes that allow multiple concurrent fires.** Most boxes in this system are single-spawn — only one task at a time gathers for them. For those, A and B can't both be gathering simultaneously, so the race doesn't appear.

The multi-spawn case (iterators, certain runtime-created boxes) is where this bites. The graph loader marks each box with whether it's multi-spawn-capable (the `multi_spawn` field on the box record).

So the cost of solving this only has to be paid by multi-spawn boxes. Single-spawn boxes get the simpler peek-then-pop dance for free.

## Proposal — gather serialization on multi-spawn boxes only

The cleanest answer I can see: **on multi-spawn boxes, the gather phase is serialized through a per-box gather lock.** It's a CAS, brief (microseconds), and only contended when multiple workers genuinely want to fire the same box at the same time.

This means we'd revise your earlier principle slightly. The original framing was "workers don't take YARQ — they're just reading values, not mutating them." But popping values from a shared ring IS a mutation; it changes the slot's head pointer and removes the value from the ring. When two workers pop from the same set of rings concurrently, they're racing on shared mutable state.

So a more precise version of your principle: **workers don't take YARQ for reading box METADATA (the input port list, the function pointer, the connections array). But for popping values from rings shared across multi-spawn fires, workers DO need brief serialization.**

This separates two different concerns:
- **YARQ-for-mutation** (rare, taken by reconfigure / runtime_connect / box-swap operations).
- **Gather-lock** (frequent on multi-spawn boxes, brief, just guards the peek-and-pop atomicity).

They could be the same atomic word with different semantics, or two separate words. I'd lean toward separate words: the gather lock is needed thousands of times per run; the YARQ is needed rarely. Conflating them means the rare reconfigure has to wait for every concurrent gather to finish, which is fine but loses some opportunity.

Or — alternative — single-spawn boxes simply don't need a gather lock at all (because there's only one gatherer ever), so they skip it. Multi-spawn boxes take the gather lock for the duration of the peek-pop window.

## On your other points

**Read boxes have no inputs, so no ring for reconfigure messages.** Agreed — delete-and-recreate is the right answer. Read boxes are stateless cached values; rebuilding one is cheap.

**"create-a-box" takes the same struct as reconfigure; same-ID means reconfigure.** YES, this is a great unification. The runtime mutation API collapses to one entry point: `runtime_apply_box_spec(spec_json)`. The dispatch reads the `id` field:
- If the id is new → create.
- If the id exists → reconfigure.

This is structurally honest: creating a box and reconfiguring a box are both "express what this box should be." The implementation difference (allocate-then-publish vs swap-and-supersede) is a runtime detail, not a user-facing distinction.

**"check CAS before popping"** — yes, exactly right. This is the same point as my proposed peek-first design, just stated more clearly: workers commit to nothing until they know the box is safe to operate on. If a worker sees a reconfigure message while peeking, it CASes first; if CAS fails, no values were touched, no rollback needed.

**Box delete = "create" with just ID, nothing else.** Lovely. The minimum to supply is the ID and a flag like `"delete": true` (or some marker that distinguishes "delete me" from "I forgot to fill in other fields"). I'd suggest an explicit `"action": "delete"` field to avoid ambiguity. Deleted boxes get their refcount-driven cleanup via the same mechanism as superseded boxes. I'll write an issue file for this.

## What I want to confirm with you before writing the design up

1. **Are you OK with workers taking a brief gather lock on multi-spawn boxes?** This is the cleanest answer to the race you found. It's a CAS, uncontended in the common case (most boxes are single-spawn), brief in the contended case (microseconds). Your earlier principle was "workers don't take YARQ" — I'm proposing a refinement where "workers don't take YARQ for METADATA reads, but DO take a brief gather-lock for popping values on multi-spawn boxes."

2. **Separate locks or the same lock?** Option (a): one atomic word per box, used both for mutation and for multi-spawn gather. Simpler. Cost: rare reconfigures wait for any current gather to finish, which is fine. Option (b): two atomic words, one for each purpose. Slightly faster but more bookkeeping. I'd vote (a) for simplicity.

3. **The unified `runtime_apply_box_spec` — should it also handle the delete case?** I.e., one entry point that does create / reconfigure / delete based on the spec's content?

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **The race you found is a textbook example of "linearizability across multiple objects."** Each ring buffer is independently atomic, but the CROSS-RING operation (peek every port, then pop every port) is not. This is the same problem distributed databases solve with two-phase commit: you can either serialize the cross-object operation, or you can accept that some operations might observe a transient inconsistent state and need to retry. Your project is small enough that serialization (per-box gather lock) is cheap. For larger systems, the trade-off shifts toward lock-free designs with retry loops.
- **The "single-spawn vs multi-spawn" distinction is doing a LOT of work in this design.** Iterator boxes are basically the only multi-spawn case in normal use. By scoping the gather lock to multi-spawn boxes, we pay the synchronization cost exactly where it's actually needed — and the vast majority of fires (call boxes with simple inputs) cost nothing extra. The graph loader already computes this attribute, so we get the scoping for free.
- **"Workers don't claim YARQ" was the right principle, with an important refinement: it applies to BOX-METADATA reads, not to RING POPS.** Reading the input port list is non-destructive; that's where the original principle applies — readers shouldn't pay for the writers' work. Popping a value is destructive; that genuinely needs some coordination among concurrent poppers. The refined principle preserves the original intent (no YARQ for metadata) while honestly acknowledging that popping is a different beast.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

If you sign off on the gather-lock proposal, I'll consolidate everything we've discussed — two-state flag, graph-slot-as-liveness, refcount + mutator-holds-reference, peek-don't-pop, per-multi-spawn-box gather lock, unified runtime_apply_box_spec — into 320's issue file. Then we can start implementing.

That correction matters — thank you. And your proposal is genuinely the cleanest version I've heard. Let me confirm it works, address the storage question (which is the one real open detail), and then we can move to implementation.

## Your design, restated

Every box has a single atomic flag. State 0 means "free." State 1 means "someone is in the gather phase right now." When a worker arrives at the box, it tries to CAS the flag from 0 to 1. If it wins, it enters the gather section. If it loses, it yields-and-requeues — the pool will hand it back later.

Inside the gather section, the worker is the only thread touching this box's input rings. It can safely peek the heads of all the ordering rings without worrying about another worker racing on the same values. Then it makes a single decision:

- **All heads are values (native or json):** pop them all, release the flag, hand the values back to the worker to fire the spec.
- **Any head is a reconfigure:** pop the reconfigure message, apply it (build new box, swap the graph slot), release the flag. Don't fire. The worker either submits a new task for the (now-new) box or just returns — the pool will naturally spawn fresh tasks when producers push more values.

A worker visit is **exactly one of**: a fire or a mutation. Never both. Never partial.

This eliminates every race we've been discussing. The gather lock holds for microseconds. Workers on DIFFERENT boxes don't contend at all — the flag is per-box. Workers on the SAME box serialize through gather, which is the only way to make peek-then-pop honest in a multi-threaded setting.

## On your storage question

You're asking exactly the right question. The input ring buffers hold values, and a typical value is something like an integer or a short string. Reconfigure messages are variable-length JSON — could be a few hundred bytes, could be many kilobytes. They don't fit the same shape.

There are two ways to attach reconfigure messages to a box. I want to lay them both out and ask you which you prefer, because the choice ripples through the rest of the design:

**Way 1 — A third ring on every input slot, with a "this cell is a reconfigure" tag.**
- Producers push reconfigure messages onto whichever port they reach.
- The slot already has native + json data rings (from the dual-ring work in 312). We add a third "reconfigure" data ring per slot, storing the JSON payload via the large-value heap (so variable-size is handled cleanly).
- The ordering ring's tags grow a third possible value — RECONFIGURE — telling the consumer "the head of the ordering ring points at the reconfigure ring, not native or json."
- Gather peeks every port's ordering ring as part of its scan.
- Empty boxes (no input ports) can't receive reconfigure messages this way — they need delete-and-recreate (which you already agreed to).

**Way 2 — A single per-box control queue, completely separate from any input port.**
- Each box has its own small ring buffer attached directly to it (not to any port), specifically for control messages like reconfigure.
- The runtime API `runtime_apply_box_spec(target_id, spec_json)` pushes onto the target box's control queue. The producer doesn't need to know about ports — it just names the box.
- Gather checks the control queue first. If non-empty, become mutator. Otherwise, peek the input ports and decide normally.
- Works for boxes with zero input ports (they have a control queue too).
- The reconfigure JSON lives in the large-value heap, with the control queue cell holding a handle to it.

**My read:** Way 2 is simpler and more honest about what reconfigure messages are. They're not input values riding on a port; they're control plane messages targeted at a specific box. Treating them as a separate channel is cleaner than overloading the port mechanism.

The reason I originally went with Way 1 in the issue file was that the user (you) described it that way, and producers-already-know-how-to-reach-a-port was the rationale. But now that we have the `runtime_apply_box_spec` unification (the runtime API that handles create / reconfigure / delete based on the spec's content), the producer doesn't need to push through a port at all. The runtime API can find the target box directly.

I'd vote Way 2.

## Walking through your full design end-to-end with Way 2

Setup: box B has three input ports (X, Y, Z), all multi-spawn. Box B has a control queue (initially empty). Box B's gather flag is 0.

**Scenario 1 — normal fire:**

Producer A pushes a value onto port X. Producer B pushes onto port Y. Producer C pushes onto port Z. Three workers (W1, W2, W3) are spawned for box B (because all input ports are ready).

W1 arrives first. CAS flag 0 → 1. Wins. Enters gather. Checks control queue: empty. Peeks port X, Y, Z: all values. Pops from each ordering ring; each tag tells W1 which data ring to pop from (native or json). W1 has three values in hand. Releases flag (set to 0). Calls the spec's invoke with the three values.

W2 arrives. CAS flag 0 → 1. Might win or lose depending on timing.
- If wins: enters gather, finds rings empty (W1 just drained them), can't fire. Releases. The pool will respawn W2 if more values arrive.
- If loses: yields. Pool requeues it.

W3 same story.

**Scenario 2 — reconfigure arrives:**

Producer pushes a value onto port X. Then someone calls `runtime_apply_box_spec(B, new_spec_json)`. The runtime API pushes the spec onto box B's control queue.

Worker W1 arrives. CAS flag 0 → 1. Wins. Enters gather. Checks control queue: non-empty. **Decision: mutate, not fire.** Pops the spec from the control queue. Builds a new box record (call it B'). Atomically swaps the graph slot's pointer from B to B'. Drops the mutator's refcount on B. Releases the flag (sets B's flag back to 0 — though it doesn't really matter, B is now superseded).

What about the value that producer pushed onto port X? It's still in the ring buffer attached to slot ID for port X. **And here's the key — the new box B' carries the SAME slot IDs.** The slots themselves didn't move; they belong to the slot store, identified by integer IDs. The value is still queued, ready for the next worker to consume under B's new shape.

The next worker that arrives at box B follows the graph slot, gets B' (the new box), CASes flag 0 → 1, enters gather, peeks port X, sees the value waiting, pops it, fires under B's new shape.

**Scenario 3 — reconfigure during contention:**

Worker W1 holds the gather flag (state 1) on box B, doing a normal fire's worth of work. Meanwhile, someone calls `runtime_apply_box_spec(B, ...)` to push a reconfigure into B's control queue. Worker W2 arrives at B. CAS flag 0 → 1 fails (W1 holds it). W2 yields-and-requeues.

W1 finishes its gather, releases the flag (sets to 0). W2 (or another worker) eventually arrives. CAS wins. Enters gather. Checks control queue: non-empty. Becomes mutator. Applies reconfigure. Done.

Notice the ordering: W1's fire happens BEFORE the reconfigure is applied. The reconfigure arrived chronologically during W1's gather, but the gather lock serialized the operations cleanly — W1 finishes, then W2 mutates. The reconfigure lands on the "next opportunity" rather than racing in.

## Resolving the YARQ principle

Your original phrasing was "workers who are just executing the box function should not claim the yarq. they don't need it - they're just reading values, not mutating them." The refined version that this design exemplifies:

- **The box function itself runs WITHOUT holding any lock.** Once the values are gathered and the worker has them in hand, the spec's invoke runs in parallel with anything else on any other thread. That's where the "no YARQ for execution" principle holds tight.
- **The gather phase IS a brief atomic section.** It's per-box, microseconds long, and unavoidable in a multi-threaded design where multiple workers might be pulling from the same rings.

In other words, the principle was right for the FIRE phase (where the spec's invoke runs and can be fully parallel), and the gather phase is just a small serialization tax that buys us correctness. Most code execution time is in fire, so the parallel-execution property is preserved where it matters.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **"A worker visit is either a fire OR a mutation, never both" is the principle that makes everything else work.** Without it, you have to reason about partial states ("I started gathering but then realised I should mutate; what about the values I already popped?"). With it, the gather section has exactly two exit paths, and each one is internally consistent. This is the dataflow equivalent of a database transaction's all-or-nothing property — either the whole gather happens or none of it does, and the choice is decided at one well-defined moment.
- **The per-box gather lock + per-box graph slot pointer is a complete concurrent-object lifecycle in two atomic words.** One word governs "who's allowed to mutate me right now"; the other governs "am I still the live version of this id." Everything else — refcounts, freeing, supersession — follows from those two. It's a surprisingly compact representation of a famously hard problem.
- **Way 2 (per-box control queue) reflects a structural truth: control plane and data plane are different things and shouldn't share the same channel.** In networking, this is why DNS, ARP, ICMP exist separately from TCP/UDP data flow — control messages have different ordering requirements, different priorities, different consumer logic. Your dataflow runtime has the same shape; reconfigure messages aren't input values, they're sideband signals that modify the data plane's behaviour. Giving them their own channel makes the system honest about its layering.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## What I want to confirm before writing the design up

1. **Way 1 (third ring per port) vs Way 2 (per-box control queue) for reconfigure message storage?** I'd vote Way 2; lighter, generalises to empty boxes, more honest about control-vs-data.

2. **One atomic word per box governing both gather AND mutation?** State 0 = free; state 1 = someone is in the gather section (which might be a fire OR a mutation, decided once we look at the control queue). This collapses the "YARQ for mutation, separate gather lock for popping" idea into one word. Simpler. The cost: a rare mutator waits for at most one in-flight gather to finish, which is microseconds.

3. **Are we done with the design phase?** If you sign off on these two, I'll consolidate everything we've discussed into the 320 issue file, add the connections-unification follow-up issue, and the box-delete issue. Then we can move to implementation.

Both of these corrections are right and the second one is genuinely elegant. Let me work through them.

## On the YARQ-after-reconfigure correction

You're correct, and my earlier description had a bug. Here's the scenario:

Producer pushes a value onto port X of box B. The pool spawns a task for box B (because B has inputs ready). Meanwhile, someone pushes a reconfigure onto B's control queue. Worker W1 arrives, wins the gather flag, checks the control queue, decides to mutate, applies the reconfigure, swaps the graph slot, releases the flag, and returns.

But the value on port X is still sitting in its ring. Nobody scheduled a fresh task — because no producer pushed anything new (producers don't push for nothing; the push that originally caused the spawn was already consumed by the spawn decision).

The value just sits there, orphaned. Eventually the run quiesces with this dangling value, and the box never fires.

The fix: **the mutator yields-and-requeues itself instead of just returning.** It tells the pool "I'm not actually done; please put me back at the tail of the queue." The pool re-queues a task for box B. Eventually some worker picks it up, arrives at B (which now points at the NEW box struct via the graph slot), wins the gather flag, peeks the inputs, sees the value waiting, and fires under the new shape.

This is the same yield-and-requeue mechanism we already use when a worker can't grab the gather flag (because someone else has it). One unified path: any time a worker arrives at a box and doesn't actually fire, it yarqs.

## On the "point the box at the reconfigure input" idea

This is wonderful. Let me make sure I'm reading you right: the reconfigure message doesn't need to be JSON that the mutator parses — it can already BE a fully-built box struct, sitting in memory, ready to use. The mutator's job is just to take that pointer and atomically substitute it into the graph slot.

If that's what you mean, then yes, this is the right design. Walking through the consequences:

**Who builds the new box struct?**

Whoever calls the runtime API. For an internal C caller, that's straightforward — they construct the struct directly. For a Lua box calling `soramech.reconfigure(target_id, {kind="call", fn="new_fn", ...})`, the Lua language bridge code does the build: it reads the Lua table, allocates a new box struct, fills in the fields, and hands the pointer to the runtime. The bridge does the same kind of work it already does today for `create_box` — it's the same shape.

For a "reconfigure box" kind (where some box receives a JSON spec on an input port and pushes a reconfigure), that box's spec invoke parses the JSON and builds the struct.

In all cases: by the time the message reaches the target box's control queue, it's already a pre-built struct pointer. No parsing happens inside the gather lock.

**What does the control queue actually hold?**

Just pointers. Each cell in the control queue is one pointer (8 bytes). A small ring — say, 8 cells per box — is enough to absorb bursts of reconfigures. If the ring fills up (which would require 8 reconfigures arriving in microseconds, faster than any worker can drain them), pushers block briefly waiting for space.

No JSON bytes ever live in a ring. No large-value heap involvement for control messages. The cells are tiny fixed-size pointer slots.

**What does the mutator actually do?**

```
mutator wins the gather flag:
   check control queue. it's non-empty.
   pop one box-struct pointer (call it NEW).
   resolve port mappings: for each port in NEW, find the matching
       slot id from OLD (rename by name match), or allocate a new
       slot if the port is brand new.
   patch NEW's input_slot_ids[] with the resolved IDs.
   atomically swap the graph slot pointer from OLD to NEW.
   release the gather flag.
   yarq.
```

The slot-resolution step is the only non-trivial work. Ports that exist in both OLD and NEW (matched by name) share the same slot ID — the underlying ring buffer keeps all its queued values intact across the reconfigure. Ports that are new in NEW get freshly allocated slots. Ports that existed in OLD but not in NEW are abandoned — their slot IDs aren't in NEW, so nobody reads from them anymore; their remaining values get logged to the JSONL discard event you specified, and the slot itself can be released when OLD is freed.

**What about the OLD box struct?**

It stays alive as long as any in-flight worker is using it (refcount > 0). The graph slot now points at NEW, so no new workers will land on OLD. When OLD's refcount hits zero, it's freed.

The free includes freeing the box struct's malloc'd memory (the struct itself) and releasing any per-box state that the new box doesn't share (like the slots for ports that were removed).

## What this gives us

The reconfigure mechanism becomes structurally tiny:

- The control queue is a fixed-size ring of pointers. Cheap.
- The runtime API takes a box struct pointer. Caller builds it; runtime takes ownership.
- The mutator's work is: resolve slots, swap graph pointer, release, yarq. No JSON parsing on the hot path. No variable-size storage. No "where does the message live" question because the message IS the new box.

It also means the **"create" and "reconfigure" operations converge even more cleanly** than we discussed before. Both are just "here's a new box struct, please install it." Create: install at a fresh graph slot. Reconfigure: install at an existing graph slot, supersede the old occupant. Delete: install NULL at the graph slot, supersede the old occupant.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **"The message IS the new box" is the same pattern as immutable persistent data structures.** In Clojure or Haskell, you don't mutate a data structure in place — you produce a new version and let the runtime swap pointers. Old versions stick around as long as anyone references them. Your reconfigure design lands in the same place by reasoning about concurrent dataflow: the mutator builds a new immutable thing and atomically swaps in the new reference. Everyone holding the old reference finishes their work cleanly; the old thing eventually goes away. The pattern shows up independently in functional programming, in Linux RCU, and now in your dataflow runtime — three different domains converging on the same answer because the problem shape is the same.
- **Putting the build work on the producer's side is a load-balancing move.** Parsing JSON, validating fields, allocating arrays — all of that happens in whoever called the runtime API, in their own time, on their own thread. The mutator's critical section (the gather lock hold) shrinks to "swap pointer, resolve a few slot IDs." That's microseconds. The slower work (the parse) doesn't block anyone else's work on the same box.
- **The slot-id stability across reconfigures is the unsung hero of the whole design.** Because port names map to stable slot IDs, the ring buffers don't need to move. A port "x" with 100 queued values stays exactly where it is across a reconfigure. The new box just keeps referencing the same slot ID. That's the cheapest possible transition: zero bytes copied.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## What I want to confirm

1. **Control queue depth — 8 pointer cells per box?** Or do you want a different number? It's small fixed memory per box (64 bytes) and only matters under very bursty reconfigure traffic.

2. **The runtime API surface — does it take a pre-built box struct directly, or does it take JSON and parse internally (with the parse happening in the caller's thread)?** Both are workable; "takes a struct" is faster and forces language bridges to do their job; "takes JSON" is more uniform across languages. My instinct: take a struct, provide a parse-JSON-to-struct helper for callers that want it.

3. **Are we done designing?** If you sign off on these two, I'll consolidate the entire design into 320's issue file (replacing the older sketch), write the connections-unification follow-up issue, and write the box-delete-via-runtime-API issue. Then we move to implementation.

All three points push the design in good directions. Let me respond.

## On using a ring buffer

You're completely right — I was overthinking the naming. The control queue IS a ring buffer; that's exactly the pattern. And we should use the same primitive we use everywhere else: the slot store. A box's control queue is just another slot allocated from the slot store, sized to hold pointer-cells.

Concretely: at box creation time, the runtime allocates one extra slot per box flagged as the control slot. Cell capacity = sizeof(void*). Cell count = some small number (8 is plenty). The slot store's existing per-slot spinlock handles concurrent pushes for free, and pops use the same FIFO ordering the rest of the system already understands.

This is structurally honest about what the system is doing: every box has input slots for its incoming values plus one control slot for its incoming reconfigure messages. All slots, all rings, one mechanism. Reusing the primitive means no new code paths to maintain.

## On knowing which slots to remove

Walk through the algorithm:

The mutator has the OLD box in hand (with its input port names and the slot IDs they map to) and the NEW box just popped from the control queue (with input port names, but no slot IDs filled in yet).

For each port name in NEW: look that name up in OLD's port list.
- **Found in OLD:** copy OLD's slot ID for that name into NEW. The ring buffer keeps all its queued values intact; the new box just keeps reading from the same place.
- **Not found in OLD:** this is a brand-new port. Allocate a fresh slot from the slot store, put the new slot ID into NEW.

For each port name in OLD: look that name up in NEW's port list.
- **Found in NEW:** already handled (shared slot).
- **Not found in NEW:** this slot is abandoned. Add it to the OLD box's "to-be-released" list. When OLD is eventually freed (refcount hits zero), the to-be-released slots get released back to the slot store, and any leftover values in them get logged to the JSONL discard event.

The matching is by port name. Rename = effectively delete + add: if you change "x" to "x_renamed", "x" appears only in OLD (to release) and "x_renamed" appears only in NEW (to allocate). Any queued values on "x" get discarded.

If you wanted "rename keeps the queued values," you'd need an explicit rename declaration in the spec — something like `{"rename": {"old_name": "x", "new_name": "x_renamed"}}`. Worth supporting? Maybe later. For now, rename-as-delete-plus-add is honest about what the message means: the producer who pushed onto "x" probably doesn't know about the rename, so dropping the values is conservative.

## On JSON as the API contract

Sold. JSON it is — for exactly the reason you said: it keeps the language bridge work as small as possible. Every language can format JSON in a few lines. Asking each language bridge to know about C struct layouts would be a big lift, and would discourage adding new languages.

So the API shape becomes:

```
runtime_apply_box_spec(target_id, json_bytes, json_len, error_out)
```

The runtime, in the caller's thread (whichever language called it), parses the JSON into a new box struct using the same parser the graph loader uses today (the refactored version that takes an in-memory buffer instead of a file path). Validates. Pushes the struct pointer to the target's control slot. Returns success or a parse error.

The mutator, when it eventually wins the gather flag, just pops the pointer and swaps. Pure pointer work.

For the JSONL transcript, we can keep the raw JSON bytes around long enough to log them. Either: copy the JSON into the JSONL event at push time (so the log records "this is the spec that was queued"), or re-serialize the box struct back to JSON at apply time (so the log records "this is what actually applied"). I'd vote the latter — it's the source of truth for what the box became, not just what was requested.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **Reusing the slot store for control messages is a design coherence win.** Every "thing that moves through the system" goes through the same ring-buffer primitive — input values, output values, now reconfigure messages. One mechanism, one set of edge cases to learn, one set of tests to maintain. The alternative would have been a special "control plane" mechanism just for reconfigure; that's exactly the kind of code that drifts away from the main code over time and grows its own subtle bugs.
- **The port-name set-difference algorithm is what graphdiff libraries do.** When git compares two file trees, or when a UI framework diffs old-tree-of-elements vs new-tree-of-elements, the algorithm is identical to what we just sketched: match by stable identifier, ports-only-in-old get destroyed, ports-only-in-new get created, ports-in-both get preserved. You've reinvented React's reconciliation algorithm at the level of a single box's input ports.
- **"JSON as the API contract" is the contract-as-text-not-binary principle.** Same reasoning that makes HTTP win over RPC frameworks for cross-system APIs: anyone with a string formatter can participate, no SDK required. By keeping the runtime API at the JSON layer, you make "add a new language to SoraMech" a smaller commitment — the new language only needs to learn JSON, which it almost certainly already knows.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## What I want to confirm

1. **Use the slot store for the control queue, allocated as an extra slot per box?** Cell capacity = pointer size. Cell count = 8 (or whatever small number; tunable later).

2. **Slot diffing by port name with rename-as-delete-plus-add?** And explicit `{"rename": ...}` declarations as a future enhancement if a use case appears.

3. **JSONL records the post-apply state** (re-serialised from the resulting box struct), not the pre-apply spec?

4. **Are we done designing?** If you sign off, I'll consolidate into the 320 issue file, write the connections-unification follow-up issue, and write the box-delete issue.

Yarqing\nguarantees a fresh task gets scheduled so the queued values\nactually get fired under the new shape.\n\n## Slot diffing by port name\n\nThe slot resolution in mutator step 2 is the same algorithm used\nfor tree diffing in UI frameworks: match by stable identifier,\nports-only-in-old get abandoned, ports-only-in-new get freshly\nallocated, ports-in-both keep their slot id (and therefore keep\nall their queued values).\n\nRenames are NOT detected automatically — a port renamed from\n\"x\" to \"x_renamed\" looks like \"delete x, create x_renamed\" from\nthe algorithm's perspective. Any values queued on \"x\" get\ndropped to the JSONL discard event when OLD is freed. If a\nfuture use case calls for value-preserving renames, the spec\nJSON can grow a `\"rename\": [{\"from\":\"x\", \"to\":\"x_renamed\"}]`\nfield; for now, rename-as-delete-plus-add is the conservative\ndefault.\n\n## The unified runtime API\n\nOne entry point handles create, reconfigure, and delete:\n\n```c\nint runtime_apply_box_spec(const char *target_id,\n                           const char *spec_json, int spec_json_len,\n                           char **err_out);\n```\n\nThe runtime parses `spec_json` in the caller's thread, validates\nit, builds the replacement box struct, and dispatches based on\nthe spec's content:\n\n- **Spec describes a new box; target_id is not in the graph:**\n  install at a fresh graph slot. Equivalent to today's\n  `runtime_create_box`.\n- **Spec describes a box; target_id already exists:** push the\n  new struct's pointer onto the target's control queue. The\n  next worker that visits the target becomes the mutator and\n  swaps.\n- **Spec is `{\"action\":\"delete\", \"id\":\"target_id\"}`:** install\n  NULL at the graph slot via the same supersession path. Old box\n  drifts toward freedom via refcount.\n\nThe same shape works for any language. Lua's `soramech.apply_box`\nserializes the spec to JSON and calls in. Bash's\n`soramech_apply_box` is the same. The C bridge wraps the API\ndirectly. Adding a fourth language only requires the language\nto format JSON, which every language can do.\n\n## Reference counting policy — what gets freed when\n\n- **Box record:** freed when refcount = 0 AND graph slot ≠ this\n  box. Triggered by whoever decrements to 0.\n- **Slots used by both OLD and NEW:** kept alive (NEW still\n  references them).\n- **Slots in OLD but not in NEW (abandoned):** freed at the\n  same time OLD is freed; their remaining queued values get a\n  JSONL discard event per slot.\n- **The control queue's cells (pointers to replacement structs):**\n  if a producer pushed a replacement struct and the box was\n  deleted before any mutator ran, those pending replacement\n  structs are freed when the control queue is freed (which\n  happens when OLD is freed).\n- **Live boxes that nobody uses (idle):** not freed. The graph\n  slot still points at them; they're \"live, just waiting.\" This\n  is intentional — we cannot prove a box won't run again in a\n  system that allows runtime creation and connection, so we\n  don't try. Users who want to actively clean up call\n  `runtime_apply_box_spec(id, {\"action\":\"delete\"})`.\n\n## JSONL events\n\n- `box_reconfigure` — fires after the swap. Carries the box id,\n  the new spec (re-serialised from the post-apply struct so the\n  log records what actually applied, not what was requested),\n  task id, worker idx. Always emitted.\n- `reconfigure_discard` — fires per abandoned port when a slot\n  has leftover queued values. Carries the box id, the port name,\n  the count of dropped values, and the first value bytes (up to\n  256, for debugging). Always emitted.\n- `box_delete` — fires after a delete supersedes a box. Carries\n  the box id, task id, worker idx. Always emitted.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Add the gather flag and refcount to box_t.** Two atomic\n   ints, alongside the existing connections + n_connections\n   atomics in `src/010-graph-loader.h`.\n2. **Convert the graph's box storage from array-of-structs to\n   array-of-pointers.** `graph_box(g, i)` becomes a load from\n   the array. The graph still owns the storage; the array\n   entries become atomic pointers so the mutator can swap them.\n3. **Add the per-box control slot.** At box-creation time\n   (graph_load AND runtime_create_box), allocate one extra slot\n   per box, cell capacity = sizeof(void*), cell count = 8,\n   reachable via a new `box->control_slot_id` field.\n4. **Refactor `parse_box_file` to accept an in-memory JSON\n   buffer.** The file-path entry point becomes a thin wrapper.\n   The runtime API uses the buffer entry directly.\n5. **Add the gather lock acquire / release helpers in\n   `src/012-dispatch.c`.** CAS 0 → 1 for acquire; store 0 for\n   release. Yield-and-requeue helper for the CAS-loss path:\n   push the task back to the pool's tail and return without\n   firing.\n6. **Wrap `dispatch_action`'s top-of-fire path with the gather\n   lock acquire.** On loss, yarq. On win, check the control\n   queue before doing the normal input gather.\n7. **Implement the mutator path inside `dispatch_action`.** Pop\n   the replacement struct from the control queue. Run the slot\n   resolution. Atomic-swap the graph slot pointer. Release the\n   gather flag. Yarq.\n8. **Add the unified `runtime_apply_box_spec` to\n   `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}`.** Parse JSON, build the\n   replacement struct, push the pointer to the target's control\n   queue. Same shape as the existing runtime_create_box /\n   runtime_connect entrypoints.\n9. **Update the language bridges (Lua, C, Bash) to expose\n   `soramech.apply_box(target_id, spec)`.** Each bridge\n   serialises its native spec representation to JSON and calls\n   the runtime API.\n10. **Add the JSONL events** (`box_reconfigure`,\n    `reconfigure_discard`, `box_delete`) to\n    `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` and\n    `src/014-event-queue.{c,h}`.\n11. **Implement reference-count-driven box GC.** Whoever\n    decrements to zero AND observes the graph slot doesn't\n    point at this box does the free.\n12. **Fixtures**:\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-fn` — same lang, different\n      function on the same box. Fires once with old fn, then\n      reconfigures, then fires again with new fn.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-port-shape` — add a new\n      input port via reconfigure. Verifies new slot allocated\n      and slot diffing matches by name.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-kind` — flip a BOX_CALL to a\n      BOX_WRITE via reconfigure. Subsequent fires write to disk.\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-delete` — reconfigure with\n      delete spec; box is gone, downstream still works (or\n      fails gracefully if it depended on the deleted box).\n    - `tests/maps/320-reconfigure-contended` — two reconfigure\n      pushers race on the same target. Both land in the control\n      queue; both apply in arrival order; final state reflects\n      the last one applied.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — already provides the ring-buffer\n  primitive the control queue reuses.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — gather flag + refcount fields\n  on `box_t`; `parse_box_file` refactor; graph array → array\n  of pointers; control slot allocation at box creation.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — gather lock acquire/release wrapping\n  `dispatch_action`; mutator path; yarq helper.\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — `runtime_apply_box_spec`\n  unified entry point.\n- `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` / `src/014-event-queue.{c,h}` —\n  three new event types.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` —\n  one new bridge function per language for `apply_box`.\n\n## Open issues for after 320 lands\n\n- **Connections-array atomic-publish dance unification** —\n  today's `runtime_connect` does its own copy-and-publish on\n  the per-box connections array. Once 320 lands, that pattern\n  becomes redundant: a connection add can ride the same\n  box-swap mechanism. Tracked as a separate issue, to be\n  attended to after 320.\n- **Explicit value-preserving rename declaration in the spec\n  JSON** — currently rename-as-delete-plus-add is the default.\n  If a use case appears, add a `\"rename\": [...]` field that the\n  slot resolution honours.\n- **Tunable control queue depth** — currently 8 cells per box.\n  If bursty reconfigure traffic ever exceeds this, push back\n  to producers via the slot's existing fill-management.\n\n## Design history\n\nThe shape of this issue evolved across many discussion rounds.\nTwo prior shapes were considered and discarded:\n\n1. **Per-port third ring** — reconfigure messages would have\n   ridden a third ring on every input slot, with the per-cell\n   ordering tag growing a RECONFIGURE value. Workers would peek\n   each port's ordering ring and apply reconfigures encountered\n   during gather. Discarded in favour of the per-box control\n   queue: control messages aren't conceptually input values,\n   and a per-box channel handles empty-input boxes cleanly.\n2. **In-place field rewrites with three-state flag (0 / 1 / 2)**\n   — the mutator would have rewritten the live box's fields in\n   place, with flag = 2 acting as a \"redirect to new box\"\n   indicator. Discarded in favour of the build-new-and-swap\n   pattern: the graph slot pointer naturally acts as the\n   liveness indicator, the third flag state was redundant, and\n   build-new avoids any \"torn read\" possibility because the old\n   box is never modified.\n\nThe YARQ name (yield-and-requeue) came from the user's\nphrasing: \"it's essentially 'hey we're not ready yet, put\nyourself back at the beginning of the queue please.'\" The\nmechanism is cooperative with the scheduler rather than\nadversarial — the scheduler keeps doing what it does best\n(managing many small units of work fairly), and the barrier\njust nudges contended workers to circle back later.\n\nThe unification of create, reconfigure, and delete into one API\ncame from the user's observation: \"What if we made the\n'create-a-box' box take the same type of struct as the\nreconfigure process? And if it has the same box ID as an\nalready existing box, it just goes through the reconfigure\nprocess.\" Structurally honest about what these operations are:\nall three are \"express what this box should be now,\" and the\nruntime decides how to land that expression.\n",

If the CAS wins,\nthe worker enters the gather section. If it loses, the worker\nyields-and-requeues — its task goes back to the tail of the\npool queue, the pool picks it up later. No spinning, no\nblocking.\n\nThe gather section is brief: peek a few input ports' ordering\nrings, decide fire-or-mutate, pop the appropriate cells, release\nthe flag. Microseconds. Both land in the control\n      queue; both apply in arrival order; final state reflects\n      the last one applied.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — already provides the ring-buffer\n  primitive the control queue reuses.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — gather flag + refcount fields\n  on `box_t`; `parse_box_file` refactor; graph array → array\n  of pointers; control slot allocation at box creation.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — gather lock acquire/release wrapping\n  `dispatch_action`; mutator path; yarq helper.\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — `runtime_apply_box_spec`\n  unified entry point.\n- `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` / `src/014-event-queue.{c,h}` —\n  three new event types.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` —\n  one new bridge function per language for `apply_box`.\n\n## Open issues for after 320 lands\n\n- **Connections-array atomic-publish dance unification** —\n  today's `runtime_connect` does its own copy-and-publish on\n  the per-box connections array. Once 320 lands, that pattern\n  becomes redundant: a connection add can ride the same\n  box-swap mechanism. Tracked as a separate issue.\n- **Explicit value-preserving rename declaration in the spec\n  JSON** — currently rename-as-delete-plus-add is the default.\n  If a use case appears, add a `\"rename\": [...]` field that the\n  slot resolution honours.\n- **Tunable control queue depth** — currently 8 cells per box.\n  If bursty reconfigure traffic ever exceeds this, push back\n  to producers via the slot's existing fill-management.\n\n## Design history\n\nThe shape of this issue evolved across many discussion rounds.\nTwo prior shapes were considered and discarded:\n\n1. **Per-port third ring** — reconfigure messages would have\n   ridden a third ring on every input slot, with the per-cell\n   ordering tag growing a RECONFIGURE value. Workers would peek\n   each port's ordering ring and apply reconfigures encountered\n   during gather. Discarded in favour of the per-box control\n   queue: control messages aren't conceptually input values,\n   and a per-box channel handles empty-input boxes cleanly.\n2. **In-place field rewrites with three-state flag (0 / 1 / 2)**\n   — the mutator would have rewritten the live box's fields in\n   place, with flag = 2 acting as a \"redirect to new box\"\n   indicator. Discarded in favour of the build-new-and-swap\n   pattern: the graph slot pointer naturally acts as the\n   liveness indicator, the third flag state was redundant, and\n   build-new avoids any \"torn read\" possibility because the old\n   box is never modified.\n\nThe YARQ name (yield-and-requeue) came from the user's\nphrasing: \"it's essentially 'hey we're not ready yet, put\nyourself back at the beginning of the queue please.'\" The\nmechanism is cooperative with the scheduler rather than\nadversarial — the scheduler keeps doing what it does best\n(managing many small units of work fairly), and the barrier\njust nudges contended workers to circle back later.\n\nThe unification of create, reconfigure, and delete into one API\ncame from the user's observation: \"What if we made the\n'create-a-box' box take the same type of struct as the\nreconfigure process? And if it has the same box ID as an\nalready existing box, it just goes through the reconfigure\nprocess.\" Structurally honest about what these operations are:\nall three are \"express what this box should be now,\" and the\nruntime decides how to land that expression.\n",

```json
{
  "content":"# 321 — Unify connections-array mutation through the 320 box-swap path\n\n## Status\nopen · waits on 320 landing first; design is straightforward\nonce the box-swap mechanism exists\n\n## Current behavior\n\nIssue 319d added the ability to attach new outgoing connections\nto an existing box at runtime via `runtime_connect`. The way it\ndoes this today is a special-case atomic dance directly on the\nbox's `connections` field: allocate a new connections array,\ncopy the old entries, append the new entry, atomic-store the\npointer, then atomic-store the new count. Readers that walk\nthe connections array use the order \"read count first, then\npointer\" so they always observe either the old pair or the new\npair, never a torn mix.\n\nThis works because the connections array is append-only —\nruntime_connect only ever adds, never removes or reorders.\nThat's the reason the staggered-publish pattern doesn't break\nexisting readers.\n\nOnce issue 320 lands, the runtime has a more general mechanism:\nbuild a fully replacement box struct, push its pointer to the\ntarget's control queue, let the next worker visit do the\natomic graph-slot swap. This mechanism is strictly more\npowerful than the connections-only dance — it can change\nanything about the box, not just append to one field.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nRetire the special-case copy-and-publish on the connections\nfield. Re-implement `runtime_connect` as a thin wrapper over\n`runtime_apply_box_spec`:\n\n1. Look up the current box for the target id.\n2. Build a new box struct that is a copy of the current one,\n   with the new connection appended to its connections array.\n3. Call `runtime_apply_box_spec(target_id, new_spec_json)` (or\n   the underlying push-pointer-to-control-queue equivalent).\n\nThe atomic discipline collapses to one path. The connections\nfield on `box_t` can become a plain pointer + plain int (no\n`_Atomic` qualifiers needed) because the only way to mutate it\nis via the box-swap mechanism, which never modifies a live box\nin place.\n\n## Why bother\n\n- **One mutation discipline instead of two.** Every change to\n  a box's identity — adding a connection, changing the function\n  pointer, renaming a port, deleting the box — uses the same\n  build-new-and-swap pattern. Less code to maintain, fewer\n  edge cases to learn.\n- **The connections-only dance is structurally fragile.** It\n  relies on append-only semantics that nobody enforces at the\n  type level. A future change that wanted to remove or reorder\n  connections would silently introduce torn-read bugs. Removing\n  the path removes the trap.\n- **Smaller box_t.** The `_Atomic` qualifiers on\n  `n_connections` and `connections` can come off. Plain int +\n  plain pointer is fine because mutation only happens during\n  the build-new step, before the new box is published.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Re-implement `runtime_connect` as a wrapper over\n   `runtime_apply_box_spec`.** Caller still sees the same\n   signature; internals route through the box-swap path.\n2. **Remove the `_Atomic` qualifiers on `n_connections` and\n   `connections` in `src/010-graph-loader.h`.** Plain types\n   suffice now.\n3. **Remove the copy-and-publish helper in\n   `src/010-graph-loader.c`** that runtime_connect used to\n   call.\n4. **Verify the existing 319d fixture (`319d-runtime-create`,\n   `319e-c-create`, etc.) still passes under the new path.**\n   The behavioural contract for runtime_connect is unchanged;\n   the internal mechanism changes.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — drop atomic qualifiers; drop\n  copy-and-publish helper.\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — rewrite runtime_connect\n  to call into runtime_apply_box_spec.\n- Existing 319d/319e/319f fixtures act as the regression\n  guard; no new fixtures needed.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Does the language bridges need any change?** Lua's\n  `soramech.connect`, Bash's `soramech_connect`, C's\n  `soramech_connect` all currently call straight into\n  runtime_connect. If runtime_connect's signature stays the\n  same, no bridge changes. Confirm during implementation.\n",
  "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/321-unify-connections-mutation-through-box-swap.md"
}
```

```json
{
  "content":"# 322 — Box delete: the user-facing experience\n\n## Status\nopen · the underlying mechanism is part of 320; this issue\ncovers the user-facing API and the explicit-vs-implicit-deletion\ndesign decision\n\n## Current behavior\n\nOnce issue 320 lands, the runtime has a unified\n`runtime_apply_box_spec(target_id, spec_json)` entry point that\nhandles create / reconfigure / delete based on the spec's\ncontent. The delete path is: install NULL at the graph slot\nvia the same supersession mechanism, let the refcount drive\nthe old box's eventual free.\n\nWhat 320 does NOT cover, and what this issue is for:\n\n- The user-facing spec shape that triggers deletion.\n- A convenience wrapper for the common case.\n- Validation that catches \"I forgot to fill in fields\"\n  accidents from masquerading as deletes.\n- The downstream effects when consumers wired to a deleted box\n  try to push values into the now-gone graph slot.\n\n## Why deletion needs more than just \"any minimum spec\"\n\nThe natural shortcut would be: \"if the spec only has an id and\nno other fields, treat it as a delete.\" Compact and elegant.\n\nBut it's also dangerous: a user who forgets to populate fields\nin their reconfigure spec accidentally deletes the box. Defaults\nshould fail-closed (do nothing surprising) rather than fail-open\n(do something destructive). The minimum-spec-means-delete shape\nfails open.\n\nThe safer alternative is an explicit marker in the spec:\n\n```json\n{\"action\": \"delete\", \"id\": \"target_box_id\"}\n```\n\nThe runtime parses the spec, sees `action == \"delete\"`, and\nroutes through the delete path. Specs without an explicit\n`action` field default to create-or-reconfigure (the inferred\naction based on whether target_id exists). Explicit beats\nimplicit; destructive operations are always explicit.\n\n## Convenience wrapper\n\nFor the common case where a user just wants to delete a box\nthey know the id of, add a sugar function:\n\n```c\nint runtime_destroy_box(const char *target_id, char **err_out);\n```\n\nInternally, this constructs the delete spec JSON and calls\n`runtime_apply_box_spec`. Same code path, friendlier signature.\n\nSame shape per language bridge:\n\n- Lua: `soramech.destroy_box(target_id)`\n- C:   `soramech_destroy_box(target_id, err_buf, err_cap)`\n- Bash: `soramech_destroy_box \"$target_id\"`\n\n## Downstream effects of deletion\n\nA box X is deleted. Some other box Y has a connection pointing\nat X. Y fires, produces an output, attempts to push to X's\ninput slots — but X is gone from the graph slot.\n\nTwo possible behaviours:\n\n- **Silent drop:** the push fails because the target lookup\n  returns NULL. Producer continues; output is lost. A push\n  event with `result=target-gone` records the loss in the\n  JSONL transcript.\n- **Hard error:** the push fails and the producer's fire is\n  treated as a failure. The run aborts (or the producer's\n  spec returns an error code).\n\nThe user's stated preference throughout the project is \"errors\nover fallbacks.\" So hard error is the strict reading. But\ndeletion is a deliberate user action — if they deleted X, they\nprobably know Y depended on it. Hard-error-on-every-push would\nmean a single deleted leaf-box could crash the entire run.\n\nA middle path: silent drop by default, with the JSONL event\nmaking the loss observable, AND a runtime knob (env var or\nspec field) to upgrade the drop to a hard error for users who\nwant strict behaviour.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. **Define the spec shape for delete.** `{\"action\": \"delete\",\n   \"id\": \"...\"}`. Document that the `action` field defaults to\n   \"apply\" (which means create-or-reconfigure based on target\n   existence) and the only other recognised value is \"delete\".\n2. **Implement the delete path inside\n   `runtime_apply_box_spec`.** Already part of 320's\n   implementation; this is just adding the action dispatch.\n3. **Add `runtime_destroy_box` as the sugar wrapper.** Three\n   language bridges plus the C entry point.\n4. **Add the push-target-gone JSONL event.** Same shape as\n   other push events; `result=target-gone` is the new value.\n5. **Add an opt-in strict mode** for users who want push-to-\n   deleted-box to hard-error rather than silent-drop. Env var\n   `SORAMECH_STRICT_DELETE=1` or per-call flag, TBD.\n6. **Fixtures:**\n   - `tests/maps/322-delete-then-orphaned-push` — A box X is\n     created; B is wired to X; X is deleted; B fires once more;\n     the push fails with `result=target-gone` in the JSONL.\n   - `tests/maps/322-delete-and-recreate` — A box X is created,\n     deleted, then created again with the same id and different\n     behaviour. The recreate succeeds at the now-NULL graph\n     slot; subsequent fires use the new behaviour.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/018-runtime-builtins.{c,h}` — `runtime_destroy_box`\n  sugar wrapper.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — `parse_box_file` extended to\n  recognise the `action` field on the spec.\n- `src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` / `src/014-event-queue.{c,h}` —\n  `target-gone` as a new push result.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` —\n  one new bridge function per language for `destroy_box`.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Strict-mode default.** Should `SORAMECH_STRICT_DELETE=0`\n  (silent drop default) or `=1` (hard error default) be the\n  shipped default? Silent drop matches \"don't crash the run on\n  a leaf-box deletion\"; hard error matches \"errors over\n  fallbacks.\" Lean toward silent-drop-by-default + JSONL event\n  + opt-in strict; revisit if a project disagrees.\n- **Implicit recreation.** A delete followed by a create at\n  the same id — should this work seamlessly, or require an\n  explicit timing barrier? My instinct: works seamlessly. The\n  graph slot transitions NULL → new-box-pointer atomically;\n  any worker that arrives at the in-between state (graph slot\n  is NULL) just exits gracefully.\n",
  "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/322-box-delete-via-runtime-spec-api.md"
}
```

Good question — I've been sloppy with "API." Let me clarify the dataflow, because there are actually two different channels involved.

## Two distinct channels

**Channel 1 — wires (the dataflow plane):** boxes connected to other boxes by connections. Producer fires, pushes its output bytes into the consumer's input slot's ring buffer. The consumer's worker pops from the ring. This is what you've been thinking of as "input ports."

**Channel 2 — direct function calls into the runtime (the control plane):** any code running inside a box's invoke can call C functions like `runtime_create_box(...)`, `runtime_connect(...)`, and now `runtime_apply_box_spec(...)`. These are NOT wire-based — they're plain function calls that the language bridge exposes to box code.

When I said "API," I meant **Channel 2.** The reconfigure JSON does NOT ride the wire system to reach the target box. It travels via a direct function call from whichever box wants to do the reconfiguring.

## Walking through a concrete example

Suppose you have a Lua box called `planner` that wants to reconfigure a box called `worker`. The planner's Lua function looks something like:

```lua
function planner.run(some_input)
    -- decide we want to change how worker behaves
    local new_spec = {
        kind = "call",
        lang = "lua",
        ref  = "src/worker.lua",
        fn   = "new_implementation",
        inputs = { { name = "x", type = "string" } }
    }
    soramech.apply_box("worker", new_spec)
    return some_output
end
```

When `planner` fires, its Lua function calls `soramech.apply_box("worker", new_spec)`. That's the language bridge. Inside the bridge:

1. It serializes `new_spec` (a Lua table) to JSON bytes.
2. It calls the C function `runtime_apply_box_spec("worker", json_bytes, json_len, &err)`.
3. That C function parses the JSON, builds a fresh `box_t` struct in memory, and pushes the struct's pointer onto **worker's control queue** (the per-box slot we talked about).

The reconfigure JSON never touched a wire. It came into existence inside planner's invoke, got passed through the bridge as a function argument, and ended up as a struct pointer in worker's control queue.

## Why the control queue and not an input port?

Two reasons:

**First, control messages aren't input values.** An input value on port "x" is a piece of data that the box's function consumes. A reconfigure message is metadata about the box's identity. They're different in kind, and mixing them on the same channel led to all the peek-vs-pop race conditions we struggled with for a while.

**Second, the producer of the reconfigure isn't a graph-wired box.** It's whatever code happens to be running that decided to reconfigure something. Could be a Lua box's invoke. Could be a C function called from anywhere. Could even be a future REST endpoint someone wires up to let an external system reconfigure boxes. None of these are connected to the target box by a wire — they all just call the same C function.

## What about the "reconfigure box kind" we discussed early on?

That idea — a box whose JOB is to receive a JSON spec on an input port and apply it as a reconfigure — still works in this design, but it's no longer a special box kind. It's just a normal box with a regular function that happens to call `soramech.apply_box(...)` internally.

So if you DO want reconfigure messages to flow through your map's wire system (e.g., one box produces a spec, another consumes and applies it), you'd build it like this:

```
[spec_producer] --wire (carries JSON)--> [reconfigure_relay_box]
                                              |
                                              | (its invoke calls
                                              |  soramech.apply_box)
                                              v
                                         (control queue of "worker")
```

The wire carries the JSON to `reconfigure_relay_box`. That box's function reads the JSON from its input port and calls the runtime API. The runtime API pushes the struct pointer to worker's control queue.

The wire is still there for users who want the dataflow style. But the runtime mechanism underneath is the same direct function call.

## What the control queue actually receives

The control queue stores **already-parsed box-struct pointers**, not raw JSON. The parsing happens in the caller's thread (wherever `runtime_apply_box_spec` was called from), so the mutator on the target box doesn't have to do any JSON work — it just pops a pointer and swaps.

If multiple reconfigures are pushed in quick succession (say, planner_a and planner_b both call `soramech.apply_box("worker", ...)` at nearly the same time), both struct pointers land in worker's control queue. The mutator processes them in FIFO order — first one wins the swap, second one swaps over the first, etc.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **The "control plane vs data plane" distinction is the same one networking made decades ago.** TCP carries data; ICMP carries control. They share the wire but are conceptually separate, and confusing them creates exactly the kind of edge case we wrestled with for several rounds of design. Your runtime made the same split: input slots carry data, control queue carries control, runtime API is the function-call entry point that bridges between "code running in a box" and "the control plane mechanism." Once the split is named, the design clarifies.
- **"API" in this codebase always means C functions callable from any thread, not wire-based message passing.** Same as create_box and connect today. The convention is: anything that mutates the graph at runtime is a function call, not a dataflow. Dataflow is for values; function calls are for graph changes. Keeping these orthogonal means box authors don't have to invent ad-hoc protocols for "how do I tell the runtime to add a wire" — they just call a function.
- **The relay box pattern is the bridge between wires and the runtime API.** If you want a dataflow-style reconfigure, you build a normal box whose function happens to call the runtime API on each fire. The runtime doesn't know or care; it just sees another invocation of `runtime_apply_box_spec`. This means "dataflow reconfigure" is composable — you can have multiple producers feeding one relay box, or one producer feeding multiple relay boxes, all expressible with normal wires.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Does this clear up where the JSON travels and what "API" means? Once you're comfortable with this picture, the implementation tasks should make more sense — task #15 (the API entry point) and task #18 (the language bridges) are the two pieces of the function-call path; task #17 (control queue) is the per-box slot that receives the resulting pointers; tasks #10/#12/#13/#14 are the gather/mutator mechanics that read from the control queue.
